text:
WASHINTON — ICE announced Nov. 2 another round of aliens who have been arrested for alleged voter fraud and election related offenses. These arrests are part of an ongoing nationwide effort to apprehend those who have unlawfully voted in U.S. elections.

“Americans should be furious when they see how frequently aliens vote unlawfully in U.S. elections,” said ICE Public Affairs Assistant Director Micah Bock. “Each vote cast by an alien disenfranchises an American citizen’s vote. The arrests will continue until every alien committing vote fraud is apprehended.”

Under President Trump, Secretary Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella’s leadership, the security of American elections is paramount to the security and stability of our nation. ICE will not rest in their pursuit of identifying and arresting those engaged in voter fraud.

Here are just a few of the illegal aliens ICE has recently arrested for illegal voting:

Alejandro Villegas Garcia, a citizen of Mexico, has been arrested for illegally voting in the 2022 and 2024 elections.

Stanley Jide, a citizen of Liberia, has been arrested for unlawful voting in the 2022 election. He has convictions for assault and fleeing a police officer in a motor vehicle.

Allan Joseph William Arseneault, a citizen of Canada, was arrested for unlawful votingin the 2024 election.

Vilmelena Dye aka Vilmelena Pereira, a citizen of Brazil and a former lawful permanent resident arrested for illegally voting in the 1996 election. She allegedly illegally voted in the 1996 election.

Julio Ceser Arias Antonio, a citizen of Mexico, was granted legal Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals status and was arrested for unlawful voting. He voted multiple times, including in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections.

Paula Stitt, a citizen of Canada, admitted to voting in U.S. elections. She has been charged with voting by an alien and fraud. She voted in at least one U.S. election.

Ayan Ahmen, a citizen of Somalia, admitted to voting in the 2021 election.

Cong Anh Nguyen is a citizen of Vietnam, who has been convicted of theft and admitted to voting in the 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections.

Andres Garcia, a citizen of Cuba, has been charged with voting by an alien in an election. Bhator Bryant is a citizen of Liberia. She was charged with unlawful voting and making a false claim of U.S citizenship to vote in the 2024 election.

Aparecido Padovan is a citizen of Brazil who’s been charged with unlawful voting and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. Records indicate he voted in 2016, 2022 and 2024 elections.

Chris Adam Pettiquoi is a citizen of Liberia who’s been charged with unlawful voting and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. Records indicate he voted in 2014, 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections.

Christian Liam Schenk is a citizen of Canada charged with unlawful voting, making a false claim to U.S. citizenship, fraud and theft. He voted in the 2024 election.

Dilea Ochoa Perez is a citizen from Mexico and was granted legal Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals. She is charged with unlawful voting and voted in the 2022 and 2024 elections.

Sade Shashauna Guppy is a citizen of Trinidad and Tobago. She is charged with voter fraud by an alien, and voted in the 2022 election[GK1] .

You can report crimes, including voter fraud, by calling 866-DHS-2-ICE (866-347-2423) or completing the online tip form.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

EVERETT — Federal immigration enforcement agents are continuing to access data about Washingtonians through the state Department of Licensing and are using the records to assist in hundreds of arrests, according to a recently released University of Washington report.

Researchers have said the practice continues to occur in Snohomish County, as well as across the state, and local community organizers said that the recent rise in immigration enforcement activities has had a chilling effect on immigrant communities.

“People are living in fear,” said Arun Sharma, the head of Utsav, a Bothell-based nonprofit that provides services to the south Asian community. “I’ve been in this county since 1992. I’ve never seen a situation like this.”

Immigration enforcement officers are able to access the data through a system called Nlets, a network that allows law enforcement officers to query databases, including criminal records or state department of motor vehicles records, and get information about a vehicle and its owner in real time. According to the report, released by the University of Washington Center for Human Rights on Oct. 13, immigration officers have submitted queries in Nlets for information about drivers in Washington, then will often cross-reference with their own internal databases to determine a vehicle owner’s immigration status and make arrests.

In an interview Monday, Angelina Godoy, the director of the UW Center for Human Rights and the principal author of the report, said that the center’s research had found 389 instances of a direct connection between an Nlets search and a confirmed arrest in Washington. The database is sorted by cities of arrest, not counties, but Godoy said that Snohomish County cities like Everett and Lynnwood are “amply represented among our data set” in terms of immigration arrests tied to Nlets searches.

Godoy said in an Oct. 13 press conference that Washington state has been a leader in immigration-related policy, through both allowing non-citizens to obtain driver’s licenses since the 1990s and through the passage of the Keep Washington Working Act in 2019, which prohibits state and local agencies from assisting in civil immigration enforcement. But Godoy said that “repeated scandals” of immigration agents accessing driver’s license data — uncovered in 2018 by the Seattle Times, in 2025 by KING 5 and earlier in 2026 by the Center for Human Rights — mean that the state can no longer be considered a leader in that regard, she said.

“If that information that the state holds is now being weaponized against those very communities, the state needs to be accountable to its own promises,” Godoy said in an interview Monday.

One woman, who has lived in south Everett for three years under asylum status and spoke with The Daily Herald on the condition of anonymity due to fear of retribution, said her husband had been arrested after immigration agents searched his vehicle registration data through Nlets. Records obtained by The Herald show that Customs and Border Patrol agents in Washington used Nlets to search the registration information of an owner of a car — a pickup matching the description of her husband’s vehicle — shortly before his arrest in July.

The woman said her husband, who was living in the United States without legal status, was later deported to Mexico. The woman and her two children are still living in Everett, and she is weighing a difficult decision whether to reunite their family in Mexico or stay in the United States and build a better future for her children, she said.

Another woman, Gabriella, who only gave her first name in a phone interview, had been living and working with her husband in Washington for about 17 years when immigration agents arrested her husband in June, she said. Neither had permits to be in the country, and her husband had previously been deported, she said. After his arrest, Gabriella sought legal help but was scammed out of $8,000 of savings by somebody impersonating an attorney, she said. Her husband was then deported to Mexico; she went with him.

Previous research by the Center for Human Rights found that immigration arrests in Snohomish County had increased significantly between 2024 and 2025, and were at the highest levels since 2011. Joomi Kim, who leads a nonprofit in south Snohomish County that serves immigrant communities, said she’s been able to see the impact as fewer people seek services and more are living in fear.

“Their daily routine of their lives are really affected, and many of them are becoming increasingly fearful of going to public places or attending religious services or even seeking resources and information,” she said.

Sharma, whose organization also serves south Snohomish County, said that communities of color are more afraid to ask for help, go to community centers or go to religious places, and it’s like “they are living underground,” he said.

“Every day, they are going to our community centers, religious places, and they are tracking those things,” Sharma said.

Kim said that the ability for immigration enforcement officers to have access to Washingtonians’ drivers licence data represents “an erosion of trust in public institutions.”

“The possibility that information is being used for immigration enforcement undermines confidence in government assurances of privacy,” Kim said. “And we want the Governor to really close that loophole.”

In a statement, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson wrote that the state is a “national leader on protecting the private information of our residents,” and that the state has taken actions to try and curtail immigration enforcement officers’ access to drivers’ data. He wrote that the state shut off ICE’s access to driver license and vehicle data and limited access for Customs and Border Patrol officers, but added that it maintained some access “necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data.”

“Shutting off the federal government’s access to our state’s DOL data across the board is not an option because there are many legitimate public safety reasons why we need to share data with some federal law enforcement agencies — such as preventing violent crime, child abductions, and human trafficking,” Ferguson wrote. “No states have fully shut off federal access to Nlets.”

Ferguson wrote that between November 2025 and mid-October 2026, Washington State Patrol has blocked over 174,000 attempts from federal agencies to use Nlets for civil immigration enforcement.

But the UW Center for Human Rights report said that the action that Gov. Ferguson has taken to this point has been “insufficient.” The state has blocked certain access to certain Originating Agency Identifiers, or ORIs — essentially usernames used by law enforcement to access the Nlets system — associated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security, and Customs and Border Patrol. Evidence obtained by the Center for Human Rights suggested that after certain ORIs were blocked, federal agents have switched to using different ORIs and are still able to perform searches on vehicles.

The report states that between January 2025 and May 2026, agencies affiliated with the Department of Homeland Security searched the driver’s license database for driver and vehicle information nearly 3.7 million times.

“This game of whack-a-mole is not providing meaningful protection for Washingtonians’ data,” the report read.

Godoy said she understands that Customs and Border Patrol has legitimate law enforcement functions, but agencies should be required to pursue and obtain a warrant before they are able to access this information, she said.

“If ICE, or the police, for that matter, want to enter my home, they have to show a judicial warrant. If they want to search my property, they have to show a judicial warrant. So why would Washington not require the same if they want to access my data, which is stored in a state repository?” Godoy said during an Oct. 13 press conference.

In Ferguson’s statement, he wrote that, as far as he knows, no state requires judicial warrants for all federal inquiries involving driver data, but his team is “reviewing what other states have done, and what is lawful, to require judicial warrants for civil immigration-related requests,” he wrote.

“My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” Ferguson wrote. “Looking ahead to the next two years, this will be an ongoing process for us to adapt to what federal government does next to work around what we do to protect our data.

The report also explores other ways immigration agents could access data from the Department of Licensing, including through third-party data brokers, although the Center for Human Rights had no specific information linking data brokers to individual immigration arrests in Washington. But in the short term, Godoy said the existence of multiple ways for immigration agents to access state driver data shouldn’t inhibit the Governor from taking more immediate action to address the primary pathway the state is aware of, Nlets.

“We’re really talking about core principles of the Constitution, which is that you should not be subjected to unlawful search and seizure, you should not be subjected to violence upon your arrest — much less for a civil infraction — you should not be subjected to racial profiling and be pulled over on the side of the road because you’re driving while broad, and that’s exactly what we see happening in our communities,” Godoy said. “And worse yet, that our own state is abetting it, is outrageous.”

text:
GivingTuesday is just around the corner on December 1st!

We believe every child fighting their immigration case should have a lawyer by their side. Your contribution to the National Immigrant Justice Center on GivingTuesday can help provide legal services that keep families together and let kids thrive.

Did you know that federal contracts that ensured unaccompanied children had access to legal advice and representation ended this summer? Since then, more children have been scheduled for interviews and hearings that could push them into deportation proceedings with no one in their corner.

Our goal for GivingTuesday is to raise $75,000 to help provide legal services to children and their families. Whatever the amount you can give, you are helping to put a lawyer in a child’s corner.

Add Giving Tuesday to your calendar:

Add to Calendar

Learn more about NIJC’s commitment to immigrant children from our Annual Report:

Immigrant children, including those who enter the United States as unaccompanied children, have limited access to attorneys but face government prosecutors who advocate for their deportation.

Having a lawyer makes a huge difference, especially for kids. Unaccompanied children with legal representation are more than seven times more likely to receive an outcome allowing them to remain in the United States, compared to those who have no representation (Vera, 2021).

For many years, the federal government has funded NIJC and similar organizations to provide legal information and representation to unaccompanied children. But in early 2025, the government sought to terminate this program, prompting NIJC and others to sue to keep the program in place. This forced the government to maintain the program, but the government did not renew the contract with existing service providers, which ended on July 31, 2026. NIJC planned for this challenge throughout the past year and remains committed to advancing access to counsel for immigrant children.

Thanks to gap funding and ongoing fundraising, NIJC will continue to represent more than 300 unaccompanied children with open cases, including more than 100 who were suddenly scheduled for asylum interviews and/or removal hearings. NIJC will also continue to identify children and families who need legal services, including through a new Illinois school-based helpdesk program.

title: I voted for Trump twice. Then ICE deported my Cuban fiancée to Mexico - The Times
description:
Wayne DeMario voted twice for Donald Trump in the hope he would make Florida great again.
But months after Trump began his second term she was arrested during a routine Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) appointment.
“Now I know better.” DeMario voted early in the midterm elections, and for the first time in decades he did so for a Democrat.
The Trump administration’s immigration sweep is so unpopular some Republican candidates in Miami are distancing themselves from Trump’s immigration policies.
How will the midterm elections unfold?
text:
Wayne DeMario voted twice for Donald Trump in the hope he would make Florida great again. The Republican was promising the kind of tough immigration enforcement DeMario thought was needed in his home state, which has one of the largest Hispanic populations in America.

That was until DeMario’s fiancée was detained and deported.

Yamile Alcantu had been living and working legally in Miami after she fled Cuba in 2000. But months after Trump began his second term she was arrested during a routine Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) appointment.

US midterm elections 2026 live: results, news and analysis

“If I had voted Democrat, I wouldn’t have lost her,” said DeMario, 57, who runs the music shop Wayne’s Guitar World. “The first time I was sticking with the party, like you do for your favourite sports team. Well that went totally wrong. That second vote, what was I thinking? Well, I am no political scientist. But this is not some sports game,” he told The Times. “Now I know better.”

DeMario voted early in the midterm elections, and for the first time in decades he did so for a Democrat.

Polls suggest he may not be alone. As Floridians head to the ballot box on Tuesday, the question is whether the immigration crackdown that helped Trump win over voters is now driving them away.

For years Republicans have made significant gains among Latino voters, particularly Cuban Americans in south Florida, by campaigning on border security, opposition to socialism and a promise to restore economic prosperity.

Trump won the state, home to his Mar-a-Lago resort, comfortably in 2024 with 56 per cent of the vote. The one-time swing state has been solidly red for a generation and largely taken for granted by Republicans, to the point that national political figures do not usually spend any time here in the final election stretch.

When will the midterm election results be announced? The key timings

Yet Trump visited twice in a week as the latest polls showed much more competitive races here than anyone had expected — some as close as a toss-up.

Trump is backing the Republican congressman Byron Donalds to replace the popular two-term governor, Ron DeSantis. Donalds’ rival, David Jolly, a former Republican who defected to the Democrats during the Trump era, is trying to sweep up independents and moderates in his old party with a promise to end the state’s mandatory co-operation with ICE.

Jolly won over DeMario, who said he voted Democratic “up and down the ticket”.

Alcantu arrived in the US from Cuba through the state department’s visa lottery programme. But after police found three Xanax pills in her handbag during a 2008 traffic stop she was put under a deportation order. Alcantu continued to report to the immigration authorities, attending check-in appointments for years without being detained.

That changed in June last year. “Once Trump became our president ICE called her in for a routine check and told her, ‘We want to finish your case today.’ Instead, they put her in shackles and chains. She’s Cuban, [but] they deported her to Mexico,” DeMario said. “I didn’t think anyone could be that cruel. I guess we all learn.”

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has characterised Alcantu as among the “worst of the worst”, citing drug-related offences. DeMario disputes the implication that she represents the kind of dangerous criminal he believed the administration had promised to target.

After months in detention, she was deported to Mexico, a third country in which she had never lived. Rather than be separated from her, DeMario decided to buy an apartment in Cancun so they could be together. “I don’t think there’s an American dream,” he said. “It’s an American nightmare now.”

Florida ranks second in the nation behind Texas for ICE detentions, with 30,000 arrests since Trump took office. Surveys suggest that most Floridians support deporting undocumented migrants with criminal records; however, that support falls sharply when they are asked whether they approve of how the removals are being carried out, or who is being targeted.

The Trump administration’s immigration sweep is so unpopular some Republican candidates in Miami are distancing themselves from Trump’s immigration policies. The congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, who is the daughter of Cuban exiles, launched a TV ad last week saying the administration had “gone too far”.

Just northwest of Miami in Doral, which is home to Trump National Doral Golf Club and often called “Doralzuela” because of its large Venezuelan-American community, Trump’s popularity surged after the capture and extradition of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro.

However, businesses were hit hard last year when Trump cancelled Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Venezuelans, in which thousands of legal workers lost authorisation to work. Donalds faced a backlash after telling diners at El Arepazo, a popular Venezuelan restaurant in Doral, that Venezuelans who had lost TPS should be deported.

El Arepazo’s owner, Maximo Alvarez, had counted himself a supporter of the president and appeared beside him at the 2020 Republican national convention. Today, he has lost an estimated 80 per cent of his business as many former customers are too afraid to eat out in fear of getting picked up by ICE agents who regularly patrol the streets of Doral.

“Those who have committed a crime, you have to fire them tomorrow. But for the others, that’s a case-by-case matter; we have to see why they arrived, who they are, and what they’re doing,” he told The Times on a quiet Monday selling his famous slow-cooked pork arepas. “We are going to lose the elections. We are going to lose everything, including the immigrants.”

Republicans had for months concentrated on tight races in battleground states such as Michigan and Ohio. However, the party began to worry after figures released in late October showed Florida Democrats holding a narrow lead in the early-vote total, despite Republicans having about 1.5 million more registered voters state-wide.

Meanwhile, Hispanic voters made up a 15 per cent larger share of Florida’s early electorate than they did in the last midterm elections.

Chris Korge, the Democratic National Committee’s finance chair and a lifelong Floridian, described the contest as a “once-in-a-20-year race” and said a combination of factors could prove “lightning in a bottle” for Democrats.

Jolly, 54, the son of a Baptist preacher, has said he is broadly supportive of immigration control at the southern border but wants the Sunshine State to offer a route to legal status and work permits for undocumented immigrants already living here.

“Our current governor is not fighting crime. He’s fighting a community,” he told voters in a campaign advert, saying that as governor he would return to celebrating the economic and cultural contributions of Florida’s immigrant population.

Still, the Democrats face serious headwinds. Donalds has a $172m war chest, largely funded by Miami billionaires. After an aggressive redistricting effort, Republicans are also positioned to pick up three additional congressional seats. Plus, no other urban county in America is as heavily Hispanic and simultaneously as heavily Republican as Miami-Dade.

Jolly is trailing Donalds by between three and five points in most polling averages, although one survey released on Sunday put the Republican’s lead at just one point.

A Jolly victory would be more than an ordinary midterm upset. The last Democrat to win the governorship was Lawton Chiles in 1994.

In the state’s Senate race, Angie Nixon, a local politician from Jacksonville who joined the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and has run an insurgent left-wing campaign, has drawn supporters with pledges of healthcare for all, taxes on the ultra-rich, rental assistance and childcare for working parents.

While the DSA platform is landing in other, more purple, parts of the country, it has risked repelling voters in south Florida whose families fled left-wing dictatorships in Cuba, Venezuela and Nicaragua. For many, Republican opposition to the government in Havana remains a powerful consideration.

How will the midterm elections unfold? Four scenarios explained

A Democratic win in Florida on Tuesday would be far more earth-shattering than one in Texas, where the rising star James Talarico is tied with Ken Paxton, a scandal-plagued Trump ally. Unlike in that race, there is not a glaring candidate-quality gap in Florida: the Republican candidate is the incumbent, Ashley Moody, a former state attorney-general DeSantis appointed last year to fill the seat vacated by Marco Rubio upon his becoming secretary of state.

But even in defeat, a sharply reduced Republican margin would be a warning shot for the party before the next election. “We could wake up saying one of two things,” Korge said. “Either ‘Oh, my God, we won a race that no one thought we could win’, or ‘What a shame that Democrats turned their backs.’”

text:
Democrats hope to take both chambers from Republicans in an election that is largely a referendum on President Donald Trump’s policies.

What to know on Election Day

CONGRESSIONAL RACES: Control of Congress hangs in the balance as voters head to the polls today in an election in which the economy and the Iran war are key issues for Americans. Recent polling suggests Democrats are in a strong position to retake the House, while the Senate majority could come down to competitive races in traditionally red states.

NBC NEWS EXIT POLLS: Nearly half of voters say they view the midterm election as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.

KORNACKI: In his latest Data Dive newsletter, Steve looks at the handful of races that could set the tone for the long night ahead. He is live at the Big Board.

TRUMP’S FINAL PUSH: Trump, whose last two years in office will be influenced by the results, led a series of telerallies for Republicans after having campaigned in person dozens of times over the past month. He’s expected to attend an election night watch party at the White House.

ELECTION RESULTS: Follow along this evening for results, detailed election data, analysis and on-the-ground reporting from correspondents across the country. NBC News primetime coverage begins at 6:30 p.m. ET.

Watch Osceola County after 7 p.m. ET for signs of Democratic strengths or weaknesses

One of the first places we got votes in Florida in 2024 was in Osceola County. It's one of the places that, when we got votes in that year, I knew Trump was going to win.

It’s a heavily Latino county and used to be reliably Democratic. Former President Joe Biden won there in 2020, but Trump won the county in 2024 by about five percentage points.

Part of Osceola is in Florida's 9th District, which features a competitive race between Democratic Rep. Darren Soto and GOP nominee Dan Green.

This will be a really interesting one for me when it comes in after polls close there at 7 p.m.

For Soto to have a good night, he wants to be leading with a vote share in the high-50s when data from early voting is reported. Like in other places, the early voting data that comes in in Florida tends to be more Democratic than the vote from Election Day.

ICE promotes arrests for 'misleading voting,' but examples aren't from Election Day

ICE posted six news releases on Election Day touting recent arrests of noncitizens' illegally voting, but all of the arrests happened last week.

ICE pushed announcements of arrests on social media alleging “misleading voting,” but it’s unclear when those arrests happened. The social media posts, which accumulated thousands of reposts, used photos of the suspects and all-capital letters while withholding the dates when the arrests took place.

The announcements were made alongside a post Election Day morning that said: “If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed the sentiment this morning on social media, saying anyone voting illegally will be hunted down.

Although Mullin previously said ICE agents would not be at polling locations, researchers have warned the social media messaging could be designed to heighten anxiety about their potential presence, possibly seeking to suppress votes.

Cases of illegal voting are rare in the U.S., which has had just a couple of hundred cases against the millions of votes cast. An analysis last week of noncitizen voting cases by NBC News found that 75% of the cases involved people who were lawfully in the U.S.

In response to one of the ICE posts, California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned agents against breaking the law. “If YOU show up to the polls illegally, we will find you,” he posted. “We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape.”

Gas prices loom large for many voters in Tarrant County, Texas

Turnout appears high here in Arlington, Texas, where many voters told us that the price of gas was the key issue driving them to the polls.

Energy costs have been on the rise nationwide since the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Shortly after the conflict began, the regime in Tehran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war.

National regular gas prices were $4.17 per gallon on Monday, according to data from AAA. A year ago, the national average was $3.03.

NBC News Exit Poll: Iran war is unpopular with voters

Amid national concerns about rising prices — particularly gas and diesel costs — voters said they had negative views of the U.S. conflict with Iran, according to preliminary results from the NBC News Exit Poll.

Sixty-two percent of voters said the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran, including a large majority of voters who backed Democrats in the House.

In contrast, voters who backed Republican candidates were far more supportive of the war: 77% said it was the right decision, while 22% said it was the wrong decision.

The Iran war was important to voters of both parties, but a far higher share of those who supported Democratic candidates for the House said it was crucial to their votes (45%), compared with 21% of voters who supported Republican candidates.

SEIU asks for every active judge on the 9th Circuit to weigh in election official threats case

The Service Employees International Union has asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for a “full court en banc review” of the 9th Circuit’s decision in the case over threats to election officials — which means asking all 29 judges on the court to weigh in.

It's a legal maneuver that's rarely made.

Today's average gas price is the highest for any Election Day in history

Gas prices have never been this high on Election Day.

The AAA nationwide average for regular gas was $4.14 per gallon as of this morning. That’s up 46% since the start of the year and up 39% since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war Feb. 28.

The high cost of fuel has been a central issue in the midterms, but what’s making the issue so much worse for consumers this year is that prices have remained elevated, rather than coming down relatively quickly as they did in 2022.

After Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the price of gas soared as high as $5.01 that June. By August, prices were below $4 again. This year, gas prices went above $4 on March 29 (one month after the start of the Iran war), and except for a brief period in June and July, prices have remained solidly above that level since.

U.S. election security agency won't hold media briefings today, unlike with previous elections

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency won't hold any scheduled media briefings today, an agency spokesperson told NBC News — a break from past major elections.

CISA, the agency devoted to protecting U.S. infrastructure from cyber and physical threats, previously held scheduled calls with reporters during every presidential and midterm election since the outgoing Obama administration designated elections critical infrastructure in 2017.

But the second Trump administration gutted CISA's election security staff and funding last year. CISA’s broader workforce has dropped by nearly one-third, from 3,178 in 2025 to 2,204 as of August, according to the Office of Personnel Management. Under Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, CISA has resumed some programs, but some states have said those changes came too late to be helpful for the 2026 midterms.

The CISA spokesperson said the agency "remains fully equipped and prepared to address any national security cyber threats that face our nation. With the top experts in the industry and most advanced tools and technology, under the Trump Administration, CISA is stronger than ever."

The Center for Internet Security, a nonprofit that previously gave CISA election security intelligence, is providing media with briefings throughout the day today. In its first briefing, it said, “As of 9:30 a.m. ET, there are no reported foreign adversary information operation incidents and analysts are not tracking any ongoing threat activity."

Polls haven't closed yet, but there's already an out of this world vote ... from space?

NASA astronaut Anil Menon posted a video to X explaining how he could cast his ballot from the space station. Menon said he filled out an electronic form from his computer to vote in Harris County.

"Yes, you can even vote from space!" he wrote in the post. "All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials."

Bernie Sanders wants an ‘extremely bold’ agenda if Democrats win Senate

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is in line to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee if Democrats win control of the Senate today.

“If I have anything to say about it, and I will: The agenda of the Democratic Party is going to be extremely bold. It is going to take on the oligarchs. The super PACs are not going to run the agenda anymore,” he told reporters recently. “We’re going to do what the American people want.”

Sanders laid out the priorities he would seek to pursue.

“At the top of my list will be a fight for 'Medicare for All,' to guarantee health care to every man, woman and child in this country," he said. "Furthermore, in an economy where 60% of our people are living paycheck to paycheck, we want to raise the minimum wage to a living wage — talking about $20 an hour. When millions of workers want to join unions and are now prohibited by their employers from doing so, I want to pass the PRO Act to make it easier for workers to join unions. And, obviously, AI and the huge implications that’s going to happen to American workers and the American people is going to be something that’s high up on the list.”

Vivek Ramaswamy casts his vote in Ohio

Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur and close ally of Trump, is running against Democrat Amy Acton in the race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.

Despite issues with voting machines in NYC suburbs, no need yet to extend voting hours, official says

Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins said in a video message that issues with paper ballots not going through the scanners is being worked on, and there's "not a need at this point in time" to extend voting hours in the New York City suburb.

"The Board of Elections has said they want to reassure every voter that their vote matters, and their ballot will be secure and their vote will be counted," the Democrat said, adding the scanner problem "is a county-wide issue."

Regardless, "people should understand that their vote will be counted — period, the end," Jenkins said. "So if you are standing in a line or you are planning on going to your polling place, continue to do so and do your vote. Circle in those ballots and then be able to hand those in into the orange bag and be directed by the poll workers, they’ll tell you exactly what you need to do."

In a separate statement on social media, the state Board of Elections said the county board "is actively working to resolve" the issue "as quickly as possible, and we remain in constant contact with them."

"Voters should rest assured that there has been no disruption to voting. Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted," the board said.

Jenkins said in a written statement, “Once these issues are resolved, I will convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again."

Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control?

In 2024, Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed that Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.

Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term.

Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s more likely that determining the winners in important races will take time.

Read the full story here.

Schumer calls mood on Election Day ‘nauseously optimistic’ after casting his vote

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., voted in the midterm election and told reporters, “We don’t want to count our chickens before they hatch.” NBC News’ Julie Tsirkin breaks down what Schumer said after casting his vote.

Unknown number of Broward County voters turned away before glitch resolved

An unknown number of voters in Broward County, Florida, were turned away this morning after a countywide software glitch left poll workers unable to submit some ballots.

At a news conference, Broward County Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott implored anyone who was turned away to return by tonight’s 7 p.m. deadline to cast a ballot. Scott said the issue, which involved a feature designed to help poll workers provide voters with the correct ballots after redistricting, was resolved within 20 minutes.

Scott said about 45,000 votes had been cast by 10 a.m. Some on social media reported initially being unable to access the county's vote totals online, but the figures eventually appeared.

Broward County has more than 1.1 million registered voters.

Equipment failures in Fulton County, Georgia, may require rescanning some ballots

An election official in Georgia says two scanners in Fulton County that experienced equipment failure during early voting last month will require a modified tabulation procedure and the potential rescanning of some of the ballots.

One scanner that had seen 708 ballots cast on it displayed a paper jam error even after troubleshooting confirmed there was no apparent obstruction, Nadine Williams, an election director in Fulton County, said in a memo. The other scanner had 361 ballots cast on it before a voter accidentally rolled over its power cable with their wheelchair, causing an unexpected shutdown, according to Williams.

The potential rescanning of the ballots tonight will require the approval of the Fulton County Board of Registration and Elections. Any tabulation would be done publicly and be available to poll watchers when the process begins, Williams added.

Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger confirmed at a news conference that about 1,000 ballots will need to be rescanned but downplayed the significance of the issue. He added that it will not delay the results.

"It’s one of those things that can happen, and we have always had procedures in place," he said.

Trump says U.S. will stop $4B in aid to Israel at end of year

Trump said this morning that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the U.S. to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel, without providing details.

The issue of U.S. aid to Israel and Israel’s war in Gaza have been among the most contentious leading up to the midterm elections.

Oil prices slid in response to Trump’s comments.

“Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” the president said in a phone interview with “Fox and Friends,” saying the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.”

Read the full story here.

Voting gets underway in the midterm elections

Voters are heading to the polls in a critical midterm election that will decide which party controls Congress. NBC News’ Ryan Nobles reports.

DOJ says it has taken 'reasonable efforts' to ensure no sworn law enforcement officers are at polling places

The Justice Department's civil rights division this morning assured a federal judge that it's taken “reasonable efforts” to ensure sworn law enforcement officers are not being used as civil rights election monitors.

As NBC News has reported, the DOJ is sending a record number of election monitors to polling places in all 50 states for today’s midterm elections.

The NAACP and League of United Latin American Citizens had filed suit to block the administration from deploying federal law enforcement agents to the polls, and the DOJ told U.S. District Judge Reggie B. Walton at a hearing yesterday that poll monitors pulled from agencies like the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Prisons and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives would only be administrative or clerical personnel, not “sworn officers” with the authority to effectuate arrests.

In the filing today, DOJ attorney Andrew Warden said the DEA had pre-emptively prohibited sworn officers from serving as election monitors, and that the civil rights division “exercised its discretion to subsequently consult with Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the U.S. Marshals Service to ensure no employee from those agencies who were signed up to monitor were sworn law enforcement agents,” and had removed several sworn law enforcement officers who had signed up to volunteer.

The civil rights division, Warden added, has concluded that utilizing the Bureau of Prisons employees as monitors "will not create a risk of an arrest at a polling location.”

At the hearing yesterday, Walton said there would be "hell to pay" if he found out he was misled.

Will Democrats flip enough seats to gain control of Congress?

Voters across the country are set to decide Washington’s balance of power, with Republicans fighting to hold on to the Senate and the House, while Democrats are hoping for a blue wave. NBC News chief data analyst Steve Kornacki joins "TODAY" with a deep dive on the numbers, and "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker gives her analysis on what to expect after polls close this evening.

Issue with paper ballots behind some voting machine difficulties in NYC suburb

An issue involving paper ballots is behind at least some of the difficulties reported at polling stations in suburban New York this morning, the Westchester County Board of Elections has said.

As voters reported issues of voting machines down at polling stations in the county, located in the Hudson Valley just north of New York City, its board of elections said it was looking the matter. It had earlier put out a statement saying the issue had to do with the "thickness" of the ballots, but retracted that shortly after.

The board said it was in "constant communication with New York state officials, Westchester County government and poll workers to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible. "It urged voters to go ahead with completing paper ballots, which it said would be placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags that would “remain secured and monitored.”

The issue could potentially delay the results of the competitive race unfolding between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, whose district includes part of the county, and his Democratic challenger Cait Conley.

In a post on X, Conley said there were "technical issues with ballot scanners in Westchester." She added: "But don’t worry: you can still vote and every vote is being counted! Don’t be dissuaded and have your voice heard."

In some Senate battleground states, the cost of gas, groceries and housing are rising faster than the national average

From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day.

In 2024, Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House.

But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters.

Read the full story here.

Where things stand on the alleged 'noncitizen' registered voter lists

The administration's belated efforts to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting in some states has ping-ponged across every level of the federal judiciary over the past 24 hours, with the courts largely ordering the government to back off.

The Supreme Court yesterday rejected the administration’s request that California separate out up to 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleges might be submitted by noncitizens. The court acted so quickly that it did not even ask California for its views first, as it normally does of the opposing party in such cases. This decision was ONLY specific to California and that disputed list of 20,000 mail in ballots.

At a separate hearing in Northern California, U.S. District Judge U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson asked Justice Department attorney Kenneth Kao about the accuracy of the list of the alleged 20,000 noncitizen voters.

At a separate hearing in Northern California, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson asked Justice Department attorney Kenneth Kao about the accuracy of the list of the alleged 20,000 noncitizen voters.

“Would you agree there is a high error rate?” Thompson asked. “I think that’s a fair statement,” Kao responded.

Overnight, a three judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals briefly blocked an order from Thompson that barred the administration from any action nationwide that may threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by the administration to be ineligible to vote.

Minutes after the panel issued its ruling, the full 9th Circuit court announced its plans to “rehear” the case, vacating the panel's decision and leaving the lower court order blocking the threats intact.

In another decision overnight out of federal court in Washington, D.C., the administration was blocked from “further disclosing, transmitting, or releasing data purporting to constitute lists of individual potential or actual non-citizen voters or registered voters, to any State, county, municipal, or other local official, employee, or officer responsible for administering voter registration, issuing or processing ballots, verifying signatures, or tabulating or certifying votes.”

In all, that means as of 7 a.m. ET, the Trump administration is blocked from sending letters filled with alleged noncitizen registered voter to states for verification, and from threatening election officials with legal action if they don’t comply with the demands set out in those letters.

Voters report broken voting machines in suburban New York

Voters in New York's Westchester County have reported issues with broken voting machines at multiple polling stations this morning, with Attorney General Letitia James' office looking into the matter.

Ben Hort, a 58-year-old commercial printer, said he went to his polling station in Greenburgh first thing this morning only to be told the machines weren't working. He said he was given the option of casting a paper ballot or returning to the polling station later.

"I'll try to go back later. I assume they'll get it straightened out," said Hort, who said he's voting "blue all the way across the board." He said he was concerned, however, that some voters might be deterred by the issue and "aren't gonna vote."

Bill Moss, a 67-year-old election inspector at another polling station in Greenburgh, said his location was also facing issues, with all three of its voting machines broken. He said voters were being asked to cast their ballots by hand as "the machines are useless to us right now."

James emphasized in a post on X that "Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations," adding: "Your votes will count."

The problem with the machines could delay the results of the highly competitive race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, whose district includes part of the county, and his Democratic challenger Cait Conley.

Lawler said in a post on X that officials didn't yet know the cause of the problem, but assured voters that "every ballot will be counted. Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting."

James said her office was monitoring the issue and was in touch with the state and local boards of elections as they work to resolve it.

"Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations," she wrote on X. Your votes will count."

Early voters turn out in Pennsylvania

Voters wait in line at a polling place in Warrington, Pennsylvania, this morning.

Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers commends Rep. Stevens endorsement

Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers commended Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens for her surprise endorsement of him and condemned his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed's views on Israel.

"His rhetoric is causing angst amongst the Jewish community here in Michigan," Rogers said in an interview on "Fox & Friends." "That’s real. That’s palpable, and you see it when young women have to hide their Star of David to walk across a college campus because they’re getting harassed for being Jewish."

"That language has consequences, and that’s why we were embracing Jewish Democrats," he added.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed months ago, endorsed Rogers on Sunday after a falling out with the Democratic candidate over her attendance at his final campaign events and after disagreements she had over his views on Israel.

In interviews and public debate, El-Sayed has declined to say whether he sees Israel, America's long-standing ally, or Iran as a greater threat to the United States.

Republicans have stepped up their anti-Muslim rhetoric in the Senate race, prompting accusations of racism and Islamophobia from Democrats.

In response to the attacks, El-Sayed has stressed his loyalty to the Constitution and said Republicans are diverting attention from voters' concerns about the economy and high cost of living, which has been exacerbated by the Iran war and Trump's trade policies.

DOJ is deploying a record number of monitors on Election Day

The Justice Department is sending a record number of election monitors to polling places in all 50 states for today’s midterm elections.

While Democratic and Republican administrations have sent federal workers to observe elections for decades, traditionally their mission has been to help ensure Americans exercise their right to vote. Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, has said monitors would also seek to ensure citizens were voting and their votes weren’t canceled out by someone who “shouldn’t be voting.”

Read the full story here.

Supreme Court hears Catholic plea to participate in Colorado preschool program

Tackling the latest in a series of cases that pit LGBTQ and religious rights against each other, the Supreme Court today will consider whether Catholic entities should be exempted from the state’s antidiscrimination rules so they can participate in a taxpayer-funded preschool program.

In the Election Day session, the justices will weigh whether Colorado’s refusal to grant an accommodation violates the religious rights of the Archdiocese of Denver and other plaintiffs under the Constitution’s First Amendment.

Read the full story here.

Polls open in Maine, North Carolina and Ohio

Polls have opened in Maine, North Carolina and Ohio, three states with Senate races that could determine control of the chamber.

In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins — the only Senate Republican representing a state Trump lost in 2024 — is seeking a sixth term in a tight race against Democrat Troy Jackson.

In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed in 2025 after Vice President JD Vance vacated his seat, is locked in a close race against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

title: Afghan ICE deportation flight via Pakistan could hand US allies to Taliban - USA Today
description:

text:
A deportation flight that was set to carry some 150 Afghans toward the Taliban on Nov. 3 – including some who served alongside the U.S. military or are relatives of those who did – will not leave this week, after a wave backlash from veterans, advocates and lawmakers and the intervention of a federal judge.

In an order issued on Nov. 3, U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni wrote the government "has effectively represented that no Afghanistan nationals will be deported from the United States to Afghanistan or Pakistan this week," and barred it from doing so through Nov. 7.

Among those facing deportation is a man who fled Afghanistan after Taliban fighters detained him, beat him and threatened him for helping their enemies, according to court records. Attorneys and advocates said the would-be passengers also included women, LGBTQ+ people and members of religious and ethnic minorities, all of whom the hard-line Islamist group has persecuted since sweeping back into power as American troops withdrew in 2021.

The plane had been scheduled to lift off from Alexandria, Louisiana, around 7 p.m. on Election Day, bound for Pakistan, according to Shawn VanDiver, the president and founder of #AfghanEvac, a coalition that helps resettle Afghans who aided the U.S. war effort. From there, he said, the passengers would have been loaded onto buses, driven through the border gate and delivered to the Taliban’s intelligence service.

"It’s just really unprecedented and egregious," said Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Her organization, which tracks deportation flights, had never seen the United States try to deport so many Afghans at once, she said.

The flight, had it left, would have tested how far the administration will reach in its push for mass deportations, returning people, by way of a third country, to a government Washington does not recognize and warns its own citizens to avoid. In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio designated Afghanistan as a state sponsor of wrongful detention, denouncing the Taliban’s "despicable tactics" of "kidnapping individuals for ransom or to seek policy concessions."

The State Department referred USA TODAY to comments Secretary of State Marco Rubio made at a Oct. 31 news conference, when he directed a reporter who had asked him about the flight to the Department of Homeland Security.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said it "does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details."

In the days before the flight, which was first reported by Bloomberg Law, the pressure built up. Veterans who had fought beside Afghan troops called their representatives. More than 900 people flooded officials with calls and letters, and 66 Democratic members of Congress urged the administration to ground the flight, warning the United States is bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture.

"That obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way," the lawmakers wrote.

They also took aim at Pakistan, urging the administration to make clear that the United States would not accept Pakistan’s help in handing the Afghans to the Taliban, and reminding officials that U.S. law allows sanctions on foreign officials who aid serious human rights abuses.

"Our nation made a promise to stand by the Afghans who risked their lives and their family safety for us," Rep. Scott Peters, the California Democrat who led the letter, said at a news conference Nov. 3. "Sending them to the Taliban breaks that promise."

The Trump administration's reversal came in a Manhattan courtroom hours before the flight's scheduled departure, when a government lawyer relayed word from a senior U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official that the agency had "no planned or confirmed chartered or commercial flights" for Afghans this week, and that such flights take weeks to arrange, according to court records. The government agreed to be held to that promise.

That account was at odds with the government’s own filings. Just last month, ICE officials and federal prosecutors told courts in Texas and Oklahoma that Afghan detainees had been scheduled for a flight departing the first week of November. An ICE supervisor in Virginia swore that its final destination would be Pakistan, with "further transport onward to Afghanistan."

Andrew Heinrich, a supervising attorney at Project Rousseau, the nonprofit legal group that brought the case, said there was "some confusion at the very least, if not discrepancy." The government is due to respond to the lawsuit on Nov. 5.

"Pressure got the plane grounded. The court makes sure it stays grounded," VanDiver said. "We made a promise to these families. Today we kept it for one more day. Our job is to keep it for good."

The reprieve may be brief, advocates fear. The plan to route Afghans through Pakistan has not been withdrawn, VanDiver said, and ICE has told some detainees the flight will now leave in a week or two.

Much about that plan remains in the dark. The government has not released details of the flight or the terms of its agreement with Pakistan, a country that has itself been fighting the Taliban government. In February, Pakistan’s defense minister declared "open war" after a round of cross-border attacks and airstrikes. The country has kept key crossings largely closed since, opening them mainly to expel Afghans.

Even the Taliban voiced unease about the flight. In a statement from Nov. 2, Afghanistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed "serious concern" about reports that the United States would send Afghans to Pakistan, where they have no legal status, and warned that third countries "should not bargain over the fate of another country’s nationals."

'They will kill me'

Among the Afghans facing deportation is a former university student. Within months of the Taliban sweeping back into power, the former student told an immigration judge, armed men came to his family’s home, accused him of helping their enemies and led him away.

For more than a week they beat him, until the bones in his foot broke, he testified. They released him only after his father promised to surrender him whenever they asked, and only after ordering him to spy on the village where he had grown up. USA TODAY reviewed his testimony in federal immigration documents and is withholding his name because he could face reprisals in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

Even after he fled, the Taliban kept coming back. They searched the family’s home, arrested his father and repeatedly asked where the son had gone, he said. When his mother and sisters were left alone, fighters warned them that women could not live without a man in the house.

So he returned, moved them into hiding in Kabul and slipped out of the country once more, carrying with him word from a relative that the Taliban were still going door to door in his village and asking about him. In December 2024, he crossed into the United States after spending months in Mexico waiting for an asylum appointment through the CBP One government app. While he waited, he testified, armed men kidnapped him and three friends, threatened to kill them and robbed them.

In July 2025, an immigration judge denied his asylum claim, pointing to gaps between his testimony and his parents' written statements and noting that his family had lived in Kabul without being harmed. He represented himself on appeal and submitted a document he said had been issued by Taliban officials, declaring him a traitor "under active pursuit and surveillance." The Board of Immigration Appeals declined to consider it.

"If I return," he had told the court, "they will kill me."

His story echoes through about 150 other people who had been slated for the flight, many of whom have final orders of removal, VanDiver said. Several were detained after routine ICE check-ins. Most made their way through the asylum system alone or found lawyers too late. Some had paid so-called immigration consultants who took advantage of them, he said.

"The tie that binds for everybody is that it is unsafe for them to go back," VanDiver said.

They are seeking refuge at a moment when it has rarely been harder to find. In September – the last month of available data – immigration judges denied 94.5% of the asylum cases they decided, the highest rate in nearly three decades, according to data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonprofit data-gathering organization at Syracuse University. That month, only 800 people were granted asylum nationwide. The courts themselves have been remade along the way, with 279 immigration judges fired or resigning since fall 2024, according to TRAC.

Many of the Afghans facing deportation, Arvey said, "have potentially really strong asylum cases that have not been meaningfully heard."

What would wait for them across the border has been documented in grim detail. Last year, the U.N. Human Rights Office reported that Afghans forced home from Iran and Pakistan had been tortured, arbitrarily detained and threatened because of who they were or the work they had once done, with investigators recording beatings with cables and sticks, waterboarding and a mock execution. Afghanistan’s rulers denied the report's findings.

The killings have continued. In the first three months of this year alone, the U.N. mission in Afghanistan counted at least five slayings of former security forces members, among them a former commander who came home from Iran and was shot dead in his own house in January. In the months after the Taliban's takeover, Human Rights Watch documented the execution or disappearance of more than 100 former soldiers, police officers and intelligence agents.

'Shoulder to shoulder'

In Garrett Cathcart’s home in Atlanta, every rug was a gift from an Afghan. One came from a village his soldiers helped free from the Taliban, another from a warlord whose fighters battled alongside his troops and a third from a police chief who stood with him until the insurgents in that village surrendered.

Cathcart, a former Army captain, commanded a cavalry troop in Afghanistan from 2010 to 2011. Before heading into a fight, he and his Afghan partners would trade a phrase in Dari, "shana ba shana," meaning shoulder to shoulder.

"It was reassuring to both sides," he said. "Like, I got your back, man."

His interpreters were civilians, but they walked patrols beside his soldiers, translating Dari and Pashto and explaining which tribe was which and whom to trust. An Afghan engineer built his combat outposts, latrines and water tanks on little more than a handshake when government contracts moved too slowly.

"I could not have done my job without them," Cathcart said.

He spent nearly a year getting that engineer and his family out of Afghanistan and into the United States on a special immigrant visa, a program Congress created to offer refuge to Afghans who risked their lives for American forces. To Cathcart, it was a promise, both moral and legal. Now, watching Afghans facing deportation feels like watching it all come undone.

"The way we left Afghanistan was one thing," he said. "But now that we’re sending folks back that fought tooth and nail to get here, that’s another level."

#AfghanEvac is tracking at least one man slated for the Nov. 3 flight who served alongside American troops and about 15 others whose relatives did, though VanDiver cautioned that the number could change. In Afghanistan, he said, the loyalties of one family member can mark all the others.

"What your brother did or what your cousin did matters," VanDiver said.

Cathcart said he did not know who was aboard the flight or whether any of them had committed crimes. But he remembers what it took to earn the trust of people who had every reason to doubt him.

"I sat under Afghan starry skies next to a fire, drinking tea, convincing some of these Mujahideen fighters to fight alongside me, to trust me," he said. "And now I feel like I’m a liar."

The cost of the flight, Cathcart fears, will reach far beyond the people on it. The next time American troops need local allies, he said, those allies will remember what happened in Afghanistan.

"My biggest fear is that whatever war we’re in next someday, the American brand and our word has been tarnished," he said. "We’re going to say, 'Hey, trust me, we’re going to be together on this.' And they’re going to point to Afghanistan and say, 'But are we, though?'"

For VanDiver, who has spent years trying to bring America’s Afghan allies to safety, the obligation is simple.

“We want to take care of these people,” he said. “That should be the easiest thing in the world.”

Here’s what officials said about the latest immigration operation targeting commercial truck drivers.

text:
Federal and state law enforcement have taken Oklahoma‘s Operation Guardian to 14 other states. Here’s what officials said about the latest immigration operation targeting commercial truck drivers.

Oklahoma’s Public Safety Commissioner Tim Tipton says commercial truckers are getting savvy to Oklahoma Highway Patrol operations targeting people in the country without legal permission.

When OHP units appeared near Oklahoma ports of entry during past operations, Tipton said truckers worked together across state lines to avoid them.

“Our intel analysts would immediately start seeing social media posts and things like that from the East and West Coast, telling each other that, ‘Hey, Oklahoma is back at it again,’” Tipton said. “You know, ‘Divert go around Oklahoma.’”

So, in preparation for the latest sting, Tipton said he reached out to 14 nearby states for support in tracking, funneling and targeting suspected immigrant truckers – and non-commercial drivers too.

The result, he said, was a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) powered, Oklahoma-led “first-of-its-kind, multi-state partnership that made it much harder for individuals to evade detection” by avoiding the state.

While the operation’s exact dates weren’t shared with the public during the press conference, Tipton called the 72-hour job a success for Oklahoma state troopers and their partners.

“Over 230 illegal immigrants were taken into custody,” he said. “Over 40 of those were driving commercial motor vehicles.”

A full list of participating states was also left out during the press conference, but Tipton said the following were involved:

Oklahoma

Kansas

Nebraska

South Dakota

North Dakota

Arkansas

Louisiana

Ohio

Indiana

Georgia

Alabama

Florida

Texas

Missouri

The Oklahoma Public Safety Department, which oversees the state highway patrol, did not immediately respond to KOSU’s inquiries for clarification.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who hosted the press conference at a facility owned by the Tulsa-based company Melton Trucking Lines, praised Tipton and Oklahoma law enforcement for their leadership, saying they “bat way above their weight,” especially when it comes to partnerships with ICE.

Oklahoma has been hyper-active in partnering with ICE since President Trump took office last year.

The latest federal data shows Oklahoma law enforcement agencies have entered into 136 partnerships with ICE known as 287(g) agreements as of October this year, allowing their officers to be deputized with various immigration enforcement powers. Of those agreements, 109 were signed in 2026.

Also at the press conference was senior ICE official Russell Hott, who oversees the agency’s 287(g) partnerships. He too commended Oklahoma’s immigration enforcement efforts, specifically around targeting commercial truck drivers, which has become the focus of Operation Guardian over the last year.

“Between January 2025 and October 31st, 2025, ICE conducted over 4,800 CDL (commercial driver’s license) operations, resulting in the arrest of 1,243 CDL holders during the same time frame,” Hott said. “ICE arrested over 710 CDL individuals in Oklahoma alone.”

text:
Last Friday, Paula Albornoz Hernandez sat in San Francisco International Airport, waiting to board a flight to Portland, Oregon with her boyfriend.

They planned to head up the coast to enjoy some of Oregon’s infamous waterfalls before midterms started. Instead, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents detained the 23-year-old Colombian asylum seeker before she could board the plane, her lawyer, Nikolas De Bremaeker, said.

ICE then transported Albornoz Hernandez to ICE’s California City Detention Facility, a remote center in the Mojave Desert that De Bremaeker called “an atrocious place where no human being should be sent.”

Albornoz Hernandez entered the country in 2022 and applied for asylum for gender-based violence “well before” the one-year deadline, said De Bremaeker.

The attorney told KQED that the arrest was illegal and that he filed a habeas petition — a federal petition used to argue that someone is being held without legal basis or being held under unacceptable conditions — on Monday.

“She has built up so many ties,” De Bremaeker said. “The government can’t just step in and say ‘Oh, I’ve changed my mind, I’m going to detain them now.’ Our Constitution prevents that.”

ICE did not respond to KQED’s request for comment.

De Bremaeker said Albornoz Hernandez is a student in U.C. Berkeley’s business administration program and is an active member of her community.

He said that the government is extensively monitoring travel to know when people enter ports or cross borders.

“It’s just a convenient way for them to carry out their agenda,” De Bremaeker said. “They’re desperate to meet their quota.”

President Donald Trump has directed ICE to arrest 3,000 per day. Data from the Deportation Data Project shows that while California arrests fell in January, they started climbing again over the summer.

“Going on a trip to Portland really should not mean that you get detained by ICE,” said De Bremaeker.

The day so far

Voter turnout has surged as Americans cast their ballots in the critical US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress and the trajectory of Donald Trump’s final years in office. With the economy and cost-of-living among the top issues in voters’ minds, these elections are widely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second presidency – and voter dissatisfaction has turned races in even ruby-red states competitive.

The first round of polls, in most of Kentucky and Indiana, will close at 6pm ET. My colleague Shrai Popat has this explainer running down hour by hour when polls will close across the country and some of the key races we’re watching in each state. The US territory of Guam was first to report (unofficial) results, which showed that Republicans had wrested away control of Guam’s governorship, while Democrats flipped the state’s nonvoting delegate to Congress blue. We also have a live-tracker for when the results start trickling in, which you can find here.

The world is also watching to see if Trump will interfere with the results of the election. In recent days, his administration has hinted at federal intervention in Alaska after a judge rejected his DoJ’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Senate race if Republican Dan Sullivan loses. The administration also sent election monitors across all 50 states today, including a last-minute surge into Los Angeles this morning, amid an ongoing legal back-and-forth with the Trump administration over California’s 20,000 contested ballots, in what is widely seen as an intimidation tactic.

We are closing this blog now and starting a fresh one to capture all the results as they come in. We’ll see you over there!

Astronaut Anil Menon has voted in the US midterm elections by casting an electronic ballot from the International Space Station. He said he filled out the ballot on his station computer and sent it to election officials in Harris county, Texas. In a social media post, he said all three US crew members onboard also had the chance to vote. Here’s the clip:

José Olivares

in Minneapolis, Minnesota

A voter from Saint Paul, Minnesota came to Minneapolis to leave his “I Voted” sticker at Renée Good’s memorial site today.

Good was killed by a federal immigration official earlier this year during the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement operation in the region.

“I felt like my vote felt a little bit more in touch with some of the things that happened earlier this year in the city,” Mike F. told the Guardian at Renee Good’s memorial site. “So I felt like it was just the right thing to do — to come pay some respects and attach my vote to what happened here.”

Voters in Minneapolis have been leaving their “I Voted” stickers at memorial sites today after participating in the midterm elections. Voters also left stickers at the Alex Pretti memorial.

Good and Pretti, both US citizens, were shot and killed by immigration officials in January.

Voters across the country have been casting their ballots in the midterm elections that are widely seen as a verdict on the second Trump administration.

Mike F, at Good’s memorial site, agrees, adding that these midterm elections also speak to the decisions under the first Trump administration.

“I felt like voting in a midterm election helps send the message that maybe what was voted on was definitely not the right direction — and we don’t have to stick with it,” he added.

Good’s family recently filed two federal lawsuits against the US government.

Share

Updated at 17.03 EST

Ed Pilkington

in Anchorage, Alaska

I’ve come to Mountain View, one of the most diverse and low-income neighborhoods of Anchorage, Alaska’s most populated city. Though it is far flung, with a time zone four hours behind Washington DC, this vast state may determine future control of the US Senate.

The voters I have just spoken to certainly affirm the diversity of this community. Rita Forbes, 80, was telling me why in her view it is important that the Republicans continue to manage Congress when she let out this little fact: she spent eight years flying helicopters in the Vietnam war.

Turns out that this slight, grey-haired woman, who uses a walking frame, was one of the first women on the front lines of Vietnam. She distributed Agent Orange to troop locations, she told me. One time her helicopter was shot down. “I broke every bone in my body, they had to piece me back together.”

She doesn’t like moves by Pete Hegseth, Trump’s defense secretary, to discourage women from frontline positions. “We showed that we could learn the job and do it. We can take a bullet like everybody else.”

Despite all that, she still supports the Republicans, and voted today on straight party lines. “I’m an old Republican,” she said. “My place is on the backline now, not on the frontline.”

Next up came Michael Comer, 40, a bouncer, bartender and comedian. His take on the election was quite the contrast, having voted for Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in the vitally important US senate race.

“I’m gay. If these mid-terms swing the wrong way then my wife, who is trans, will have even less rights and could be in danger,” he said.

He sees 2026 as a tipping point. “We are on the edge right now. If Trump wins again it will validate all that hatred.”

My last interlocutor is an African American Alaskan, Tenesha Williams, 41. She also voted Democratic.

She works in a school for low-income kids, many of whom have migrant backgrounds. She has witnessed the fear sweeping through her classrooms.

double quotation markWe’re in dark times and it’s easy to lose hope. That’s why we vote. I don’t only vote for me, I try to look out for other people. Everyone deserves rights and choices.

The US justice department sent a last-minute surge of election monitors into Los Angeles this morning, the LA Times (paywall) reports, amid an ongoing legal back-and-forth with the Trump administration over California’s 20,000 contested ballots.

The Golden State and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the DoJ’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls.

The administration’s demands to set aside the contested ballots were struck down by the supreme court on Monday, but in a series of rulings later last night and earlier today, the San Francisco-based 9th circuit court of appeals cleared the administration to threaten state election workers with criminal charges.

That came just after the justice department announced it was sending out “1,000 election monitors and observers” across the United States in what it described as “the largest monitoring effort in DoJ history” – in a move widely viewed as an intimidation tactic.
