title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls to decide control of Congress
authors: Lucy Campbell, Chris Hippensteel, Yohannes Lowe, Ed Pilkington, Richard Luscombe, Adria R Walker, Lex McMenamin, David Smith, José Olivares, Gaya Gupta
description:
We can take a bullet like everybody else.” Despite all that, she still supports the Republicans, and voted today on straight party lines.
Share Americans are voting today in the midterm elections, which will decide whether Republicans retain control of the House and Senate.
And though they can’t vote today, they’ll be old enough to do so in 2028.
In Tuesday voting, Republican voters outnumbered Democrats by almost half, 856,000 to 445,000, according to Florida Vote Tracker.
The midterm elections have been largely seen as a national verdict on the second Trump administration, including its immigration enforcement crackdown.
text:
Key events

Ed Pilkington

in Anchorage, Alaska

I’ve come to Mountain View, one of the most diverse and low-income neighborhoods of Anchorage, Alaska’s most populated city. Though it is far flung, with a time zone four hours behind Washington DC, this vast state may determine future control of the US Senate.

The voters I have just spoken to certainly affirm the diversity of this community. Rita Forbes, 80, was telling me why in her view it is important that the Republicans continue to manage Congress when she let out this little fact: she spent eight years flying helicopters in the Vietnam war.

Turns out that this slight, grey-haired woman, who uses a walking frame, was one of the first women on the front lines of Vietnam. She distributed Agent Orange to troop locations, she told me. One time her helicopter was shot down. “I broke every bone in my body, they had to piece me back together.”

She doesn’t like moves by Pete Hegseth, Trump’s defense secretary, to discourage women from frontline positions. “We showed that we could learn the job and do it. We can take a bullet like everybody else.”

Despite all that, she still supports the Republicans, and voted today on straight party lines. “I’m an old Republican,” she said. “My place is on the backline now, not on the frontline.”

Next up came Michael Comer, 40, a bouncer, bartender and comedian. His take on the election was quite the contrast, having voted for Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in the vitally important US senate race.

“I’m gay. If these mid-terms swing the wrong way then my wife, who is trans, will have even less rights and could be in danger,” he said.

He sees 2026 as a tipping point. “We are on the edge right now. If Trump wins again it will validate all that hatred.”

My last interlocutor is an African American Alaskan, Tenesha Williams, 41. She also voted Democratic.

She works in a school for low-income kids, many of whom have migrant backgrounds. She has witnessed the fear sweeping through her classrooms.

double quotation markWe’re in dark times and it’s easy to lose hope. That’s why we vote. I don’t only vote for me, I try to look out for other people. Everyone deserves rights and choices.

Share

The US justice department sent a last-minute surge of election monitors into Los Angeles this morning, the LA Times (paywall) reports, amid an ongoing legal back-and-forth with the Trump administration over California’s 20,000 contested ballots.

The Golden State and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the DoJ’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls.

The administration’s demands to set aside the contested ballots were struck down by the supreme court on Monday, but in a series of rulings later last night and earlier today, the 9th circuit court of appeals cleared the administration to threaten state election workers with criminal charges.

That came just after the justice department announced it was sending out “1,000 election monitors and observers” across the United States in what it described as “the largest monitoring effort in DoJ history” – in a move widely viewed as an intimidation tactic.

Share

Richard Luscombe

in Fort Lauderdale

There was no school on Tuesday for 10-year-old Lily Ferguson, but she still received an Election Day civics lesson from her grandmother Robin Pace as she accompanied her to the polls in Coral Springs, Florida.

Lily is a student at Ramblewood elementary school, in use on Tuesday as a polling site where a steady stream of voters had passed through by early lunchtime.

“I was telling her in the car on the way here that when she’s 18, she can vote too,” Pace said.” I think the younger generation needs to be more engaged. A lot of them have no clue what they’re voting for, half of them don’t study, read, or watch the news.”

Pace didn’t say who she was voting for and considers participation in democracy to the fullest extent critical for the country’s future. Younger voters, she says, are too easily swayed.

“They just hear someone tell them to vote Democrat, and for everything that’s Democrat, or it could be Republican, and they don’t really research what you’re actually voting for. They hear, ‘Oh, he’s gonna do this for us’, but guess what? Anybody can say anything on TV. They still have to go through Congress and the whole nine yards to get anything approved.”

Other Florida voters who spoke with the Guardian expressed similar sentiments. Hetty Dubois, 20, a first-time voter from Tamarac, said she tuned out a tsunami of television adverts from candidates from both parties.

“All they do is attack each other, you never hear what they actually stand for, it’s what the other one doesn’t,” said Dubois, a shop assistant who voted before work at her city’s multi-purpose center. “I voted on the information I found out myself.”

Dubois said she voted Democratic “all the way down the ticket” largely because of the economy, and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“I have friends whose family members won’t go out much because they worry about being detained. Is that how they have to live now?” she said.

Meanwhile, Coral Springs residents Orlando and Irene Roman said they also based their vote on the national picture, but voted Republican. “We’re conservative, we vote for the policies, not the party,” Orlando Roman said.

He added that he always voted in person on election day and would not trust his vote to a mail-in ballot.

Share

Americans are voting today in the midterm elections, which will decide whether Republicans retain control of the House and Senate. A Democratic victory in either chamber would significantly constrain Donald Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda. Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make passing legislation more difficult, and could pave the way for Democrats to launch investigations into the administration.

My video colleagues have this report:

Share

Technical issues reported across several Mississippi counties

Adria R Walker

in Mississippi

People across the Magnolia State have experienced issues with voting, according to Mississippi Voters Action Fund [Msvaf], which supports voting in the state.

Lily Moens, policy and research director at Msvaf, said that the team received reports from Jackson county, on the Gulf Coast; Hinds county, in central Mississippi and DeSoto county, one of the northernmost counties in the state, along with other counties. Jackson county, which has received international scrutiny since Nolan Wells, a Black teenager, disappeared and died there, reported the largest number of incidents.

“There were a lot of reports coming from Jackson county that all of the machines were down,” she said. “We were told that, at at least one location, it was an internet connectivity issue.”

In a midday statement, the Mississippi secretary of state’s office said they are “experiencing high call volume on the Elections Hotline.” The office received reports of late-opening precinct; voting machines being temporarily down; state agency websites experiencing accessibility issues; and voters verifying registration status.

Debbie Price said that she arrived to vote at the civic center in Ocean Springs, which is in Jackson county, about twenty minutes after the polls opened. There was already a long line. Eventually, a poll worker told those gathered that the voting machines weren’t working and that there were no paper ballots available. People who wanted to vote would have to wait until the ballots were delivered.

“Everyone was waiting and, of course, people were leaving because those are people that vote early to go to work,” Price told the Guardian. She said that she saw about 25 to 30 people leave. “I didn’t vote until 45 minutes later.”

Though the civic center serves many voters in the coastal city, Price said that there were only two voting machines available when she finally made it in to vote. One of the machines kept breaking down. Price said that she received text messages from voters at four different locations who were experiencing similar issues.

“It was horrible,” she said. “There was no preparation, they didn’t know what they were doing. It was very discouraging.”

Kelly Jacobs, who lives in DeSoto County, was driving to a voting precinct to ascertain whether or not reports that the precinct had run out of ballots were true when she spoke to the Guardian. When she arrived there, a precinct manager told her that they opened on time, but ran out of pre-printed ballots. They were told that they would not receive any more, but that voters could use blank ballots.

By then, Jacobs, who is chair of Indivisible Desoto county, had been to two other precincts. One, she said, opened an hour late and still ran out of ballots by 10am. When she made it to that precinct, at 10:35, they had resolved the ballots, but were dealing with a very long line. A different polling precinct was also out of ballots early on.

“This is business as usual for the Republicans,” Jacobs said. “This is how they cheat at voting. There’s no penalty for running out of ballots. We saw that for the gubernatorial election … In my opinion, we don’t have a system that is set up in favor of voters. This is not the first time that DeSoto county has run out of ballots.”

Share

Updated at 16.14 EST

Lex McMenamin

in Durham, New Hampshire

Halfway through Voting Day on the campus of the University of New Hampshire, many students wore “I voted” stickers on their hoodies and t-shirts as they scurried between classes.

In a state with one of the nation’s oldest overall populations - and despite a recent supreme court ruling making it more difficult for New Hampshire college students to vote - hundreds of students dropped by the multiple on-campus areas to catch a ride to go vote.

One “ride to the polls” program was from the New Hampshire Youth Movement, a grassroots organization launched during the 2016 election cycle. Organizers handed out Dunkin Donuts in hopes of luring in students, some of whom averted their eyes while trying not to hear the volunteers asking them, “Hey, have you voted yet today?”

At the NHYM tent, two volunteers calling out to potential voter passerby were there in part because they themselves weren’t old enough to exercise their voices through voting. Local high school students Maddie Denham and Viola Landry, both 16, were motivated to get involved in politics while watching the struggles of their trans friends and classmates; New Hampshire has passed anti-trans legislation targeting youth in recent years.

“One of my big fears is that there’s going to be more legislation that’s targeting trans youth, and trans and queer people in general,” said Denham. She said she had previously met current Republican governor Kelly Ayotte, up for re-election, and was distrustful of her.

Voting age or not, the impacts of Trump administration policies have been felt inside their school, whether that’s the economy - Landry immediately brought up gas prices - or vitriolic political rhetoric.

“Because of how diverse our school is, there’s a lot of differing political opinions. And it feels very unsafe for some people at our school sometimes,” Denham said, mentioning that fights broke out in school after the death of Charlie Kirk. A few months ago, a classmate of Landry and Denham’s threatened to call Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on another classmate.

And though they can’t vote today, they’ll be old enough to do so in 2028. “For most of our lives, Trump has been president,” said Denham. “I personally want to see a change, and not what’s been happening.”

While the New Hampshire Youth Movement is providing rides to the polls on four campuses today, Kirk’s organization, Turning Point USA, has had a heavy presence today both on campuses as well as at New Hampshire voting locations.

The young people manning their tents handed out sandwiches to potential voters, with signs telling voters to vote “red” all down the ballot propped up on their tables.

The organization appears to have plunged significant resources into the state amid the heated race between Republican John Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat. At one polling place in Manchester, multiple elderly voters were dropped off by Turning Point USA’s rides to the polls program.

Share

Technical issues with Florida county's voting machines resolved, election officials say

Richard Luscombe

Election officials in Florida’s Broward county, the largest Democratic party stronghold in the state, say they have resolved issues with voting machines in a number of precincts that prevented early election day voters from casting their ballots.

Joe Scott, the county’s supervisor of elections, said in a statement that the technical problems, which became evident as soon as polling opened at 7am ET, were quickly ironed out.

“The system was telling them it was the wrong ballot when, in fact, it was not,” he said.

“Those people were not able to move forward until the problem was fixed, so nobody voted on the wrong ballot.

“The impact is that some people weren’t able to wait.”

Elsewhere in the county, one of many in Florida that experienced heavy overnight rainfall, a precinct had to be moved because of flooding.

By 3pm ET, more than half of Florida’s eligible 13.6 million voters (7.22 million) had cast a midterm ballot, state officials said, either in early voting that ended Sunday, or in person on election day.

In Tuesday voting, Republican voters outnumbered Democrats by almost half, 856,000 to 445,000, according to Florida Vote Tracker. In all votes cast, Republicans led 3.06 million to 2.5 million, with another 1.6 million independent or no party affiliated votes cast.

The figures, of course, reflect only the number of returned votes by affiliation so far, not who voters actually voted for.

Share

Updated at 15.44 EST

David Smith

in Austin, Texas

Election day hopes are running high for Senate candidate James Talarico in Austin, the capital of Texas and the Democrat’s home city.

Regina Montoya, a lawyer wearing a “Talafreako” t-shirt, said: “He’s honest, he’s thoughtful, he’s going to make a difference for our country. He’s going to ensure that Texas has good education for its students, that we are able to have health care. He understands the issues of Texans.”

Addressing a potential shift among Latino voters who previously backed Donald Trump, Montoya, who is Latina, said: “I absolutely think it’s going to change because the issues of ICE, the deportation that has been occurring has been horrendous for so many people. It’s been so thoughtless. It has been so insensitive.”

She added: “People were told so many lies and they understand now that these were lies that were given to them and they’re not buying it anymore.”

Household economic pressure is also acting as a major catalyst for voters, according to Montoya, who pointed to petrol costs exceeding $4 per gallon and steep rises in essential food prices.

“The economy was supposed to improve. It did not improve for people. Paying over $4 a gallon for gas, going to the grocery storeand what used to cost $4 now is $8 and $9. People’s grocery bills are astronomical and it’s because of what has been happening in DC and because of what’s been happening and the state as well.

Texas has not elected a Democratic candidate to the US Senate since 1988. Asked what a victory would signify, Montoya said: “It’s going to be a brave new world and I’m excited about it. I’m excited about the opportunities.”

Share

Alex Pretti’s memorial site adorned with “I Voted” stickers

José Olivares

in Minneapolis, Minnesota

Voters in Minneapolis have been leaving their “I Voted” stickers at the Alex Pretti memorial site after participating in Tuesday’s elections. Pretti, a US citizen and nurse, was shot and killed by federal immigration officials in January this year.

“I knew Alex Pretti,” said a retired physician in Minneapolis who worked with Pretti. “I just knew that he was a competent nurse — a really, really liked guy. And he was assassinated.”

The physician, Arne, who only gave his first name, left his “I Voted” sticker at the memorial site. Arne choked up when speaking about his vote, Pretti and when federal immigration officials killed him.

Pretti was killed by federal immigration officials during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation in the Minneapolis region this year, days after an immigration official in the city shot and killed another US citizen, Renee Good.

The midterm elections have been largely seen as a national verdict on the second Trump administration, including its immigration enforcement crackdown.

“The country has humiliated itself by putting in a bad man, a very very bad character,” Arne said of President Donald Trump. “Today is a chance for America to say whether they support this kind of thing.”

If they don’t oppose it, “then fuck America,” he added.

Share

Updated at 15.51 EST

Gaya Gupta

in Lawrence, Kansas

Zachary Hijaz, 20, cast his ballot for the first time at the Checkers grocery store in Lawrence, KS, along with his roommate at the University of Kansas, Brendan Stanley, who turned 21 today.

“Felt amazing,” Hijaz said.

“It was fantastic being able to participate in democracy,” added Stanley.

Both cast their ballots for Adam Hamilton, who was Stanley’s pastor growing up. Though they had never formally met, Stanley viewed him as a “really kind” and “even-keeled guy,” and added that he wants to see a Democratic majority in the Senate

“He seems like he’s a good champion for the American people, and he has a lot of common interests that I think are just common sense ideas,” he said.

Both men said they have cars and neither were on meal plan at the University of Kansas, so they’ve both noticed the rising price of gas and groceries.

“Meat’s expensive,” said Stanley.

“Stuff’s overall expensive,” added Hijaz.

“I think it’s probably because of the fuel prices from the war. I think this is an unjust war,” Stanley continued.

Share

Updated at 15.22 EST

Robert Tait

in Lewiston, Maine

Election monitors from the US Department of Justice spent several hours observing voting at a polling station in Lewiston where ballots were cast by the city’s sizeable immigrant population, including Somalis, a local official confirmed to the Guardian.

Armed police officers were also present inside and outside the polling station.

Two DoJ observers watched proceedings at the Memorial Armory polling station after quizzing local election wardens about their training, Steve Bannister, the senior warden at the center said.

The deployment followed reports of voter intimidation and suspected fraud during early voting last month, he added.

The Memorial Armory station is a venue for voters from Lewiston’s ethnic Somali, Angolan and Eritrean communities, according to local election chaplains, who were on duty outside.

Bannister said the justice department monitors were present for three hours. “They were not obtrusive,” he said. “They asked what training I got, where I got it from and asked the same of other wardens.

“From what I understand, it’s done at every election but this time it was more stated from the federal government that they were doing it.”

However, the deployment comes against a backdrop of Donald Trump’s allegations of widespread election fraud, which he has made repeatedly despite an absence of evidence.

It also followed Trump’s frequently bigoted and racist attacks on the US’s Somali community, which the US president has accused of rampant fraud. Federal agents raided the home of one of the community’s most prominent members, the Democratic Congress member Ilhan Omar last month amid allegations that her US citizenship was based on fraudulent paperwork submitted by her late father.

One chaplain observing outside the polling station, who declined to give his name, said he had never known DoJ observers to be sent to Lewiston in past elections.

Share

Updated at 15.02 EST

Rachel Leingang

in Des Moines, Iowa

Charlyn Fordyce, a 65-year-old Democrat, voted at a polling place at a Presbyterian church in Des Moines on Tuesday. She came a long way - she lives part of the year in Scotland, on the Isle of Skye. Voting in person felt important this year, and she arrived on Monday to cast her ballot in time.

She said she was raised Republican but is now a Democrat. She voted for a slate of Iowa Democrats today, saying she believes the party has better policies that look out for everyone.

Immigration and schools were top issues for her. On immigration, she thinks there needs to be “compassion for people who come here to seek a better life”. And as a former teacher, she thinks school and childhood should be safe for children here.

double quotation markI think it’s a very dangerous thing for a child to go to school in America.

Stacey, an independent voter at the Presbyterian church who didn’t want to share her full name, said she voted a straight ticket for Democrats, which isn’t the norm for her.

“I wanted to vote for no Republicans,” she said, citing “empty promises” and a “lack of common sense” from the party.

The economy, especially for young families, played into her vote, she said. The job market doesn’t seem great, and everything from gas to healthcare costs a lot.

She, like most Iowans, is ready for the campaign contact to end. “The best thing about today is the text messages will end, the mail will stop being wasted,” she said.

Westchester county official addresses voting machine malfunctions affecting up to 250,000 ballots

In New York state, Westchester county executive Kenneth Jenkins has told a news conference that voting machines have been unable to scan as many as 250,000 ballots in 332 polling locations across more than 40 of the county’s municipalities.

Jenkins stressed that people will still be able to vote, and would be directed to cast their vote on emergency ballots (via orange bags that will be counted later).

double quotation markLet us be absolutely clear: every eligible vote will be counted. No voter should be discouraged from participating in this election because of this issue. Your voice matters and your vote matters. Please stay in line and vote.

Republican representative Mike Lawler, who is seeking re-election in New York’s 17th congressional district, reassured voters on social media: “Every ballot will be counted. Stay on line and vote.”

His challenger, Democrat Cait Conley, also urged voters: “Don’t be dissuaded and have your voice heard.”

The Westchester County Board of Elections said it was in communication with New York state officials and the Westchester county government “to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible”.

New York attorney general Letitia James also wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count,” she said.

Updated at 15.09 EST

US territory of Guam is first to report election results

The first election results of the 2026 midterms have come in from Guam, the Pacific island territory across the International Date Line where America’s day – and its elections – officially begin.

The unofficial results published by the Guam Election Commission show that Republicans wrested away control of Guam’s governorship, with the GOP ticket headed by Vicente Ada. Democrats, meanwhile, flipped the state’s nonvoting delegate to Congress blue, as voters opted to send Democratic candidate Alicia Anne Garrido Limtiaco to Washington.

Donald Trump took to his personal social media platform to remark on the results, which he considered a strong showing for the Republicans.

“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada! Also, the Republicans have the Majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come!”

“It is devastating,” De Bremaeker said. “It shocks the conscience.”

Described by her lawyer as an exceptional student, Hernandez quickly received her GED diploma upon arrival in the U.S., where she earned several awards at San Jose City College before transferring to one of the most competitive programs in the country at UC Berkeley. On Monday, the school’s chancellor’s office issued a campuswide email addressing her detainment and said the university is maintaining contact with Hernandez’s family while mobilizing legal support.

“This student is a valued member of our community, and campus leadership is doing everything within our power to support them so that they may return to their life at Berkeley to continue their studies with us,” the letter from Chancellor Richard K. Lyons reads.

Now, Hernandez is being held at California City Detention Facility in the eastern California desert, which De Bremaeker describes as one of the worst ICE facilities in the nation.

“It is horrifying,” he said.

“I’ve been to many of our detention centers in the country, and that one certainly stands out as a dark page in our nation’s history,” he told SFGATE. “It’s a detention center that looks like a concentration camp in every way.”

“The treatment that people are undergoing there is inhumane. The medical treatment has been described as being wholly insufficient by independent auditors,” he said, adding that Hernandez has been distressed and suffering from cold temperatures ever since her detainment. According to the American Civil Liberties Union, which published an external report of the facility’s medical operations, the facility was understaffed and lacked clinical oversight, making it an “unsafe” environment.

“It is just not a place where any human being should be kept,” De Bremaeker said. He recently filed a petition challenging the legality and constitutionality of the ICE arrest, and he says Hernandez was detained without ever being given due process.

Lyons says the university will continue to provide updates in accordance with the student’s family’s wishes. ICE press and media representatives did not respond to SFGATE’s request for more information by the time of publication.

text:
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former Attorney General Pam Bondi have been thrust into an explosive federal court ruling after a judge found that an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fabricated arrest records and lied under oath, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

According to court documents obtained by Radar, U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai issued a 50-page ruling on November 2, finding that federal immigration authorities repeatedly violated an injunction restricting warrantless arrests in Oregon.

In a stunning finding, the judge determined that an ICE officer had falsified information in official government records to justify an immigration arrest.

The court also found that the officer gave false testimony under oath while attempting to explain discrepancies in the documentation.

The findings emerged during proceedings examining whether federal immigration authorities had complied with an earlier court order governing arrests without judicial warrants.

The ruling raises serious questions about the accuracy of federal immigration records and the government's compliance with judicial oversight.

Noem and Bondi are among the federal officials named as defendants in their official capacities in the litigation, placing two of the Trump administration's most prominent law enforcement figures at the center of the legal dispute.

However, the ruling does not accuse either official of personally falsifying records or providing false testimony.

Instead, the case concerns the conduct of federal immigration authorities and whether their arrest practices complied with constitutional requirements and the court's injunction.

The findings represent a significant judicial rebuke of enforcement practices carried out under the administration's immigration crackdown.

The controversy began after the court issued a preliminary injunction on February 4, requiring ICE officers to assess whether an individual was likely to escape before making a warrantless civil immigration arrest.

Officers were also required to document the circumstances surrounding those arrests and submit regular reports detailing their actions.

But the latest ruling found that authorities consistently failed to follow those requirements.

The plaintiffs accused ICE of conducting arrests before assessing escape risks, using improper standards, failing to document arrests adequately, and withholding information.

Federal officials disputed the allegations and maintained that they had complied with the injunction.

Privacy advocates warn this creates a pathway for information collected by Illinois jails to enter commercial databases used by ICE to identify and locate people for immigration enforcement.
In 2022, The Guardian reported that ICE paid about $4.8 million to access Appriss data.
Commissioners approved an ordinance restricting how county employees and contractors share residents’ information with ICE and data brokers.
Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law said the ordinance doesn’t solve the problem of data sharing elsewhere in Illinois.
text:
A multimillion-dollar contract with Appriss Insights LLC, which runs the state’s crime victim notification system, contains a provision that allows the company to share jail data with third parties, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, immigrant advocates say.

The state’s victim-notification system known as VINE alerts crime victims when someone is released from jail, transferred or experiences a change in custody status. Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul signed the current contract with Appriss in May 2021, initially committing approximately $6.07 million. The contract runs through June 2028.

A clause in that contract allows Appriss to share jail records with third parties. Privacy advocates warn this creates a pathway for information collected by Illinois jails to enter commercial databases used by ICE to identify and locate people for immigration enforcement.

Illinois’ sanctuary laws limit state and local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration authorities— including sharing information about anyone held at a local jail or prison — unless that person has a federal criminal warrant. But advocates say even though the state isn’t sharing this information directly, the loophole in the state’s contract offers a back door around the sanctuary laws.

“This is why we’ve been raising alarms for years,” Jacinta González, a former policy director at Mijente who is now head of programs at MediaJustice, told the Sun-Times in June. “When these loopholes are allowed to exist, they’re going to lead to concrete harm. They’re going to lead to people being detained and people being deported.

How ICE uses jail records

Federal procurement records show that in 2021, ICE sought access to Appriss records that contained information about bookings and incarcerations from more than 2,800 jails and correctional facilities nationwide. In 2022, The Guardian reported that ICE paid about $4.8 million to access Appriss data.

As of November 2024, 88 county jails, 96 court systems and 31 Illinois Department of Corrections-affiliated facilities participate in the statewide victim-notification system, according to a report from the attorney general’s office.

Privacy advocates have argued for years that data provided to Appriss could move beyond state and county systems and into commercial databases like LexisNexis that are accessible to agencies like ICE. They allege ICE is able to access information that includes names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, custody status dates, release information, court hearing details and other sensitive personal data. Advocates say ICE’s contract with LexisNexis includes an add-on for a database called Justice Intelligence, a product offered by Appriss that collects release data from U.S. jails and prisons and makes it easily searchable.

“Basically, this is a loophole paragraph,” said Steven J. Kochevar, an attorney and law fellow at the University of Chicago, who has reviewed the state’s contract. Kochevar said the language in the contract leaves unclear exactly how Appriss may use the data it collects.

Without effective restrictions, companies can combine government records with information from other sources into commercial databases sold to customers, including government agencies, he explained.

“They package it and they sell it through these systems like LexisNexis,” he said.

Such databases can combine booking records with addresses and other personal information, creating profiles of people regardless of immigration status, including those arrested but never convicted.

“It’s not like one straight pipeline,” Kochevar said. “They [ICE] get a bunch of data in a lot of different ways.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office said they were committed to protecting residents’ information from improper use, including for immigration enforcement.

“We are engaged in ongoing conversations with Appriss Insights LLC,” the spokesperson said.

The attorney general’s office did not say whether information from the statewide system had reached ICE and they did not identify any specific restrictions preventing access to the data. The office would not answer questions about whether the attorney general plans to change or retain the contract’s data-sharing provision.

Appriss also did not respond to questions about its contract with the state.

Cook County as a model

Last month, Cook County moved to strengthen protections against this type of data sharing with ICE. Commissioners approved an ordinance restricting how county employees and contractors share residents’ information with ICE and data brokers.

For Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, the county ordinance addresses a basic concern: information residents provide to government offices being used to target them.

“We wanted to make sure that that information that we are providing to the county — at the very least, to county offices — does not get weaponized against us for immigration enforcement purposes,” he said.

Tsao said Cook County’s ordinance could provide a model for restrictions elsewhere in Illinois.

Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law said the ordinance doesn’t solve the problem of data sharing elsewhere in Illinois.

“The fact remains that this company is still obtaining the personal information of people across other parts of Illinois, and that information is being shared with ICE through this contract,” Rivera said. “So there’s a lot of work to do.”

title: ICE Is Inspiring Latinos to Vote in Historic Numbers - WIRED
description:
Civil society groups have feared that the mass anti-immigration surges across the US this year would have a chilling effect on voter turnout in Latino communities.
Trump’s immigration policies have disproportionately targeted Latino neighborhoods, and many law-abiding US citizens have been caught up in the ICE dragnet.
By October 27, 3.8 million Hispanic and Latino voters had cast a ballot nationwide, a massive increase from the 2.35 million Hispanic and Latino voters who had voted by the same date in 2022.
In one recent week, volunteers knocked on thousands of doors, César Fierros, a spokesperson for the group tells WIRED.
“We’re hearing it everywhere our Vote Safe team members are,” Mary Corcoran, cofounder and executive director of the Save America Movement, tells WIRED.
text:
Civil society groups have feared that the mass anti-immigration surges across the US this year would have a chilling effect on voter turnout in Latino communities.

In reality, they have had the opposite result.

”We have not seen here at the local level people worried to show up to vote because they think ICE is going to be there,” Michael Mireles, a canvassing organizer with LUPE Votes, a get-out-the-vote group in southern Texas, tells WIRED. “People are driven right now by their anti-ICE sentiment, and it's not stopping them from going to the polls.”

Advertisement

Mireles is one of a dozen activists, volunteers, and organizers WIRED spoke to in recent weeks about the impact Trump’s hard-line immigration policies were having on communities that turned out in surprising numbers for the president in 2024. Trump’s immigration policies have disproportionately targeted Latino neighborhoods, and many law-abiding US citizens have been caught up in the ICE dragnet. For weeks now, the Department of Homeland Security and the Trump administration have claimed that they have no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on election day, but President Donald Trump and administration officials like DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin and attorney general Todd Blanche have repeatedly hinted at some sort of deployment.

While there is certainly still fear about what may happen on Election Day, the overwhelming message coming from the Latino community is that rather than being cowed, they are defying the administration to turn up in record numbers.

These experiences are backed up by data. Early voting figures indicate people are casting their ballots at a much higher rate than in recent elections. By Monday afternoon, more than 57million people had voted early, 10 million more than the total early voting figure in the 2022 midterms. In many states, Latino communities are accounting for a larger share than in previous years, according to data from the University of Florida’s Election Lab.

In Texas, there have already been over 400,000 people who didn’t vote in 2024 who have cast their ballot in 2026. Of that figure, 50 percent are Latino voters, Tom Bonier, a Democrat strategist and adviser to data company TargetSmart, revealed in an interview last week.

And what’s happening in Texas is being replicated across the country, according to data from TargetSmart. By October 27, 3.8 million Hispanic and Latino voters had cast a ballot nationwide, a massive increase from the 2.35 million Hispanic and Latino voters who had voted by the same date in 2022.

“Where large Hispanic communities exist in Texas, there is elevated turnout even above the blistering statewide pace,” Michael McDonald, who runs the University of Florida Election Lab, wrote in an analysis last week. “Texas Hispanics are voting at higher levels than in past elections, as we can see in Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina.”

This analysis was backed up by data shared with WIRED by the League of United Latin American Citizens, the largest Latino civil rights group in the country.

The league’s data shows that in Texas’ 15th congressional district, which includes a part of the Rio Grande Valley, over 12,000 people who have voted early did not vote in the previous elections. Those votes could have a significant impact in a district where incumbent Republican congresswoman Monica De La Cruz won in 2022 by around 12,000 votes.

Dozens of organizations and individuals across the country have worked tirelessly for months to convince these communities that they need to stand up and have their voice heard, and the best way to do that is to vote.

“We didn't try to pacify people or make it seem like it wasn't going to be that bad,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with 614 ICE Watch and Ohio Good Neighbor Network tells WIRED. “We didn't want to exaggerate either. We said this is the reality of what's been happening. These are examples of what we've seen. You've told us that it's really bad and that you don't want this to continue, so you have a choice. You're either going to show up and vote and make sure that your voice is counted, or you're going to stay home and continue to deal with this for the next two or three years, possibly longer. I really think that motivated a lot of people.”

The experiences of citizens who have faced down ICE’s massive surges have played a huge factor.

“Folks in these places that have really come face-to-face with some of the worst of the ICE violence are feeling like they understand that preparation is key,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, a group that combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They understand how traumatizing this is, how chaotic it is. I think they want to be as prepared as possible for any scenario.”

But Garvey says that facing down ICE already means these communities are “frankly, a little less scared. They have faced this already, and it's scary, but they also know that it's possible, and that the escalation can happen very, very quickly.”

Living United for Change in Arizona is a group that targets working-class Latino voters with its get-out-the-vote efforts. In one recent week, volunteers knocked on thousands of doors, César Fierros, a spokesperson for the group tells WIRED. 1,000 people told the group they voted early or mailed their ballots back. “That's a really good sign; that's something that we have really never seen before,” Fierros says. “People are saying ‘Yes, there are threats out there, looming, but we're still going to show up regardless.”

In DeKalb County in Georgia, volunteers from the Save America Movement, an anti-Trump group, heard similar messages from people streaming into early polling locations earlier this month.

“We’re hearing it everywhere our Vote Safe team members are,” Mary Corcoran, cofounder and executive director of the Save America Movement, tells WIRED. “Voters came through in a steady stream from the moment the polls opened until they closed. Person after person told our team that nothing was going to keep them from voting this year. People know what this administration is trying to do, and they are refusing to be scared out of their own democracy.”

In Nevada, secretary of state Cisco Aguilar, who is running for reelection against election denier Jim Marchant, believes that in order to convince reticent voters to show up, elected leaders need to “get real.”

“I did a Latino community event [and said] we have to actually fucking vote to tell these motherfuckers to fuck off,” Aguilar tells WIRED. “And when you get real with them about that, and they know that you're willing to stand up and fight for them, then they are willing to consider showing up to vote.”

This is a sentiment echoed by Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states with voting rights group Common Cause, who says it’s important to “lean into that defiance” and tell voters “that the opposition wouldn't be making it so difficult if there wasn't power in voting.”

“The threats are real, but so is the joy, and there is a real joy that comes in participating in democracy,” Almeida says.

text:
The Kabul Tribune (KT)— A bipartisan group of 66 U.S. lawmakers is pressing the Trump administration to abandon plans to deport more than 150 Afghan nationals, warning that sending them back could put their lives at risk under Taliban rule.

The lawmakers, led by Democratic Rep. Scott Peters of California, addressed a letter Monday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, urging them to cancel planned removal flights involving Afghan and Iranian nationals.

The appeal comes after reports that U.S. authorities intended to move detained Afghans from Louisiana to Pakistan before arranging their return to Afghanistan. The first flight could take place as early as Tuesday, according to the lawmakers.

The group includes family members of Afghans who assisted U.S. forces during the 20-year military presence in Afghanistan, as well as individuals who could face reprisals because of their backgrounds or perceived connections to the former government, The New York Times reported.

"Do not hand over the people who stood alongside our troops to the Taliban, either directly or through Pakistan," the lawmakers wrote.

They warned that deportees could face threats, torture and even death if returned to countries where they may be targeted.

The lawmakers said Washington had an obligation to protect Afghans who supported American forces and placed themselves and their families in danger by doing so.

Court records cited by The Associated Press indicate that U.S. authorities were considering transferring at least some Afghan detainees to Pakistan before sending them onward to Afghanistan.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to discuss possible removal operations, citing security concerns. It remained unclear whether the planned flight had taken off or whether the administration would reconsider the operation.

In Kabul, the Taliban-led Foreign Ministry said Monday it was willing to engage with Washington on the return of Afghan nationals. The ministry called for responsible handling of the issue and cautioned against using citizens of other countries as bargaining chips for temporary political concessions, Reuters reported.

The dispute comes as the Trump administration pursues tougher immigration policies, including expanded deportations and changes to refugee protections.

The proposed removals have raised particular concerns because Afghanistan remains under Taliban rule, where people associated with the former government and international military forces could face security risks.

Lawyers are scrambling to free a 23-year-old Colombian asylum seeker and U.C. Berkeley student after she was detained by ICE Friday while waiting to board a flight to Portland.

Paula Albornoz Hernandez is currently in detention in California City Detention Center in Kern County, her lawyers confirmed.

Hernandez’s boyfriend, who asked only to be identified by his first name, Anthony, said he’d planned the trip because he wanted to treat Hernandez to a weekend getaway.

“She does so much work and she’s on top of her things and I thought she deserved a break,” Anthony said.

When ICE detained Hernandez on Friday, agents said she was being held because she’d overstayed her visa, Anthony said. His attorney confirmed his account.

Anthony said he immediately called the Alameda County Rapid Response Network, which provides resources and legal aid to undocumented residents detained by ICE. He wasn’t able to contact her until midday Saturday, he said, by which point she’d been taken to an ICE detention facility in Stockton (San Joaquin County). Over the next few days, he said, ICE shuttled Hernandez to a lockup in Sacramento, then back to Stockton and then down to California City, at least five hours drive from San Francisco.

“She’s been moving around a lot,” he said. “She said she’s doing ok, she’s calm, a little more calm than we are.”

Back in the Bay, Hernandez’s friends and family began working to get her freed from detention.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Her attorney, Nikolas De Bremaeker, said that Hernandez had followed immigration rules. After fleeing Colombia in 2022, she’d submitted her biometric information to the federal government and applied for asylum within a year, and received a work permit.

She had all these points of contact with the government and the government didn’t detain her (before),” he said. “She’s an important member of the community and her future should be protected.”

Late Monday night, he filed a habeas petition on her behalf, arguing that the government was holding her illegally.

Hernandez’ detention comes amid the Trump Administration’s ongoing crackdown on undocumented immigrants, and after ICE announced the launch of “Operation Safe California,” a 45-day immigration enforcement operation across the state. The federal government has also increasingly targeted asylum seekers, and last week announced plans to deport Afghan refugees, including relatives of those who helped the U.S. military during its war against the Taliban. In recent months, ICE agents have also been observed detaining more travelers at airports, even though such individuals had not previously been traditional targets for detention or deportation.

When ICE detained Hernandez on Friday, agents said she was being held because she’d overstayed her visa, Anthony said. His attorney confirmed his account.

De Bremaeker contended that ICE didn’t have a warrant when they arrested Hernandez, violating her Constitutional rights, and said that because she had spent years living in the U.S. while pursuing an asylum claim and building a life here, she had a “strong liberty interest,” and should be released.

“Here’s someone who’s been complying every step of the way, done everything necessary, and the government was able to detain her but didn’t,” De Bremaeker said. “In the meantime, she’s built up this life for herself. Her detention affects not only her but also her community.”

ICE officials did not respond to a request for comment.

According to De Bremaeker, Hernandez came to the U.S. in 2022, fleeing gender-based violence in her home country of Colombia.

After settling in the Bay Area, she obtained an associate’s degree from San José City College, and then applied to U.C. Berkeley, De Bremaeker said. After being accepted there earlier this year, she began pursuing a masters in business administration and conducting research in artificial intelligence, he said.

Anthony said he and Hernandez met in school in 2023. Even though she had been in college in Colombia, she’d “had to start all over” after arriving in the U.S., her boyfriend said. She’d been determined to study at Berkeley, he said, and ecstatic when she was finally admitted. “That was her goal.”

Hernandez’s detention has sparked significant concern in her community at UC Berkeley. On Monday evening, the Daily Californian reported that university officials sent a letter to students informing them that the school had been working with Hernandez’s family and was providing legal support.

UC Berkeley Chancellor Richard K. Lyons also wrote a letter Saturday to federal immigration officials on Hernandez’ behalf, noting that “Paula has rightfully earned an opportunity to study at UC Berkeley, an institution with an extremely competitive admissions process. …It takes remarkable dedication and perseverance to complete a degree at UC Berkeley, and I am deeply concerned that her current situation will unnecessarily interfere with the opportunity that she has earned, potentially impacting her academic progress.”

text:
The Trump administration has made plans to deport nearly 200 Afghan nationals by first sending them to Pakistan, where officials would then return the deportees to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, a U.S. official told CBS News.

The official cautioned the plans are still in flux, and that it's unclear when such deportations could take place.

The Afghans in question are in ICE custody, accused of violating U.S. immigration law.

The plan has triggered alarm among advocates for Afghans, who warn that the proposal could lead to the deportation of Afghans who could be persecuted by the Taliban because of the connections they or their relatives had to the U.S. war effort in Afghanistan.

The U.S. suspended operations at its Kabul embassy in 2021 and does not have official diplomatic relations with the current Taliban government, which would complicate any efforts to deport people directly to Afghanistan.

A U.S. immigration enforcement official confirmed in a sworn court declaration that a planned deportation flight originally scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3, would land in Pakistan before an Afghan national would be transported onward to Afghanistan via land.

Sergio Aguilar, a supervisory detention and deportation officer at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said he initially understood that the charter would land in Afghanistan but subsequently learned that Pakistan would be its destination.

"The plane's final destination would be Pakistan with further transport onward to Afghanistan," Aguilar wrote in the Oct. 30 declaration, adding, "The alien's intended removal destination was Afghanistan, as reflected in his removal order."

The declaration was filed in Sadat v. Mullin, a federal case involving Said Mansor Sadat, a 30-year-old Afghan national assigned to a special charter flight scheduled to depart from Alexandria, Louisiana, after U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff ordered federal officials to explain whether the planned charter would fly directly to Afghanistan or stop in Pakistan.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney representing Sadat and another Afghan national facing deportation, said both clients were told independently they would be flown to Pakistan on Tuesday before being transported overland to the Afghan border.

"They were not told who would be taking them overland and in what manner," Sandoval-Moshenberg said in an email to CBS News on Monday.

Sadat has since been removed from the flight list and released from ICE custody, according to his attorney, after a judge ruled his continued detention violated his due process rights. His second client, however, was awaiting a decision on an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order as of Monday night.

The disclosures raise significant questions about whether Pakistani authorities have agreed to receive the deportees and which government would ultimately oversee their transportation to Afghanistan.

Most Afghans who arrived in the U.S. in recent years came after the 2021 fall of Kabul, either through a Biden administration-era resettlement effort or through their own means, with some even first traveling to Latin America and crossing via the U.S.-Mexico border.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to address the planned removal flights, citing operational security concerns in a statement to CBS News, but defended its broader third-country removal practices.

"Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal," a DHS spokesperson said, adding that ICE receives diplomatic assurances from destination countries that deportees will be safe.

The department did not specify whether Pakistan had provided such assurances for this operation or whether any guarantees would extend to the deportees' onward transportation and treatment in Afghanistan.

"When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them," the spokesperson said.

The Pakistani embassy did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

DHS referred questions about third-country agreements to the State Department. However, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pressed about the planned Afghan deportations during an Oct. 31 news conference, he directed the question back to DHS.

CBS News has reached out to the State Department, but did not receive a response.

Afghanistan's Taliban-led Foreign Ministry aired its own concern Monday over reports that the United States intended to transfer Afghan nationals to Pakistan, calling for coordination and urging that the rights and dignity of Afghan citizens be respected.

"Third countries should not bargain over the transfer of another country's nationals in pursuit of short-term, limited concessions or other considerations, nor should their decisions and actions undermine human dignity, rights, or established ethical and humanitarian standards," a spokesperson for Afghanistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president and founder of #AfghanEvac, a nonprofit focused on supporting Afghan allies who resettled in the U.S. following the U.S. military's withdrawal from the country, said in a statement, "When even the Taliban are voicing 'serious concern' about this plan, the administration should stop and ask what it is doing."

"Handing the families of our allies to Pakistan, a government that has no plan for them and every reason to send them to the Taliban, is not immigration enforcement," he said. "It is abandonment with a boarding pass."

As of Monday, 66 members of Congress in a letter called on Rubio and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to cancel deportation flights of Afghans and Iranians.

The planned removals of Afghans through Pakistan have also surfaced in separate federal court proceedings in Texas and Louisiana.

In an Oct. 15 order, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone said ICE had acknowledged that Basir Ahmad Ahmadi, an Afghan detainee in El Paso, had been "nominated for an Afghanistan removal mission tentatively scheduled for early November."

Ahmadi then sought emergency relief, arguing that Pakistan could arrest him and turn him over to Taliban authorities. Cardone denied his request on Oct. 29, ruling that the district court lacked jurisdiction to halt his removal.

In Louisiana, another Afghan national, Khaled Khaleeq, sought emergency intervention after learning through news reports and conversations with other detainees that he might be deported to Pakistan or Afghanistan. A federal judge denied his request on Oct. 30, though subsequent reconsideration notices have been filed.

text:
One of the joys, or perils, of a weekly Tuesday newsletter is coming out every year on Election Day, right when the world is on hold for those 13 or so hours the polls are open. If you live, as I do, in a corner of Pennsylvania without a hotly contested congressional race, and with Gov. Josh Shapiro up by double digits, the day might seem less consequential. That’s wrong. Not only is control of the state legislature on the line, but we’re fighting for a bigger principle: the right to vote again in a free and fair election in two years. Vote as if your life depends upon it, because in a sense, it does.

In Maryland, a man named Julian Curo Churata arrived more than a decade ago from Peru to work as a carpenter and build a new life with his wife, Veronica Ramirez, their two children from previous marriages, and eventually their own daughter, now age 6.

In June, as President Donald Trump's campaign of mass deportation was surging across America, agents from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Curo Churata in a targeted operation, and the undocumented immigrant was flown to detention in Louisiana. He managed to call his daughter every day—pretending he was out of town on a job—until September 29, when ICE said he suffered cardiac arrest, was rushed to a nearby hospital, and pronounced dead. He was just 47.

The most despicable campaign promise in American history proved to be the only one Trump kept.

Ramirez went public with her grief, her unanswered questions about her husband’s death, and the lack of information she was receiving from ICE, in a story on the front page of The Washington Post.

“He wasn’t a criminal,” Ramirez said at the time. “All he wanted to do in this country was work. He paid his taxes, he wanted a better future for his children and for me—for his family. He didn’t deserve this at all. I want justice.”

What Ramirez got instead from ICE was a notice to appear for an immigration court hearing that could lead to her deportation to El Salvador—dated just three days after the newspaper article. Now she fears for the future of her already traumatized daughter, who may lose a second parent. “She’s afraid—afraid of being alone,” Ramirez said.

This case of seeming retaliation by an uncaring and increasingly tyrannical US government where the ultimate victim is a defenseless 6-year-old girl is the kind of article that makes your blood boil. But it’s also just one of a series of stories of heartlessness and violent thuggery toward the undocumented on our soil that have polluted my social media feed in recent days.

I saw a video of an ICE agent pointing a gun in the face of an innocent bystander in North Hollywood, California during the arrest of an immigrant; read about the Afghani refugees that ICE plans to fly back to their native country even after their relatives risked everything to aid US troops; and noted the Cuban-American lawyer who voted for Trump in 2024, tried and failed to stop his cousin’s deportation during the ensuing ICE crackdown, and then cried that, “This isn’t what I voted for.”

No, this is exactly what you voted for. I was inside Milwaukee’s Fiserv Forum on the night of July 16, 2024—watching in horror as white Trump delegates in their red MAGA garb or Texas cowboy hats waved placards that read, “MASS DEPORTATION NOW.” The most despicable campaign promise in American history proved to be the only one Trump kept.

And you still don’t think that elections have consequences?

There are millions of people—who live on our blocks, and pray in our houses of worship, and work the backbreaking jobs in our communities that no one else seems willing to do—who face the greatest consequences from the results of Tuesday’s midterm election. People like Veronica Ramirez and her 6-year-old girl.

Our neighbors with the most to gain or lose from the election results, for whom Tuesday’s election is about a lot more than paying a few cents less per gallon at the gas pump, are also people who cannot vote.

They desperately need you to cast a vote for them.

Hubert Humphrey, the former Democratic vice president known for his outspoken defenses of civil rights in the postwar era, said most famously that “the moral test of government is how that government treats those who are in the dawn of life, and those who are in the shadows of life...”

In today’s United States, no one is forced to retreat into those shadows more deeply than the 14-million-or-so undocumented immigrants and the American dreams of their children, many of whom are US citizens who might have to watch masked government goons rip their parents away.

Unfortunately, it’s a nightmare that won’t end on Wednesday morning no matter who wins, since Trump and his xenophobic henchmen like Stephen Miller will still be in the White House and—barring the unexpected—will be there until January 20, 2029.

But your vote will still make a huge difference. One party will hold public hearings, subpoena top officials, expose evil, and refuse to provide any new dollars to co-opt our local police to arrest our neighbors, hire more masked thugs, or open the squalid equivalent of concentration camps. The other party will continue, and look to expand, a mass-deportation crusade that has become a dark moral stain on our nation.

It’s fine to vote your pocketbook, but Tuesday’s ballot is about so much more. This is a moral imperative.

I know when I vote Tuesday, I’ll be thinking about Wendy Martínez, a woman I met this summer in Pottsville. With her four kids, Martínez rarely left their cramped apartment with the windows covered in blankets after ICE took away her husband, Carlos Moreno. There are thousands like her—women whose family breadwinner was arrested by ICE in a deliberate strategy to drive their families out of the United States.

Martínez won’t be voting Tuesday, but you can.

I think about the family members like Maryland’s Ramirez or Ly Wang, the stepdaughter of a Philadelphia Amerasian immigrant from Vietnam named Tuan Van Bui. whose loved ones died this year in the ICE-detention gulag archipelago, with little or no explanation

Ramirez won’t be voting Tuesday, but you can.

Tuesday’s election caps a year that started with the brutal murders by immigration officers in Minneapolis of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who objected to what the government is doing in our name.

Good and Pretti won’t be casting ballots on Tuesday, but you can. If you care about justice, you must.

Many are. Tuesday morning, I woke up to see a photo online of the ever-growing memorial to Pretti on the Minneapolis street corner where the protester was gunned down nine months ago. A number of Minnesotans have traveled straight from their early-voting site to the memorial, and attached their “I Voted” stickers.

Immigration, of course, isn’t the only important issue on the ballot. It’s not even the only moral one. You can play a role in ending the erosion of gains for Black and brown Americans in the classroom and the voting booth; turning the tide back toward the LGBTQ community, including our transgender neighbors; and electing more opponents of US militarism from Iran to the Caribbean.

But the fiercest battle for the soul of America is being waged in the streets of our immigrant communities. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) used to ask his rally goers, “Are you willing to fight for that person who you don’t even know as much as you’re willing to fight for yourself?”

This Tuesday, the existential question is, are you willing to vote for the immigrant who can’t—even more than you’re willing to vote for yourself?

SANTA BARBARA COUNTY, Calif. (KEYT) Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents spent more than four hours Monday inside the lobby of the Santa Barbara County jail.

They chose not to comment, but could be heard discussing agitators over a walkie-talkie device.

Members of S.B. Resiste said they call themselves observers and used their phones to record the men.

Some wore masks and bodycams.

All appeared armed.

"They have been here all day on our taxpayers dime, originally 7 agents driving up in I don't know how many vehicles and this is just happening too often," said Celine Eising.

"We have been here since 11, no breaks, no nothing, just waiting here to see what happens and then they just leave, that to me is as successful day," said Ana Arce.

Some of the observers said the ICE activity on the eve of Election Day could suppress the vote.

Other said it may give some people a reason to vote.

text:
PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - A federal judge has determined that federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have repeatedly failed to follow his order requiring a warrant before an arrest is made in Oregon. In one case, the judge determined an agent lied about having a warrant.

The judge released a 50-page opinion on the matter. The order was issued in February.

The judge discussed several arrests as evidence of the defiance. In one case, he determined an ICE agent lied on official documents.

That arrest took place in July. A man identified only as “HDGH” was on a trip with a friend in Ashland.

The agent testified he was running license plates and got a hit on the friend, who had a warrant for being in the United States illegally. The agent followed the two and eventually arrested both.

The agent said both men had warrants. HDGH said agents did not know who he was. The agent then said he made a mistake and that his testimony was false.

In the arrest record, known as an I-213, the agent said agents had a warrant for HDGH. The agent later admitted they did not. He said he “wrote it as if I already knew who the person was, but I did not.”

The judge wrote in his opinion: “It defies logic that such consequential errors in the I-213 form are merely a mistake.”

Based on the testimony of the agent and HDGH, the judge determined the agent intentionally lied.

The judge is ordering the agency to meet new reporting requirements to show compliance with his ruling. He is ordering ICE agents to provide unedited documents and body camera footage of all arrests.

Since the injunction blocking warrantless arrests in February, ICE agents have made more than 500 arrests in Oregon. Attorneys representing the federal government say only 15 of those arrests were warrantless.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have been asked for a response to the ruling. This story will be updated when a response is received.

text:
One Friday this past June, a man who lived in The Dalles with his wife and kids was making Walmart deliveries in Hood River. From the parking lot, he collected an order and left to bring it to the customer. Then, a federal judge recently wrote in a summary of the encounter, about six U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles surrounded the man. They told him to get out of his vehicle, handcuffed him and put him inside their own.

These officers did not, the judge wrote, ask the man questions, show paperwork, or declare they had a warrant, but as they drove along, they began making inquiries and checking his ID. After two hours by some train tracks in the Columbia River Gorge, the agents then drove the man to a secluded parking lot in Portland—at which point, after another two-hour wait, another ICE vehicle drove up, an agent forced the arrested man to sign paperwork without explaining what it was, and took him to Tacoma, Wash., where he remained for nearly the entire summer until, in mid-September, a judge in Washington state got him out.

As it turned out, the judge concluded, the ICE agents seem to have taken the wrong man.

When the arrestee, who in court papers is identified only by the initials JCCV, got some of ICE’s paperwork, it turned out that it described the vehicle of his brother, not his, and misstated the location of the arrest, claiming it occurred near Napa, Calif.

This story of a man “appallingly” detained for several months because of ICE’s errors was one of several that U.S. District Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai recounted in a blistering Monday ruling as evidence of the sloppiness and lawlessness with which the agency has been arresting people in Oregon over the past year.

The Eugene federal judge has evidently lost patience with the agency, which he has now ordered to supply drastically more documentation of its work—including body camera footage of all civil immigration arrests in the state of Oregon—after he found that agents routinely violated his past orders, lied in at least one case, and showed incompetence in many more.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment. But the agency has argued the judge was hamstringing their efforts to enforce federal immigration law.

Moreover, the case of JCCV demonstrates how convoluted and contradictory the U.S. immigration system has become for millions of people. According to court papers, JCCV came to the U.S. more than three years ago, was arrested but released and granted temporary protected status, had that status revoked last year, but retains a pending asylum claim and authorization to work in the U.S.

While ICE, Judge Kasubhai pointed out, did not offer any testimony to contradict the man’s account of his apparently accidental arrest, JCCV’s is the sort of immigration status that the Trump administration has routinely characterized as “illegal,” and the agency argued his arrest was justified.

Kasubhai rejected this argument, and his scathing order adds his voice to the mounting chorus of judges who have found the Trump administration and its agents to be unreliable narrators of events.

Where courts would generally give the benefit of the doubt to a public agency, the judge writes, ICE has broken trust. Its many errors, he wrote in his order Monday, “prove that, without external accountability or supervision, ICE is not capable or competent in conducting its investigative and enforcement activities with integrity.”

The case in question, M-J-M-A v. Wamsley, originally centered specifically on the matter of a Woodburn woman whom ICE arrested in late 2025. But it soon expanded into a class action case, representing a broad range of people ICE has arrested in Oregon without a warrant.

Making an arrest without a warrant is not forbidden in itself, the judge writes, but it tends to require certain predicates, like probable cause and concern that the person would flee. To ensure these conditions were in fact met, Kasubhai in February ordered ICE to record the circumstances of its warrantless arrests and provide the plaintiffs with basic documentation.

At the time, the judge wrote, he believed the disclosure of a particular form (called the I-213 narrative) would be sufficient for plaintiffs to monitor whether ICE was complying with the law. But 500-plus ICE arrests later, “evidence of Defendants’ poor recordkeeping has changed the Court’s stance,” he wrote, noting that ICE has failed to report all of its warrantless arrests, and those reports it did submit were inadequate. “The I-213 narratives produced by Defendants in this case have been boilerplate, vague, or outright fabricated.”

Indeed, the judge’s 50-page order began by describing an ICE officer admitting to falsely stating facts in documentation as the basis for an arrest. This was, the judge noted, the only ICE officer who had testified in the case, and “there is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct, which calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon.”

For these reasons and others, the judge set down new terms. ICE will have to remind its agents of his orders every 30 days. It cannot redact documents (“the Court has little confidence that Defendants will comply with any instruction that would allow some redaction,” he wrote), and it will have to produce more documentation overall. This, he wrote, would include all body camera footage of civil immigration arrests in the state of Oregon.

Judge Kasubhai made clear one of his goals was to produce a robust evidentiary record. “This case,” the judge wrote, “underscores what happens if people were not called to testify under oath in a courtroom, if as a society we do not demand that government agents explain their actions, and if the public fails to shine a spotlight on what is happening under cover.”
