title: We went to court to check on California illegal voting cases. Here's what we learned - CalMatters
description:
The government charges say he voted in three elections in violation of the law that bans noncitizens from voting for president or Congress.
Many of the defendants are not charged with illegally voting, but with illegally registering to vote or lying on their naturalization applications.
On Monday, the Supreme Court denied an appeal by the Department of Justice to wade into its fight with California over voter rolls.
The federal statute prohibits anyone who isn’t a U.S. citizen from voting to elect the president or members of Congress.
“We are investigating thousands of more similar cases throughout the nation,” Bill Essayli, U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, told reporters.
text:
A 51-year-old business owner and father of seven was the first of more than three dozen California residents to appear in court to face allegations by the federal government that they violated voting laws because they are not U.S. citizens.

Camilo Giles Jimenez, a U.S. legal permanent resident from Mexico who, according to the criminal complaint, has lived outside Kerman, in Fresno County, since at least 2017, pleaded not guilty to three misdemeanor counts Wednesday afternoon in federal court in downtown Fresno. The government charges say he voted in three elections in violation of the law that bans noncitizens from voting for president or Congress.

During the 10-minute hearing before Judge Stanley A. Boone, federal public defender Erin Snider said Jimenez, who was dressed in a peach polo shirt, faded jeans and white Nike sneakers, owns a paving company. Neither Jimenez nor Snider answered questions from reporters.

Justice Department officials announced the charges against Jimenez and 27 other California residents on Oct. 19 as part of a coordinated effort they said was designed “to root out fraud” in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity. On Monday, the department announced charges against 12 more people in California.

Many of the defendants are not charged with illegally voting, but with illegally registering to vote or lying on their naturalization applications.

More court appearances are set for the coming days and weeks.

Legal experts say that to gain convictions for illegal voting prosecutors must prove that these people willfully committed a crime, which could be difficult. Regardless of any criminal convictions, even legal residents could be deported whether or not they knew they were breaking the law.

The cases

Twenty-three of hose accused are from Southern California, six are from the Bay Area, four are from the Sacramento region and seven are from Fresno County and the Central Valley.

One of those arrested in the mid-October sweep, 72-year-old Omar Muñoz of Commerce, told KCRW that six police vehicles, a helicopter and at least six reporters arrived at his home just after 5 a.m. on Oct. 19.

“It’s a show,” Muñoz told the station. “I said, ‘Wow!’ I said, ‘I’m not a killer.’”

Muñoz was still wearing pajamas when he was shackled around the waist and legs and transported to downtown Los Angeles. He was released that afternoon but would not speak to the specifics of the charges against him.

Justice department officials have said these indictments are the tip of the iceberg in what they allege is widespread voter fraud in California.

“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a news release. “Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week. California refused to look at that list. Today’s charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk.”

Wednesday, a federal judge sided with California by rejecting a bid by the Trump administration to separate out any ballots sent in from people on that list. The decision by U.S. District Judge David Carter is a setback for the federal government in its efforts to exert more control over state-run elections ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm. On Monday, the Supreme Court denied an appeal by the Department of Justice to wade into its fight with California over voter rolls.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote in his 26-page decision. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”

The California Newsroom tried to speak with many of the defendants, and their lawyers, but except for Muñoz, all inquiries were turned down or received no response.

In its case against Jimenez, the government alleges the Fresno County resident submitted a voter registration application to the Fresno County Registrar in 2022, and checked a box indicating he is a U.S. citizen. Jimenez is also accused of voting in recent elections.

The complaint says Jimenez subsequently told agents that he registered to vote after receiving his green card. Jimenez also said that he had been voting since 2023, according to the complaint, although he denied ever claiming he was a citizen.

Standard of proof

To prove its case against Jimenez and the other defendants, the government must show they deliberately broke federal law by voting as noncitizens, according to UCLA law professor Rick Hasen.

The federal statute prohibits anyone who isn’t a U.S. citizen from voting to elect the president or members of Congress. Doing so is punishable by up to one year in prison, a fine or a combination of both.

“In order to violate the statute, there has to be proof that the person did so intentionally,” Hasen said. “That is, they knew they were not eligible, and they did it anyway.”

For example, Hasen said it is not necessarily considered intentional if a government office, like the Department of Motor Vehicles, mistakenly offers someone who is not a citizen the chance to register to vote.

“Suppose you are told by a government official you can register to vote, even if you’re not a citizen, and the person registers, then they might be doing so knowing that they registered but not knowing that they were violating the law,” Hasen added.

Even a statement that a defendant makes acknowledging that he or she voted would not automatically prove the government’s case, Hasen said. Prosecutors must still show defendants were knowingly and willfully breaking the law.

He said successful prosecutions or guilty pleas by noncitizens accused of voter fraud are rare.

“It seems to be a very small problem relative to the number of voters in the country,” Hasen said, adding that it is more about, “trying to make an example of some people, rather than showing evidence that there’s a massive problem of election fraud in the United States.”

Potential immigration consequences

While intentionality is key to a criminal case, it may not matter when it comes to immigration consequences. Regardless of whether someone meant to break the law, unlawful voting and falsely claiming to be a citizen, including by signing a voter registration form, can be grounds for deportation and for denial of an application for U.S. citizenship.

Many of the people charged have lived in the U.S. legally for years and are in the process of applying for citizenship, according to the federal complaints against them. That could now be denied to them, even if the government doesn’t move to deport them.

Stanford University Law Professor Jennifer Chacón says that one reason noncitizen voting is rare, is because the price to pay is so steep.

“The fact that these individuals can be criminally prosecuted, barred from naturalization, subject to deportation, all demonstrates why, as a general rule, noncitizen voting is not a problem,” she said, “because there are many, many consequences to it, and people are generally aware of that.”

Federal prosecutors said that the names they provided in California are only a small fraction of a wider problem. “We are investigating thousands of more similar cases throughout the nation,” Bill Essayli, U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, told reporters.

While the Department of Justice has emphasized that the number of noncitizens charged with voting and related offenses has grown to more than 150 in this Trump term from a total of 13 under Biden’s entire term, other analysts point out that it is small compared to the number of registered voters.

California has 23 million voters, Attorney General Bob Bonta noted, saying those who face charges in the state are “just a drop in the bucket numerically, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”

Speaking on KQED’s Forum program, Hasen cast doubt on the federal government’s statements. “What I think they’re actually trying to do,” he said, “is to project the image that there’s a widespread voter fraud problem in this country, and to kind of mimic the claims that President Trump has made, that noncitizens are voting in droves and affecting the outcome of elections.”

text:
Americans will head to the polls Tuesday, Nov. 3, to vote in the 2026 midterm elections, with control of Congress, dozens of governors' offices and thousands of state and local positions at stake.

Midterm elections take place halfway through a president’s four-year term, and the results will determine who serves in Congress for the next two years.

Control of Congress is on the line

All 435 voting seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for election. House members serve two-year terms, so every seat is contested every two years.

Voters will also decide 35 Senate contests. Senators serve six-year terms, so only a portion of the 100-seat chamber is normally up for election at a time. The party that wins a majority in each chamber will control it for the next two years.

The results are also likely to be seen as a measure of how voters view the president and the party in power. Midterm outcomes can shape the administration’s ability to advance its agenda in Congress.

What issues are shaping the vote?

The economy and cost of living are prominent concerns, while recent polls also point to government corruption, health care, Iran, immigration and abortion. In a Harris Poll for The Guardian released Friday, 36% of likely voters named the cost of living as the single most important issue in their midterm vote. Government corruption ranked second at 12%, followed by immigration at 9% and health care at 7%.

A Gallup poll asked registered voters to rate several issues rather than choose just one. Half said the economy and health care were “extremely important” to their vote, while 47% said the same about Iran. Immigration and abortion also ranked among voters’ concerns. Because the polls asked different questions, their results offer different measures of what is influencing voters.

Governors and state lawmakers will be chosen

Voters in 36 states will elect governors. Governors and state legislatures have influence over policies affecting schools, crime, taxes and other issues, and can either support or oppose federal policies.

State legislative races are also widespread: voters in 46 states will elect more than 6,100 state lawmakers. The offices and candidates on each ballot depend on where a voter lives.

Battleground races to watch

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the Senate. Citing Cook Political Report ratings, The Washington Post identified seven toss-up races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. The Post’s average of recent polls showed Democratic candidates narrowly ahead in all seven, though most leads were within the margin of error. Trump carried six of those states in 2024, five by double-digit margins.

North Carolina is another key race: Democrats are favored to flip the Republican-held seat, according to the Post. Republicans’ best pickup opportunity is Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is defending an open seat against Republican Mike Rogers. The Post did not classify Georgia as a toss-up, saying Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff was favored there.

Ballot measures and local races vary by location

In addition to candidates, voters in 39 states and the Northern Mariana Islands will decide on 146 statewide ballot measures. The questions cover topics including taxes, budgets, elections and abortion. Local ballots may also include city, county, school board or judicial races and local ballot questions.

There is no single ballot that every American will see. A voter’s choices can vary by state, county and district.

How to find your ballot

Voters can check their sample ballot, polling place and voting rules through their state or local election office. Early voting and mail voting are also available in many states, though the rules and deadlines differ.

text:
Editor's note: This story was updated at 8:55 a.m. Nov. 3 to include a chancery court judge’s temporary restraining order.

A Nashville judge has temporarily stopped Tennessee from enforcing a new policy that denies driver’s licenses to thousands of immigrants in the state.

For years, non-U.S. citizens could get a temporary driver’s license using a valid work permit to show they had federal permission to be in the U.S. In recent weeks, the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security has stopped accepting work permits as documentation for license applications and renewals.

The change means asylum seekers and immigrants protected by DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, won’t be able to obtain or renew their licenses, making it impossible for them to legally drive in the state.

On Friday, a coalition of immigration attorneys sued the state over the law. Now, Nashville Chancellor Russell Perkins has granted a temporary restraining order, requiringthe state’s Department of Safety and Homeland Security to once again accept work visas as part of the license application while the lawsuit moves forward.

The real impact on immigrants

L.R., a nurse and DACA recipient in East Tennessee, has an hour-long commute to the rural hospital in which he works. At a Friday press conference, he told reporters it’s impossible to find a ride to work and too costly to Uber.

“We are already experiencing a nursing shortage,” he said. “With one less nurse on the floor, this has left them dealing with higher patient-to-nurse ratios.”

L.R., like the six plaintiffs who signed onto the lawsuit, is not using their full name to protect their identity.

For many, losing the ability to drive has meant losing their job. Ale Z. had been working as a therapist for children with disabilities before the state rejected her license renewal. Now, she said, she’s out of work and doesn’t have the means to take her own son to medical appointments.

State response

The new rule stems from a 2025 omnibus immigration law that established a new state division to coordinate immigration enforcement between federal and state agencies. Although the law has been fully in effect since Jan. 1, the department didn’t announce the change until September.

Department of Safety may have violated its own rules around policy changes, according to the lawsuit filed Friday by the National Immigration Law Center, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and law firm Bass, Berry & Sims. The agency did not allow for public comment or wait to 90 days to implement the change after formally announcing it, as required by Tennessee code.

Gov. Bill Lee told reporters Wednesday that he had just been made aware of the change and was looking into the possibility of legislative “unintended consequences.” The 2025 sweeping immigration law was the product of a special session Lee called to, in part, address immigration enforcement in the state.

The Tennessee General Assembly has continued focusing on immigration, passing a host of laws crafted in coordination with the Trump administration. One law requiring beneficiaries of public programs to prove their immigration status drew similar scrutiny in June when it jeopardized the medical care of severely sick and disabled children.

At the time, the legislation’s sponsor, Sen. Ed Jackson, R-Jackson, said he hadn’t intended for the restrictions to apply to children. A group of doctors sued on behalf of their patients, and a judge temporarily blocked the law’s enforcement.

The lawsuit over licenses has been granted a similar injunction, stopping enforcement of the law while the legal challenge moves forward. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Nov. 16.

text:
During her troubled tenure as secretary of homeland security, Kristi Noem prioritized the purchase of warehouses, which she intended to use to detain and effectively imprison undocumented immigrants. That plan did not go well: In June, a few months after her departure, the Department of Homeland Security decided to abandon seven of the warehouses, which were vacant.

By all appearances, the incident pointed to an important example of DHS misusing public resources — which looked even worse two months later, when the public learned that the agency also spent nearly a half-billion dollars on a no-bid contract for several used airplanes that went largely unused. The no-bid contract went to a company whose chair donated to a political committee aligned with Noem.

Late last week, this ugly pattern got messier still when we learned about the story of the Prairie Correctional Facility in Minnesota.

Last year, a private prison company called CoreCivic reached out to the Minnesota Department of Corrections with an offer: The state could buy the long-shuttered detention facility for $75 million.

Officials in Minnesota declined, concluding that it did not need and could not afford the prison, though things apparently worked out quite well for CoreCivic anyway. The New York Times reported:

Last summer, to their astonishment, the 1,600-bed prison sold for more than $495 million. The buyer: the Department of Homeland Security.

“The price tag is so different than the conversations we were having last year,” said Safia Khan, the deputy commissioner and chief of staff for the Minnesota Department of Corrections. “It was a shock.”

The Times’ report added that CoreCivic, which received almost seven times the amount of money it had sought from the state of Minnesota a year earlier, “donated $500,000 to President [Donald] Trump’s inauguration committee” after the Republican’s 2024 victory.

Minnesota’s Democratic attorney general, Keith Ellison, said in a statement, “Trump scamming taxpayers out of almost half a billion dollars is outrageous, especially at a time when Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran are already raising prices for Minnesotans.” (Neither the White House nor DHS commented in response to the Times’ request.)

In theory, this seems like the sort of thing the Republican administration should take quite seriously. After all, Team Trump loves to talk about the suspected misuse of public funds in Minnesota, right?

More articles

And yet, on Friday, amid local reporting on the Prairie Correctional Facility story, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was there to talk about the Trump administration’s faltering efforts to root out fraud. A reporter asked about the apparent DHS overpayment, and Bessent did not seem to appreciate the question.

“I don’t know anything about that,” the treasury secretary replied, adding that he considered the question “a waste of our time.”

Oh, I see. By the Republican administration’s own estimate, Minnesota’s Feeding Our Future fraud controversy cost taxpayers roughly $250 million, and the White House considers that one of the most significant scandals of the 21st century. But if the Department of Homeland Security overpaid $420 million for an unused prison in the same state, the only thing that’s wasting is the secretary’s precious time.

A cynic might wonder if Team Trump only cares about alleged waste and fraud when it thinks it can be used as a political cudgel against blue states and racial minorities.

Bakersfield, California – In a nondescript car park, a memorial with orange marigolds and prayer candles has been erected in honour of recently deceased labour organiser and civil rights leader Dolores Huerta.

Huerta was a well-known figure in California’s Central Valley, where she helped found the United Farm Workers union (UFW) and win better wages and working conditions for migrant and Latino labourers, who were vital to the state’s huge agricultural sector in the 1960s and 1970s.

list 3 of 3‘Fields were solitary’: Migration raids send chill across rural California

The term “si, se puede”, coined by Huerta and translating to “yes, it can be done”, has also been placed on the display of a local theatre in her honour.

If Huerta represents a tradition of social and economic justice and labour organising that continues to resonate, an uptick in immigration raids across the valley over the last month has underscored the degree to which insecurity, both economic and political, remains a stubborn reality for many of the region’s agricultural workers.

Since early October, federal immigration agents, often masked and in unmarked vehicles, have fanned out across the Central Valley as part of a 45-day effort titled “Operation Save California” by the Trump administration.

Those raids, part of the administration’s mass deportation campaign, have become a flashpoint in the race for California’s 22nd congressional district, one of several contests in the state that Democrats hope will help deliver them a majority in the United States House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3.

While Republican incumbent David Valadao has been a fixture of the Central Valley for years, winning six of his last seven races, progressive challenger Randy Villegas is seeking to capitalise on popular frustration over the rising cost of living, healthcare cuts and immigration raids.

In a small building down the road from the Huerta memorial in Bakersfield, one day before the election, a room full of volunteers chant her slogan, encouraged by labour leaders and Democratic representatives such as California Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, before they knock on doors.

“I’ve spoken to local business owners who have told me how their businesses are now struggling as a result of these ICE raids, and many of them have now pivoted to delivering things like groceries,” Villegas told Al Jazeera, noting that some residents are afraid of leaving their homes amid the increase in raids.

“It’s having an impact on people who just want to go to work, want to go to school,” he added.

‘Unlawfully targeted’

Immigration authorities say the raids have targeted criminals and deny that they are racially discriminatory.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the Department of Homeland Security said in an email. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the US – NOT their skin colour, race, or ethnicity.”

But the administration’s depiction of targeted operations focused on people with serious criminal backgrounds is at odds with accounts from farmworkers, labour organisations, local officials, and advocacy groups, who describe aggressive methods and a dragnet approach.

“These are not criminals. These are hard-working, long-term members of our communities being unlawfully targeted simply for looking Latino and working class,” Teresa Romero, president of the UFW, whose members have campaigned for Villegas, said in a statement on October 10.

“We are seeing car windows being smashed and farm workers dragged from vehicles in the middle of the road while on their way to work.”

A woman who spoke with Al Jazeera over the phone on condition of anonymity said her husband, a farmworker in Fresno County, had been detained by immigration agents while returning home from work during the first week of October.

“I understand that if they [those arrested] are criminals or have done bad things, they have brought it on themselves,” the woman said of immigration arrests over a phone call. “But my husband has not done anything. The only thing he has done is work.”

She adds that her four children, all of whom are citizens born in the US, became anxious after the incident, and that some now begin to cry when they hear a knock at the door and fear that their mother will be taken away as well.

‘Word spreads’

Local officials say such stories have reverberated through their communities.

“When you have a small community like ours, and folks are actually detained, word spreads,” said Olivia Calderon, mayor of the city of Arvin.

“I had pastors ask me whether ICE takes a day off on Sunday because people don’t want to go to church,” she added.

Villegas has drawn a link between the raids and Valadao’s vote in favour of a bill that is set to transform ICE, often accused of excessive force and disregard for civil liberties in its operations, into the most well-funded law enforcement agency in the country.

Asked about the impact of the raids in a debate with Villegas in early October, Valadao responded by mirroring the government’s claims that many of those targeted have criminal backgrounds and that “it is what it is.”

As Republicans and Democrats jostle for control of the House, the race has also received national attention.

Prominent figures such as leftist Senator Bernie Sanders, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson have visited in recent months to rally in support of their respective candidates.

Labour organisations, such as UFW, have also mobilised members to knock doors for Villegas.

But polls suggest a tight race between Valadao and Villegas, even after a partisan redistricting measure passed by California voters in 2025 resulted in a series of newly drawn maps, including parts of the 22nd district, meant to favour Democrats.

Valadao has proven himself to be a resilient candidate. His upbringing in the Central Valley, where his Portuguese parents settled and worked as dairy farmers, has helped him build close ties with ranchers, growers, and conservative voters who play an influential role in the region. While California in general is a bastion of support for the Democratic Party, rural areas are often favourable terrain for Republicans.

While Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris defeated Donald Trump in California by nearly 20 points in 2024, Trump carried Kern County, where Bakersfield is located, by a similar margin.

Still, Villegas and his supporters are hoping that concerns over the rising cost of living, driven in part by the Trump administration’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has sent energy prices soaring, will help him dislodge the resilient Republican incumbent.

“It was really unnecessary,” she said of the war on Iran, adding that rising fuel costs have made her commute to her job as a warehouse worker in the region much more expensive.

“That could have gone to food for my household or bills that need to be paid,” she added. “People are sick of the prices increasing.”

text:
The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency is calling on the federal government to remove Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles parked in a downtown, city-owned parking garage.

The request comes after Mission Local first reported Friday that ICE vehicles were assigned spaces in the Golden Gateway Garage, a few blocks from ICE’s downtown field office.

“I learned for the first time on Friday, October 30 that GSA is providing dedicated parking spaces for ICE vehicles at the facility,” wrote SFMTA’s director of transportation, Julie Kirschbaum, in a letter Monday to the federal government’s General Services Administration.

“I did not approve this arrangement, nor would I, because it is inconsistent with the City’s laws and policies.”

Kirschbaum requested that the federal agency “immediately and permanently cease parking ICE vehicles” at the Golden Gateway Garage, which is owned by the SFMTA.

State and local sanctuary laws prohibit municipal governments from collaborating with federal immigration agencies. Among those laws is San Francisco’s “ICE-Free Zones” legislation, which explicitly bars ICE from using city-owned property to stage operations.

Kirschbaum wrote that she “intends to pursue available options to bring the use of Golden Gateway Garage for ICE vehicles to an end.”

The city contracted a private firm, IMCO Parking, to operate the garage. IMCO then subcontracted to the General Services Administration, which handles logistics for other federal agencies and in turn assigned parking spaces to ICE.

The SFMTA was aware that its parking operator, IMCO Parking, had a sub-contract with the federal government. But it is unclear who, if anybody, at the SFMTA knew that ICE vehicles were parked there under the sub-contract.

Activists monitoring immigration enforcement vehicles in and around the federal building in downtown San Francisco said they have observed ICE vehicles exit and enter the Golden Gateway Garage for at least a year, and have occasionally seen officers standing around and loading bags into their vehicles.

The parking garage is just blocks from 630 Sansome St., the immigration field office that was last year the epicenter of arrests in San Francisco. Pitched battles between protesters and ICE agents took place in the streets around the building, some of them involving ICE vehicles.

In one, a woman was thrown from the hood of an ICE SUV that barrelled through a crowd.

Angela Chan, who helped draft both local and state sanctuary policies, called the letter a first step but “far from enough.”

She said that SFMTA should also investigate how this agreement came about, and cancel the contract.

Across the country, New York City is confronting a similar situation. Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday threatened to sue ICE for using city-owned parking lots to stage operations there.

Here in San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office has stayed quiet. Under city code, the city attorney can sue to enforce sanctuary laws. So far, the city attorney’s office has declined to comment, citing attorney-client privilege. The mayor’s office referred Mission Local’s questions to the SFMTA.

Supervisor Bilal Mahmood said he will introduce a letter of inquiry at Tuesday’s Board of Supervisors meeting asking the SFMTA and the Recreation and Park Department for lists of their contractors and subcontractors to see whether there are other possible violations around the city.

The letter will also look at how city departments are trained to approve contracts to ensure they comply with the city’s sanctuary policies.

“Our belief is this shouldn’t have happened to begin with,” Mahmood said.

Key Points:

Arizona state attorneys have asked a federal judge to dismiss a Trump administration lawsuit targeting in-state tuition for undocumented students

Assistant Attorney General Hayleigh Crawford argues the federal government lacks standing to sue

Arizona voters approved a 2022 measure that allows students who graduated from a state high school and meet other conditions to pay in-state tuition rates, regardless of immigration status.

PHOENIX — State attorneys are urging a federal judge to dismiss a Trump administration lawsuit targeting reduced tuition for undocumented students at Arizona’s public universities, arguing the federal government lacks legal standing to challenge state education policies.

Assistant Attorney General Hayleigh Crawford noted that Arizonans voted in 2022 to change the law and allow lower tuition for those who meet certain requirements, “regardless of residence and lawful immigration status.” The Trump administration sued earlier this year to block the policy, claiming it violates federal law and a Trump executive order.

But Crawford told U.S. District Court Judge Murray Snow that the only people who can sue in federal court to overturn Arizona’s law are those who can show an injury that is “concrete and particularized, and actual or imminent.” And the government can’t, she argued.

“The government lacks standing,” she wrote. “Instead, the government points to alleged economic harm suffered by Arizona universities.” The Department of Justice put the alleged damages at $10.5 million for the last school year.

Aside from the fact that Crawford told Snow the reduced tuition amount is wrong — she doesn’t say what it actually is — she said it’s irrelevant.

“Any alleged economic harm from reduced tuition payments to state universities accrues to Arizona and its institutions, not the United States,” Crawford said.

The tuition issue for noncitizens traces back to the Obama administration, which created the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program in 2012. It allows people who arrived in this country illegally as children before 2007 — colloquially called “Dreamers” — to remain and even to work if they meet certain conditions.

As a result, the Maricopa Community College system and, later, the Arizona Board of Regents agreed to let DACA recipients pay in-state tuition. But the Arizona Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that Proposition 300, a 2006 ballot measure that denies various public benefits to those not legally in the country, including any form of subsidized tuition, precluded that.

Proposition 308, approved in 2022 by a 51.2% to 48.8% margin, was crafted to say that no longer applies to tuition and scholarships.

A 1998 federal law says someone who is not lawfully present in the United States can’t get any postsecondary benefits based on state residency unless the same benefits are available to citizens of any other state.

President Trump issued an executive order last year directing the Department of Justice to take action against any state whose practices give benefits to aliens that all American citizens don’t receive. The order says that includes “state laws that provide in-state higher education tuition to aliens but not to out-of-state American citizens.”

The financial difference is significant. At the University of Arizona, for example, in-state undergraduate tuition is $13,906 a year. The annual out-of-state cost is $43,068.

Prop. 308, the 2022 ballot measure, allows certain individuals who graduated from an Arizona high school and meet other conditions to pay the same tuition as state residents, regardless of immigration status. At the same time, U.S. citizens from another state can be required to pay the higher non-resident tuition.

The state law says in-state tuition requires students to meet two conditions. They must have attended a public or private school (or have been homeschooled) “while physically present in this state for at least two years. They must also have graduated while physically present in Arizona.

For example, Crawford said, a student who crossed into Arizona daily from another state would be a resident of that state but could qualify for in-state tuition by attending and graduating from an Arizona high school.

She also said someone from elsewhere who graduated from an Arizona boarding school could qualify for the lower in-state rate even though, strictly speaking, that person is a resident of the state where her parents lived.

Anyone who met the conditions but later moved to another state could also qualify, even after being gone for years.

Conversely, Crawford said someone whose family moves to Arizona in a final year of high school does not qualify. Ditto an Arizonan who attends and graduates from an out-of-state boarding or private school.

She said rulings in favor of the Trump administration in Illinois, Texas and Nebraska are irrelevant because the wording of the laws in those states are different.

Snow has not said when he will consider the arguments.

text:
The grandfather of the current president of the United States, Friedrich Trump, arrived penniless from Germany at the age of 16 in 1885. He worked as a barber in New York before heading west, eventually opening a restaurant in a mining town. Like so many immigrant stories, his is unremarkable in one sense, and quintessentially American in another. It reminds us that history often looks different when viewed from a distance.

Today, however, history is being written in real time. And the images now emerging from the United States tell a troubling story.

Across many American cities, armed and masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are conducting highly visible raids. Videos show people being detained in the streets, families disrupted, and communities thrown into fear. Other footage captures American citizens confronting federal agents in their own neighborhoods amid tear gas, pepper spray, and rubber bullets. These scenes dominated evening news broadcasts not only in the United States, but in Europe and elsewhere. Footage related to the fatal shootings in Minneapolis spread globally. Now, California’s Central Valley faces raids and accusations of voter intimidation ahead of Tuesday’s elections. They project an image of a nation in distress, one in which fear appears to be overtaking everything.

The nation’s greatness has always rested on the idea that people from every corner of the world came here to live under the same laws, to contribute, to succeed, and—eventually—to become citizens.

Some of these encounters raise serious constitutional questions. When force is used during immigration enforcement actions, concerns arise about the Fourth Amendment’s protections against unreasonable searches and seizures, the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee of due process, and the First Amendment rights of citizens who protest in public spaces. These are not abstract legal matters. They go to the heart of what it means to live under a constitutional democracy.

Why are so many people willing to stand in the streets to protect their neighbors? Because those neighbors are deeply woven into the fabric of American life. Undocumented immigrants often perform jobs that others are unwilling to take: picking apples, tending livestock, washing dishes, cleaning hospitals, and caring for the elderly. They work hard, pay taxes, and spend money in local economies. Economist Paul Krugman has noted that immigrants played a critical role in stabilizing the US economy after the pandemic, continuing essential work when much of the country shut down. Have we already forgotten that?

Most Americans either descended from immigrants who once lacked legal status or know family stories that began that way. This country has always been a mosaic of people who arrived with little, worked relentlessly, and eventually earned not only stability but admiration. They learned to love this land. Many still feel a surge of pride when they hear the national anthem or see the Stars and Stripes.

That is why what is happening now should concern all of us. Fear is spreading through immigrant neighborhoods—fear of going to work, going shopping, seeing a doctor, even answering the door. Parents worry about what will happen to their children. Communities are learning to live with the anxiety that a knock at dawn could change everything.

History teaches us that when societies normalize fear directed at a particular group, the consequences are rarely confined to that group alone. The United States has long defined itself by its rejection of such thinking. Dystopian novels were not written as instruction manuals, but as warnings to recognize the early signs of authoritarian drift and stop it.

As America celebrates the ongoing 250th anniversary year, it should be recommitting itself to the ideals articulated in 1776: liberty, dignity, and equal protection under the law. The nation’s greatness has always rested on the idea that people from every corner of the world came here to live under the same laws, to contribute, to succeed, and—eventually—to become citizens.

Thus, America must find the courage to honor its own history. That means recognizing the contributions of immigrants, including undocumented ones; rejecting policies that force people into hiding like thousands of Anne Franks; and pursuing reforms that help them obtain citizenship and integrate them into civic life. In doing so, the nation would not only honor its founding principles, but also the generations of immigrants—like Friedrich Trump—who believed in America enough to come here with nothing and help build it.

The 2026 midterms are about more than congressional majorities. They are an opportunity for Americans to hold their representatives accountable and decide whether fear should remain an instrument of government. They offer Americans an opportunity to remember those who made America their home but now live in constant fear.

After all, a president may wear many hats—or, in Trump’s case, many MAGA baseball caps—but no president should forget that his own family has an immigrant past. And that includes immigrant brides. text:
Orlando, Florida – Thirteen foreign nationals from Brazil and Cuba have been charged by indictment for their roles in a conspiracy to defraud the United States and other aliens. The charges include conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, visa fraud, unlawful employment of aliens, and marriage fraud. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

Vagner Sorares De Almeida (age 54), Juliana Colucci (age 47), Lucas Felipe Trindade Silva (age 34), and Ronaldo De Campos (age 35) are each charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and two counts of wire fraud. They are also charged with four counts of conspiracy to commit visa fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud, and one count of unlawful employment of aliens.

Erick Bruno Goncalves De Assis Pinto (age 34), Nathalia Da Costa Ferreira (age 43), Nathalia Gomes Ciriaco (age 29), and Kelen Cristina Da Silva (age 37) are each charged with charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, and four counts of conspiracy to commit visa fraud.

Issac Antonio Narvaez (age 69) is charged with three counts of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud.

Ronay Castillo Salazar (age 51), Rebeca Aldama Garcia (age 40), Mijail Cabera Nunez (age 52), and Lorraine Soares Oliverira (age 32) are each charged with one count of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud.

According to court records, from August 18, 2023, through April 20, 2026, Vagner Sorares De Almeida owned and operated a corporate entity registered in Florida called Legacy Imigra Solutions LLC (“Legacy”). Juliana Colucci, Lucas Felipe Trindade Silva, Nathalia Da Costa Ferreira, Nathalia Gomes Ciriaco, Ronaldo De Campos, Erick Bruno Goncalves De Assis Pinto, and Kelen Cristina Da Silva were employees of the company. Legacy falsely purported to be a professional establishment employed by immigration experts and attorneys who could assist individuals with immigration-related legal work. It was part of the conspiracy to give false, inaccurate, and incomplete legal and immigration advice to prospective clients to induce them to retain Legacy’s services. Legacy would falsify immigration documents to fraudulently obtain immigration status and benefits for their clients. The defendants also engaged in a regular practice of hiring aliens knowing that the individuals were unauthorized for employment in the United States. Vagner Sorares De Almeida, Juliana Colucci, Ronay Castillo Salazar, Rebeca Aldama Garcia, Mijail Cabera Nunez, Lorraine Soares Oliverira, and Issac Antonio Narvaez also conspired to commit marriage fraud.

If convicted, each count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud carries a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment. The conspiracy to commit visa fraud offenses are each punishable up to 10 years’ imprisonment. The maximum penalty for conspiracy to commit marriage fraud is 5 years in federal prison, and unlawful employment of aliens carries a maximum penalty of 6 months’ imprisonment.

An indictment is merely a formal charge that a defendant has committed one or more violations of federal criminal law, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless, and until, proven guilty.

This case is being investigated by the Homeland Security Investigations (Orlando, Tampa, and Brasilia), the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, the United States Department of Labor Office of Inspector General, United States Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General, United States Citizenship and Immigration Services, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations, the United States Marshals Service, the Orange County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Highway Patrol and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Bianca Bansal.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. title: He fled Afghanistan fearing the Taliban. Now a judge has temporarily halted his deportation
description:
Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.
Sardar Akbari, the 31-year-old Afghan being held at Camp East Montana, is among those with deportation orders to Afghanistan.
The next day, U.S. authorities issued a determination of inadmissibility, according to a document cited in the court filings.
In March, an immigration judge ordered Akbari removed to Afghanistan and his removal order became final in April.
But ICE transferred Akbari from the Torrance County Detention Facility to Camp East Montana early Oct. 27, without notifying his attorneys.
text:
A New Mexico federal judge paused the deportation of an Afghan detainee at Camp East Montana on Monday, just as the Trump administration is reportedly preparing to deport Afghans detained in the United States to their home country through Pakistan this week.

Advocacy groups say the move could put the Afghans’ lives at risk, as those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban, the governing entity in Afghanistan since 2021. Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

Sardar Akbari, the 31-year-old Afghan being held at Camp East Montana, is among those with deportation orders to Afghanistan. He had been detained in the Torrance County Detention Facility in Estancia, New Mexico, southeast of Albuquerque for almost two years before being transferred to El Paso on Oct. 27. Court documents show the transfer was for “staging for execution” of his final removal order.

“We believe this client is at high risk of being put on a plane to Pakistan,” said Rebecca Sheff, a senior staff attorney with the ACLU of New Mexico. “It’s cruel, heartless and reckless for the federal government to be doing this, especially to people like Afghans who have helped us, taking on risking their lives to support us in the war efforts in Afghanistan.”

Akbari fled his home country after the Taliban “severely beat him” while members of the group searched for his wife – targeting her because of her prior service with the Afghanistan military, according to New Mexico district court records.

Making his way to the United States, Akbari said he was robbed and assaulted in Peru and in Mexico before crossing into South Texas on Dec. 28, 2024. Seeking asylum, he surrendered to Border Patrol agents and was taken into federal immigration custody. The next day, U.S. authorities issued a determination of inadmissibility, according to a document cited in the court filings. He has been in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention since.

SEE MORE: 298 days: Iranian asylum seeker released after judge rules ICE violated his rights

His wife and child also fled Afghanistan, though court records don’t offer any other details about their whereabouts.

In March, an immigration judge ordered Akbari removed to Afghanistan and his removal order became final in April.

After a flurry of court activity the past week, New Mexico Chief District Judge Kenneth J. Gonzales on Monday stayed the execution of Akbari’s removal order for 14 days and until he is satisfied that adequate safeguards are in place to protect against the risk of suicide.

“The ruling was based on the acute mental health crisis that Akbari suffered when he learned of the government’s intention to deport him to Pakistan,” the ACLU of New Mexico said in a statement Monday.

The court also directed the government to transfer him back to the District of New Mexico.

Shaw Drake, co-counsel for Akbari, said the case is a window into the horrors of our immigration system.

“If ICE is able to deport vulnerable immigrants like Mr. Akbari to a country other than his own without any notice or opportunity to claim fear, the fundamental due process safeguards to which we are all entitled are rendered virtually meaningless,” said Drake, an assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law.

Because the government hasn’t provided Akbari or his attorneys information about his planned deportation, it’s unclear whether that removal flight would be from El Paso.

Biggs Army Airfield at Fort Bliss served as a major military staging and deployment hub during the Afghanistan war and later became a temporary home for thousands of Afghans evacuated during the U.S. withdrawal.

U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the Associated Press, the organization reported Saturday, saying the deportations could happen as early as Monday and likely from Louisiana.

The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg last week, with the New York Times reporting that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.

Those targeted for deportation could include Afghans and family members of Afghan allies who worked alongside U.S. military forces and aid organizations in the two-decade U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, the organization Human Rights First said in a recent news release, citing the Oct. 26 Bloomberg Law report.

“For operational and security reasons, we would not confirm removal operations,” the Department of Homeland Security said in an email response to El Paso Matters. DHS did not respond to questions about the concerns cited by Human Rights First.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025, the administration has suspended or stopped refugee programs and visa pipelines for Afghans, which human rights advocates say has left Afghans open to removal to Pakistan or Africa under what’s called third-country deportations.

If the deportations were to happen, they would mark the first large-scale U.S. deportation flight of Afghans “into the hands of the Taliban,” Human Rights First said in an Oct. 29 news release.

The Taliban – an Islamic fundamentalist and militant group – took over Afghanistan when the United States and its NATO allies withdrew from the country in 2021 following a 20-year war.

Thousands of Afghans began fleeing the country with their families, and under the Biden administration, many were granted special visas or asylum in the United States. Others were granted “withholding of removal” by immigration judges, allowing them to remain in the United States as they faced imminent danger in Afghanistan.

“Sending our Afghan allies back to Afghanistan – knowing full well that they face retribution, and possibly certain death – is a level of cruelty that is impossible to comprehend,” U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-El Paso, said in a statement.

“The Trump administration’s lack of appreciation for their service and sacrifice to our country, and the disregard of the promises we made to them will haunt our nation for generations,” Escobar said. “This administration continues to sink lower by the day, and the consequences innocent people face are heartbreaking.”

Akbar filed a federal habeas corpus petition Oct. 23, arguing his detention exceeded the six-month period addressed in the 2001 U.S. Supreme Court’s Zadvydas decision that established immigration detention cannot be indefinite for people who can’t be deported.

SEE ALSO: A year in ICE detention: Cuban man’s case tests Supreme Court detention ruling

Three days later, Gonzales ordered the government to respond and restricted his transfer outside New Mexico without court approval. But ICE transferred Akbari from the Torrance County Detention Facility to Camp East Montana early Oct. 27, without notifying his attorneys.

They filed an emergency motion seeking to prevent his deportation to any country other than Afghanistan without notice and an opportunity to raise a fear-based claim, citing concerns he could be sent to Pakistan. On Oct. 28, Gonzales denied the request, ruling the court lacked jurisdiction to block the final removal order and that the transfer restriction did not prevent moving Akbari to carry it out.

A flurry of filings followed Friday to Sunday, with Akbari’s attorneys submitting an ICE officer’s declaration in another case that identified Pakistan as the flight’s final destination with further transport to Afghanistan. They then filed a renewed emergency motion to block his removal on an ICE charter flight to Pakistan, arguing he had received “no meaningful notice or opportunity” to raise fears of persecution there.

Akbari’s attorneys have also expressed concerns that he might be sent to a third country in Africa where he would also face imminent danger, they said. That’s because the government hasn’t stated that any direct flight to Afghanistan is planned, court records state.

“Neither Afghanistan or Africa are good options, but in Afghanistan he could at least defend himself in his own language,” Drake, of the UNM School of Law, said. “It’s hard to say that he’d prefer that, but he has a lot more fear of being sent to another country.”

Human Rights First said its research shows individuals returned to Afghanistan “face grave, systematic dangers, including arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence.”

The organization said reports from attorneys also indicate the Trump administration may soon send a deportation flight forcing Iranians back to Iran – the fourth since 2025 and the first since the start of the Iran war in February.

“By creating arrangements with countries such as Kuwait, Qatar, and now Pakistan, the Trump administration is effectuating removals to active war zones and severe security crises where individuals may be at grave risk,” Uzra Zeya, president and CEO of Human Rights First, said in a statement.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) reported use of city-owned parking lots to stage immigration enforcement operations without the city's authorization.

In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations," which the mayor said is unauthorized and illegal.

DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

title: US lawmakers ask Trump administration to stop deportation of Afghans - Al Jazeera
description:
The Trump administration has forcibly sent at least 25,000 people to third countries, according to a tally by nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First.
Since taking office, Trump has attempted to put an end to resettlement programmes for Afghans started by former President Joe Biden.
The Trump administration has instituted record-low quotas for asylum applications globally.
Trump ordered a halt to processing applications from Afghans after a man from Afghanistan allegedly shot two National Guardsmen in Washington, DC, in November 2025.
The Trump administration also included Afghan nationals in a blanket visa ban earlier this year, saying it would review immigration applications filed by anyone from the country.
text:
A group of 66 lawmakers in the United States has written to the administration of President Donald Trump asking it to halt a planned mass deportation of Afghans, including some who worked alongside coalition forces in Afghanistan before the military withdrawal in 2021.

In Monday’s letter, the lawmakers cited advocacy group reports that at least 150 Afghans were scheduled to be deported from Tuesday – flown from detention facilities in Louisiana to Pakistan.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Outrage as Afghan asylum seeker who fought alongside US dies in ICE custody

list 2 of 3Biden administration shields Afghans in US from deportation

list 3 of 3Afghan Adjustment Act: What does it mean for refugees in US?

end of list

The Associated Press news agency also reported that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials had said in court filings that they eventually planned on returning some of the Afghans to their home country.

The US does not have diplomatic relations with Afghanistan, which has been governed by the Taliban since US troops withdrew in August 2021.

“Sending dozens of people back to one of the most dangerous countries on earth, and where they are likely to be targeted for their or their family’s suspected support of the US government or criticism of the Taliban, is a death sentence,” the lawmakers wrote in the letter addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin.

“Our country made a promise never to abandon the Afghans who sacrificed their own and their family’s safety to stand with American service members.”

Third-country deportations

As part of its crackdown on immigration, the Trump administration has made agreements with at least 35 countries to take in third-country nationals, in many cases because it cannot send them back to their home countries for fear they would be tortured, killed, or otherwise persecuted.

Critics of the practice have said it undermines decades of global humanitarian norms around asylum seeker and refugee protection. They say deportees often end up in countries with a record of human rights abuses, or places that are so dangerous the US tells its own citizens not to travel there.

The Trump administration has forcibly sent at least 25,000 people to third countries, according to a tally by nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First.

Human Rights First said it has confirmed that a flight carrying some of the Afghans from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan is scheduled for Tuesday.

Rights advocates say the batch of deportations to Pakistan may also include Iranians, small numbers of whom the Trump administration has previously sent to third countries to eventually be returned to Iran, despite the ongoing war the US is waging on the country.

Pakistan has deported millions of Afghans to Afghanistan in recent years, as relations with the Taliban have deteriorated.

Afghans in US left in limbo

Most of the Afghans scheduled for deportation did not have the opportunity to properly fight their removal in court, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the AfghanEvac advocacy group, said.

“They were placed into removal proceedings because they didn’t have attorneys to fight,” he said.

VanDiver said he spoke to one man on Monday, a former police officer in the Afghan government toppled by the Taliban, who expected to be deported and feared for his life if he ended up back in Afghanistan. Others, VanDiver said, had also either worked in the Afghan government or with the US, or had family that did so, and would be in danger in Afghanistan.

Since taking office, Trump has attempted to put an end to resettlement programmes for Afghans started by former President Joe Biden. More than 120,000 Afghans were evacuated from Afghanistan in 2021 after the chaotic withdrawal of US forces.

Some ended up in facilities abroad, like in Qatar. This September, the US granted a nine-month extension for Camp As Sayliyah, a facility in Qatar housing more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted US forces in Afghanistan.

Afghans evacuated to the US were initially granted humanitarian parole, allowing them to stay in the country. In 2022, the Biden administration granted them Temporary Protected Status for 18 months, allowing them to live and work legally in the US after their parole period expired, and while their immigration status was resolved.

But since then, few Afghans in the US have been able to move their applications for asylum, or other special protected status relating to their work with coalition forces, through the severely backlogged immigration system.

“These people are in dire straits; they have been stuck in this limbo for five years, waiting for permanency, waiting for green cards, waiting to hear about their status,” VanDiver said.

The Trump administration has instituted record-low quotas for asylum applications globally. However, he made an exception for white Afrikaners from South Africa, giving them sanctuary after alleging they had faced racial discrimination against white people.

Trump ordered a halt to processing applications from Afghans after a man from Afghanistan allegedly shot two National Guardsmen in Washington, DC, in November 2025. The Trump administration also included Afghan nationals in a blanket visa ban earlier this year, saying it would review immigration applications filed by anyone from the country. Both policies were challenged in court.

Many Tennesseans, including Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, have consequently been denied temporary drivers licenses when they tried to renew them.
“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” said Peter McGraw, Legal Deputy Director of the National Immigration Law Center.

text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — The National Immigration Law Center, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition (“TIRRC”), and Bass Berry & Sims PLC, filed a lawsuit today challenging a new rule from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security (TDOS) that blocks many non-U.S. citizens from getting temporary driver’s licenses, even when they have authorization from the federal government to be present in the U.S.

For many years, TDOS issued temporary driver’s licenses to Tennesseans who could show they had permission from the federal government to be in the country. TDOS routinely accepted work permits and other federal government documents as proof of a person’s legal stay in the U.S. for a period of time.

However, in recent weeks, TDOS abruptly changed that policy. Under its new rule, TDOS only issues driver’s licenses to certain non-U.S. citizens who can present a valid visa, I-94, I-94W, or a temporary green card. The new rule excludes thousands of people living in Tennessee with federal authorization who have relied for decades on the agency’s prior practice. The lawsuit also argues that TDOS made this change without following proper legal steps, overstepped its authority, and failed to give the public a chance to provide input.

Many Tennesseans, including Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, have consequently been denied temporary drivers licenses when they tried to renew them. Most didn’t learn about the new rule until they were already at the Driver Services Center offices. As a result, Plaintiffs and many other people are without the ability to drive, making it harder for them to go to work, take their children to school, and manage their daily lives. For many, losing the ability to drive also threatens their livelihoods and ability to support their families.

“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” said Peter McGraw, Legal Deputy Director of the National Immigration Law Center. “TDOS issued its new driver’s license policies without first seeking community input or approval, and a state agency must consult the public before implementing extreme policies that affect all of us. Tennesseans should be able to drive safely and freely, and we look forward to putting driver’s licenses back in the hands of people who depend on them.”

The lawsuit asks the court to block the new rule and require TDOS to return to its previous process for issuing temporary driver’s licenses.

“Regardless of where they were born, Tennesseans rely on the ability to drive in order to work, care for their families, and access the basic needs of life – groceries, medical appointments, their children’s education. The plaintiffs in this action, like so many others across the state, have found their lives upended by the state’s abrupt rule change, which was implemented without warning or explanation” stated Spring Miller, Senior Legal Strategy Director at TIRRC. “This is why we are taking legal action. All Tennesseans expect to be treated fairly before the law, and expect their own government to follow it too.”

text:
[co-author: Katie Applebaum]*

On September 18, 2026, President Trump issued a proclamation extending the $100,000 supplemental payment requirement imposed on employers filing certain H-1B visa petitions through September 21, 2027. The Trump administration previously imposed the steep H-1B fee in September 2025, but a federal court in Massachusetts vacated the fee policy and blocked USCIS from collecting the fee in June of this year. Less than two weeks after the extension, on September 30, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California issued a second order blocking the fee. As a result, employers are not currently required to pay the $100,000 fee, but the government has appealed, and further developments are likely.

Background: The $100,000 H-1B Fee and Ensuing Litigation

On September 19, 2025, President Trump issued a proclamation imposing a $100,000 “supplemental payment” on employers submitting petitions for new H-1B visas. Notably, the fee did not apply to H-1B petitions for change of status, extension of status, or change of employers. USCIS collected the $100,000 H-1B fee for approximately ten months until federal litigation halted enforcement.

On June 8, 2026, a federal judge vacated the $100,000 fee requirement, holding that the payment functions as a tax rather than as a permissible fee. The court reasoned that the Immigration and Nationality Act does not grant the President power to levy taxes and that the taxing power resides exclusively with Congress under the Constitution.

On June 12, 2026, the court temporarily stayed its order to allow the government to appeal and to give the appellate court time to rule on the government’s request for a stay of the June 8 decision. During this brief window, USCIS resumed collecting the fee.

On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit dissolved the stay, effectively reinstating the district court’s order and once again blocking USCIS from collecting the fee. The government has appealed the First Circuit’s decision, but the court has not yet issued a final ruling on the merits. USCIS has indicated that it intends to collect the fee retroactively if the order is reversed on appeal.

Trump Administration Extends the $100,000 Fee Despite Court Order

On September 18, 2026, President Trump issued the “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers” proclamation, extending the $100,000 H-1B fee for an additional twelve months. The proclamation states that the extension was necessary in the interest of national security, asserting that the current administration of the H-1B program without the supplemental payment poses a “threat to the labor market that would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.”

Because the administration’s policies implementing the fee had already been vacated in the Massachusetts litigation, many immigration law practitioners expected the fee to remain blocked, but there was concern that USCIS would argue that the new proclamation fell outside the scope of the existing order. However, the Northern District of California’s recent decision in Global Nurse Force v. Trump has resolved much of that uncertainty.

U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California Blocks the Fee and Its Extension

On September 30, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted, in part, a motion for preliminary injunction in Global Nurse Force v. Trump, Case No. 4:25-cv-08454 (N.D. Cal. 2026). The lawsuit was filed in October 2025 by a coalition of labor unions, employers, and nonprofit organizations.

According to U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam, Jr., the extension violates key provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA): “There is no question here that Agency Defendants failed to consider any alternatives or the reliance interests of the regulated parties. As such, Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claim that the Agency Policies are arbitrary and capricious.”

The court prohibited USCIS from enforcing or implementing the fee policies until the required notice-and-comment rulemaking and regulatory flexibility analyses have been conducted. The government has appealed this decision.

What This Means for Employers

The fee, including the extension, is blocked. Two federal courts have now barred the government from collecting the $100,000 H-1B fee, and the Northern District of California’s order expressly covers the September 2026 extension. Employers are not currently required to submit the $100,000 payment with new H-1B petitions.

A similar fee could return through rulemaking. The California order bars enforcement only until agencies complete notice-and-comment rulemaking and the required small-business analysis. DHS’s separate, pending proposal for a $103,265 H-1B cap fee suggests that the administration may pursue a different path. The current proposal does not appear to impact “cap exempt” entities, but the rule language could change during the notice and comment process.

The legal landscape could change. The California litigation is far from over – the government has already appealed the preliminary injunction to the Ninth Circuit. Until the appellate courts weigh in, employers should treat the current reprieve as temporary. USCIS has indicated it intends to collect the fee retroactively if the fee is reinstated on appeal.
