title: Deportation Judges: Executive Capture of the Immigration Court | Yale Law Journal
description:
This Essay analyzes recent changes to immigration courts in light of the scholarship concerning the purposes and impact of courts in authoritarian systems, concluding that the Trump Administration’s immigration courts reflect a slippage into authoritarianism.
Last, the Board has revamped substantive immigration law to make it more difficult to obtain relief in immigration court.
Part II analyzes recent changes to immigration courts in light of the scholarship concerning the purposes and impact of courts in authoritarian systems, concluding that the Trump Administration’s immigration courts reflect a slippage into authoritarianism.
C. Making Deportation Judges Historically, the goal of immigration courts has been to provide a system for fairly and accurately deciding deportation cases.
A growing consensus of scholars favors the creation of an independent Article I immigration court similar to the Tax Court.
text:
abstract. Recent changes to immigration courts have transformed them from tribunals organized around evidentiary adjudication to immigration-enforcement collaborators. This shift can be seen in the adoption of summary removal policies, the rise of in absentia orders of removal, and the decrease in evidentiary hearings. These changes have begun to collapse the distinction between expedited-removal proceedings, which historically only applied to noncitizens apprehended near the border soon after entrance, and immigration-court cases for noncitizens in the interior, which traditionally involved greater due-process protections, including evidentiary hearings.

The Trump Administration has achieved this change by radically reworking immigration-court procedures and substantive immigration law through Board of Immigration Appeals and Attorney General precedential decisions and Executive Office for Immigration Review policy memoranda. The changes both streamline removal proceedings and make it harder for noncitizens to win relief. In addition, the Administration has purged the corps of immigration judges and hired replacements consisting largely of former military lawyers, lawyers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and other prosecutors. Tellingly, in its recruitment materials, the Administration refers to the position as “Deportation Judge.” These Deportation Judges have presided over a sharp decline in grant rates for asylum and other relief and a sharp rise in deportation orders.

It is not normal in a democratic system for a president to tell judges how to decide cases, even when it comes to courts housed in executive agencies. Decisional independence is critical for the rule of law, the separation of powers, and the protection of individual rights. Indeed, court manipulation is normal in authoritarian systems, where courts serve to enforce social control, legitimize the system, and delegate controversial reforms to judicial institutions. This Essay analyzes recent changes to immigration courts in light of the scholarship concerning the purposes and impact of courts in authoritarian systems, concluding that the Trump Administration’s immigration courts reflect a slippage into authoritarianism. Relatedly, it considers how to approach immigration-court reform from a transitional-justice framework. The Essay presents a proposal for a path forward that establishes judicial independence, copes with the large backlog of immigration-court cases generated by heightened immigration enforcement, and reckons with an era of immigration injustice.

Introduction

In June 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved to dismiss thousands of removal cases pending before the immigration courts. DHS is the prosecutor in immigration courts, which are housed in the Department of Justice (DOJ) and presided over by immigration judges (IJs) who are DOJ employees. In many immigration-court cases, DHS made the motion for the first time in open court, surprising the noncitizen respondent, who likely assumed that the dismissal of their removal case would benefit them. However, DHS’s intent was not to abandon its removal efforts, but to detain and remove these noncitizens much more quickly and with less due process. Instead of immigration court, where noncitizens can seek forms of relief and pursue defenses, DHS transferred these noncitizens’ cases to “expedited removal,” a streamlined process in which DHS officials rapidly remove mandatorily detained noncitizens without a hearing and with minimal judicial review.

One of the noncitizens unexpectedly transferred from court proceedings to expedited removal—and subsequently to a detention center—was John Doe 1. He entered the United States at age nineteen and sought asylum before an immigration court in New York City. Because his father had died and his mother had neglected him, he also filed an application for a benefit called Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS) that provides a pathway to permanent residency for abused, abandoned, and neglected immigrant children. With the hope of earning his high-school-equivalency diploma and eventually working in the medical field, he enrolled in English-language classes at the New York Public Library and a New York-based nonprofit organization called The Door. According to court filings by The Door, he appeared for a preliminary “master calendar” video hearing in June 2025 with a private attorney. However, the IJ ordered him to attend the hearing in person, so he appeared in court later that day. At that hearing, the DHS attorney moved to dismiss the case, and the IJ granted the motion. Immediately afterward, DHS arrested John Doe 1 and placed him in expedited removal where he would be held in detention and unable to seek forms of relief like SIJS.

John Doe 1’s case was one of 6,210 cases in which Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) filed motions to dismiss from May 20, 2025, to July 28, 2025. Most of these motions were granted the same day they were made. These dismissals are emblematic of a larger shift in immigration-court culture and procedure. They reflect a transition from a court organized around evidentiary adjudication to an immigration-enforcement collaborator. Part I of this Essay describes this shift, which has occurred through transfers to expedited removal, summary removal policies, an increase in in absentia orders of removal, and decreases in evidentiary hearings. This change has partially collapsed the distinction between expedited-removal proceedings, which historically applied only to noncitizens apprehended near the border soon after entrance, and immigration-court cases for noncitizens in the interior, which traditionally involved greater due-process protections, including evidentiary hearings. Even while shifting more noncitizens, like John Doe 1, from immigration court into expedited removal, the Trump Administration has also made immigration court itself more like expedited removal.

Several factors help explain this shift. First, the Trump Administration has purged the corps of IJs. In 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, 203 out of the approximately 735 IJs who were on the bench at the start of the Trump Administration were fired, retired, or resigned, with many taking advantage of early-retirement or deferred-resignation options. Moreover, from 2025 to the end of August 2026, about 338 new IJs were hired, amounting to a wholesale makeover of the IJ corps. About two-thirds of the replacements consist of judges with experience as officers or prosecutors for DHS, or military lawyers. Tellingly, in recruitment materials, the Administration has referred to the advertised position as “Deportation Judge.”

Second, the Administration has radically reworked immigration-court procedures through Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) and Attorney General (AG) precedential decisions and Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) policy memoranda. The new case law and policy memoranda encourage the summary dismissal of cases, reinforce EOIR hierarchy, and not-so-subtly signal to IJs that deportation is the preferred—indeed, expected—case outcome.

Third, EOIR has implemented new “court-based performance metrics,” which require the completion of cases on an expedited time frame—sixty days for detained cases and one year for nondetained cases. Relatedly, it has rescinded a memo stating that it would facilitate pro bono legal services, for example, by cooperating in scheduling with law-school clinics or helping immigrant children obtain representation. Last, the Board has revamped substantive immigration law to make it more difficult to obtain relief in immigration court.

These changes have transformed IJs from neutral decision-makers into “Deportation Judges.” EOIR’s own statistics reveal a shift that is so stark that it strongly suggests that the Trump Administration, through its hirings, firings, performance metrics, case-management policies, and substantive legal changes, has dictated IJs’ decisions.

It is not normal in a democratic system for a president to tell judges how to decide cases, even when it comes to courts housed in executive agencies. Rather, decisional independence is critical to the rule of law, the separation of powers, and the protection of individual rights. Courts, in societies that prioritize these principles, serve the purpose of independently deciding cases based on the law and facts applicable to the case. In contrast, in authoritarian systems, courts serve to enforce social control, legitimize the system, and delegate controversial reforms to judicial institutions. Part II analyzes recent changes to immigration courts in light of the scholarship concerning the purposes and impact of courts in authoritarian systems, concluding that the Trump Administration’s immigration courts reflect a slippage into authoritarianism.

IJs do not need to be Deportation Judges under the thumb of the Executive. Part III considers how to approach immigration-court reform from a transitional-justice framework, grounding its analysis in lessons learned from countries that have rehabilitated their institutions in the aftermath of authoritarian governance. It presents a proposal for a path forward for immigration courts that establishes judicial independence, copes with the large backlog of immigration-court cases generated by heightened immigration enforcement, and reckons with an era of immigration injustice.

I. courts as collaborators

In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, deportation cases were decided by nonlawyer officers who served as both the prosecutor and judge of the case. But by the middle of the twentieth century, this approach was inconsistent with the prevailing view that administrative adjudication impacting individual rights should come with some of the safeguards of courts, including a neutral decision-maker. In 1946, Congress adopted the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which required an impartial adjudicator in agency hearings, independent from the investigator or prosecutor. Soon afterward, Justice Jackson wrote that the requirement of a neutral judge seemed especially appropriate in immigration-court cases, which concerned “a voteless class of litigants who not only lack the influence of citizens, but who are strangers to the laws and customs in which they find themselves involved and who often do not even understand the tongue in which they are accused.” Congress clarified in 1951 that the APA did not apply to deportation proceedings, but incremental reforms eventually led to the same result: an adversarial immigration-court system, presided over by IJs who were part of a separate agency from the prosecutor.

In less than two years, the Trump Administration has largely reversed decades of reforms, creating a court system in which Deportation Judges collaborate with DHS to summarily deport noncitizens. It has achieved this sea change by purging IJs who do not deport enough noncitizens, pursuing policies to limit relief and facilitate summary removal, and instructing Deportation Judges to collaborate with the prosecutor to terminate removal proceedings so that noncitizens can be arrested in court and have their cases transferred to expedited removal. As IJs have become deportation collaborators, noncitizens fear showing up for court. The result has been a surge of in absentia removal orders, allowing the Administration to achieve through terror what it could not accomplish by law.

A. The Purge

The current adversarial system for immigration courts, with separate judges and prosecutors, developed gradually from an inquisitorial model. This shift has also been accompanied by a movement, until recently, for greater IJ professionalism and autonomy. That trend has come to a hard stop during the current Administration, which has fired judges based on how they have decided cases and replaced them with Deportation Judges, most of whom are former prosecutors, DHS officers, or military attorneys.

From the eighteenth through the late nineteenth century, state officers exercised considerable authority over immigration, but the 1891 Immigration Act empowered federal immigration officers to exclude noncitizens seeking entry into the United States. In 1893, Congress added an additional layer of review for exclusion cases by creating boards of special inquiry. These boards were staffed by immigration inspectors who could conduct further proceedings and overturn the initial inspector’s exclusion decision based on a vote of the board members. However, the boards did not adjudicate proceedings for noncitizens already in the United States, who could be deported based on the order of a single officer who served as both prosecutor and judge.

The 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) abolished the boards and replaced them with “Special Inquiry Officers” who, again, could serve as both prosecutor and judge for exclusion and deportation proceedings. But that system was in tension with trends toward reforming administrative courts to resemble Article III courts, and in 1956, DOJ made a prosecuting officer mandatory in every case in which deportability was contested. Moreover, in 1973, the regulations governing Special Inquiry Officers were amended to rename them as “Immigration Judges,” and some IJs began to wear robes. The IJs, however, were still housed in the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), which was also the prosecuting agency in deportation cases.

To create greater separation between prosecutor and adjudicator, in 1983, the AG created EOIR to house IJs in a new subagency within DOJ. In 2002, Congress erected further space between adjudication and prosecution by abolishing the INS and transferring immigration enforcement functions from DOJ to the newly created DHS, while leaving immigration adjudication in DOJ. Prosecutors were then part of a different cabinet-level agency, DHS, than IJs, who were part of DOJ.

Yet even under this revised structure, IJs remained under the control of the executive branch; they were not, by any stretch, part of independent courts. The governing statutes gave considerable power to the AG to appoint, supervise, and control IJs. Their decisions are subject to review not only by the BIA but also by the AG, who may self-certify BIA decisions for unilateral review. In theory, IJs are protected from arbitrary or discriminatory dismissal by the civil-service removal provisions of the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), but the Trump Administration contends that these protections conflict with the President’s authority to manage the executive branch under Article II of the Constitution. The Merit Systems Protection Board recently agreed that the CSRA is unconstitutional as applied to IJs, and that case is presently on appeal before the Federal Circuit.

The legal question of what, if any, protection IJs enjoy from arbitrary or discriminatory dismissal is significant because the Trump Administration has pursued a sweeping purge of the IJ corps. During the first day of the second Trump Administration, it dismissed senior EOIR leadership. Next, it began terminating Biden Administration IJ appointees who were still in their two-year probationary period. From 2025 through the first quarter of 2026, approximately 203 IJs have been dismissed, retired, or otherwise left service. Twelve immigration courts lost over half of the judges present at the beginning of the second Trump Administration. Those dismissed are almost entirely judges appointed by Democratic presidents, with backgrounds that include representation of immigrants and with higher asylum grant rates. Two judges were dismissed after they ruled in favor of international students placed in high-profile deportation proceedings based on their pro-Palestinian advocacy.

To replace these judges, the Trump Administration has installed about 338 new IJs as of August 27, 2026. About 262 of the appointments have been indefinite, around 87 have been temporary six-month appointments, and about 11 temporary appointments have been made indefinite. About two-thirds of the new judges have either DHS experience or military legal or judicial experience. In contrast, only about eleven of the new IJs have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience. That one IJ served for sixteen years as a Louisiana state prosecutor.

Being a former officer or prosecutor for DHS or military attorney does not necessarily guarantee that a judge will rule in a particular way. In at least one instance in which a newly appointed IJ (and former military lawyer) granted a high percentage of asylum claims, he was summarily dismissed. The dismissals and hirings reveal a pattern in which the Administration has dismissed IJs with higher asylum grant rates or a background viewed as immigrant friendly, replacing them with IJs with prior DHS or military service. If these new IJs do not fall into line, they too are dismissed, creating a chilling effect on any IJ who might be inclined to rule in favor of noncitizens.

B. The Border Is Everywhere

Immigration law has long offered dichotomous procedures for those at the border and interior, with greater protections for noncitizens in the interior who have resided in the United States long enough to have developed ties to the country. A more draconian version of the Constitution operates near the border, where courts have allowed law enforcement to target noncitizens with less protection from the Fourth Amendment and Due Process Clause. In keeping with this framework, Congress has created summary removal procedures, referred to as expedited removal, that the government has used for decades to deport noncitizens near the border without an evidentiary hearing. The Trump Administration, however, has increasingly brought the summary enforcement and adjudication practices of the border into immigration courts across the United States, applying them even to noncitizens with strong connections to the country.

All noncitizens in removal proceedings before immigration courts are entitled under the INA to an evidentiary hearing at which they have a right to obtain counsel (at their own expense) and to present evidence. However, the nature of these proceedings and the level of procedural fairness associated with them have varied over time. Even taking into account the diminished constitutional due-process standards in the immigration context, a host of federal-court judges, commentators, and nonprofit organizations have criticized the quality of immigration-court adjudication. For example, in a 2005 federal court opinion, Judge Posner cataloged cases in which IJs had engaged in speculation unsupported by the record, made logical errors, ignored key facts, used unfair procedures, and adopted an unprofessional or even abusive tone, concluding that “the adjudication of these cases at the administrative level has fallen below the minimum standards of legal justice.”

Soon after, EOIR undertook a new round of efforts to formalize its procedures and professionalize the corps of IJs. In 2006, AG Alberto R. Gonzales instructed the EOIR Director to create an Immigration Court Practice Manual, and in 2008, EOIR released the new manual. It set out a clear protocol for preliminary “master calendar hearings” for “pleadings, scheduling, and other similar matters,” as well as for the “[e]videntiary hearings on contested matters” that it called “individual calendar hearings” or “merits hearings.” In 2007, EOIR also revamped its Immigration Judge Benchbook, which it posted publicly in 2009.

Yet the growing professionalism of the immigration courts soon faced pressure from rising caseloads. Beginning around 2018, the number of respondents in removal proceedings filing “defensive” applications for asylum increased considerably. Asylum is a complex form of immigration relief, which requires the applicant to prove a well-founded fear of persecution on account of certain protected grounds. This complicated and fact-bound standard regularly resulted in immigration-court hearings that could last hours or days and involved multiple witnesses and difficult legal questions. As the number of asylum cases increased, the average life of an immigration-court case went from 685 days in 2017 to 925 days by 2021.

During President Trump’s first term, he pursued a series of policies designed to ramp up immigration enforcement and restrict the ability of noncitizens to seek asylum. One of the centerpieces of this immigration policy was the “Migrant Protection Protocols” (MPP), under which migrants arriving at the southwest border of the United States were returned to Mexico to wait for immigration-court hearings held in the United States near the border. As a result of the MPP, a de facto refugee camp cropped up near the border in Matamoros, Mexico. Forced to wait in chaotic and sometimes dangerous conditions, many MPP respondents never received notice of the time and date of their removal hearings, and over half were ordered deported in absentia after failing to attend.

Soon, however, the MPP became less relevant as the Trump Administration closed the border entirely to asylum seekers during the COVID-19 pandemic. After it was reopened, the number of new immigration-court cases and defensive asylum applications rose dramatically. Following his reelection, President Trump characterized the rise in cases as an “invasion” justifying radical new enforcement measures. While the first Trump Administration had centered its immigration policy around making asylum seekers wait outside the United States border, the second Trump Administration brought treatment typically reserved for those at the border into the United States interior.

1. Transfers to Expedited Removal

In 1996, Congress created a new process of “expedited removal” for those who could not prove that they had been in the United States for two or more years. These noncitizens could be deported by immigration-enforcement officers without any hearing and with minimal judicial review. But despite the sweeping scope of the expedited-removal provision, the government has historically limited its application, first applying it only at ports of entry and then, beginning in 2004, to those apprehended within 100 miles of the border who could not prove that they had been in the United States for longer than two weeks. Persons apprehended further from the border and residents of more than two weeks received standard immigration-court hearings with more procedural protections, consistent with the Supreme Court’s longstanding recognition of a right to procedural due process for persons being deported from the interior.

By 2016, expedited removal and other fast-track forms of removal had come to significantly supplant immigration court and comprise the majority of deportations from the United States. After taking office in 2017, President Trump sought to expand expedited removal even further—to its full statutory maximum of anywhere in the United States and to anyone who could not prove they had been present for two years or more. DHS attempted to do so in July of 2019, although the expansion was challenged in federal court and ultimately applied in only a small number of cases. The Biden Administration reversed the expansion, but after his reelection, Trump immediately ordered the reexpansion of expedited removal. To date, litigation has not succeeded in halting the nationwide expedited-removal regime.

In 2025, DHS and EOIR collaboratively pursued an effort to shift thousands of cases from immigration court to expedited removal. From late January through the end of May 2025, ICE issued a series of memos increasing ICE agents’ authority to apprehend noncitizens at courthouses and encouraging ICE lawyers to terminate pending removal cases in order to place noncitizens into expedited-removal proceedings.

EOIR collaborated with this effort. On Friday, May 30, 2025, EOIR leadership sent an email to Assistant Chief Immigration Judges around the United States, telling them that “DHS is carrying out enforcement actions in or near EOIR space. Further, DHS attorneys have moved to dismiss cases that are currently pending in court.” The email explained that noncitizens who had not been continuously present for two years before being charged with a notice to appear for removal proceedings were subject to expedited removal under Trump Administration policy and that, according to its interpretation of the regulations, DHS could move to dismiss removal proceedings upon the ground that “circumstances have changed to such an extent that continuation is no longer in the best interest of the government.” It stated that DHS attorneys could make oral motions to dismiss, which could be decided from the bench, and it admonished IJs to not reset cases for an oral decision, but to complete them immediately as “no additional documentation or briefing is required.” It noted that respondents who were shifted from removal proceedings into expedited removal could be subject to mandatory detention.

In the coming days, reporters described hundreds of arrests occurring at courthouses throughout the United States after DHS attorneys moved to dismiss removal cases based on the new Trump Administration policies. FOIA data obtained by the American Immigration Council documented 6,616 ICE motions to dismiss filed between May 1, 2025, and July 28, 2025. Some of those whose cases were dismissed, like John Doe 1 (described in the Introduction), were eligible for forms of relief that could not be pursued in expedited removal. Given how much was at stake, IJs could have required ICE attorneys to file written motions and given noncitizens time to respond and seek counsel if unrepresented. In some of the cases, like John Doe 1’s, granting ICE’s motions effectively foreclosed legal options or defenses. In those cases, the IJ’s grant of dismissal could raise due-process issues unless the IJ explained the implications of dismissal to the noncitizen and gave them a chance to object. Yet there is little evidence that Deportation Judges considered these issues when dismissing thousands of cases at ICE’s behest in mid-2025.

2. Summary Removal Policies

At the same time that immigration courts were collaborating with ICE to shift cases into expedited removal, the agency also reformed immigration-court procedures, making them more like expedited removal. In the first months of the Trump Administration, all nine of the members of the BIA who had been appointed by President Biden were removed. Since then, the BIA has issued a barrage of decisions narrowly interpreting immigration-law remedies, restricting procedural opportunities for noncitizens, empowering IJs to summarily dismiss cases, and signaling in various ways to IJs that removal is the preferable outcome.

EOIR has also issued policy memoranda at a breathtaking pace. There have already been fifty-eight EOIR policy memoranda issued during the second Trump Administration (as of September 22, 2026), as compared to thirty EOIR memoranda concerning immigration courts during the entire Biden Administration. Fourteen were issued in the first twelve days of President Trump’s second term. The memoranda adopt a series of measures clearly designed to truncate proceedings or otherwise expedite cases, and to signal to IJs that they are subordinate to agency policies and hierarchy. One memo rescinded prior initiatives to facilitate pro bono legal services, such as by cooperating in scheduling with law school clinics or helping immigrant children obtain representation.

One of the most significant reforms allows for the routine summary dismissal of asylum cases, which traditionally have received an evidentiary hearing in immigration court. EOIR has issued a policy memorandum permitting immigration courts to pretermit cases; that is, to deny an asylum claim without holding a hearing on the claim when the application is “legally deficient.” Simultaneously, the Board has issued a decision enhancing pleading requirements for asylum, making it more likely that cases will be found legally deficient.

The Board has also held that IJs can pretermit asylum claims based on the existence of “Asylum Cooperative Agreements” (ACAs). In 1996, Congress amended the INA to allow the government to deny asylum to individuals if they can be removed to a “safe third country” that has a formal agreement with the United States and has a fair process for adjudicating asylum or a related benefit. Initially, the only such agreement was with Canada, entered into via a 2002 treaty, and implemented essentially as a procedural rule limiting the ability of individuals to seek asylum in either country if they had passed through the other. However, the second Trump Administration has entered into ACAs with Belize, Cabo Verde, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Liberia, Paraguay, and Uganda, which have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims filed by persons in the United States. IJs have pretermitted thousands of asylum cases pursuant to these ACAs, despite the fact that many of these countries have nascent or ineffective asylum systems and questionable human rights practices. The safe third country statute requires the AG to consider whether the noncitizen “would have access to a full and fair procedure” in the third country and whether it is in “the public interest” for the noncitizen to receive asylum in the United States irrespective of the existence of the safe third country. However, the Board has foreclosed the possibility of IJs considering these issues in removal proceedings, raising a question as to whether noncitizens are receiving due process if they have no forum to litigate necessary factual predicates for applying the safe third country bar.

The Board has also issued a decision holding, contrary to decades of prior practice, that noncitizens who entered without inspection are ineligible for bond. Faced with mandatory detention, many noncitizens decide not to pursue claims that can take months or even years to work through, opting instead to stipulate to orders of removal or accept voluntary departure. Moreover, the ineligibility of persons who entered without inspection for bond means that IJs conduct far fewer bond hearings than previously—yet another way that IJs are deciding matters summarily rather than based on evidence. A circuit split has developed concerning whether the new approach violates the INA, and the Supreme Court has taken certiorari over the issue for this term.

3. In Absentia Orders

As a result of these changes, immigration court has shifted from an institution centered around factual adjudication to one focused on summary removal. In 2025, IJs entered 376,856 removal orders at master calendar hearings—the largest annual total since EOIR’s electronic records began and roughly a fourfold increase from 2018. Of those orders, 289,517, or 76.8%, were issued in absentia, without the respondent appearing at the scheduled hearing. In absentia removal orders at master calendar hearings have climbed every year since the pandemic-era trough of 2021, from 11,251 in 2021 to 289,517 in 2025. Some of the recent increase is likely due to ICE’s 2025 courthouse arrest policy and to widespread reports of noncitizens being detained at master calendar hearings and placed into expedited-removal proceedings, leading many noncitizens to fear attending court.

Recently, immigration courts have even begun holding “mega master calendar hearings” for pro se respondents, sometimes involving 100 or more respondents at a time. According to reports, the court conducts the hearing like a classroom roll call, issuing in absentia orders to everyone not present. With so many respondents in attendance at once, it is unlikely that an IJ could fulfill any of the traditional steps of a master calendar hearing, such as taking pleadings, setting call-up dates for evidence and briefs, scheduling an individual calendar hearing, evaluating competency or interpretation needs, providing resources to help identify counsel if unrepresented, and making sure the noncitizen is aware of the next steps in the case. Instead, these mass hearings are geared towards efficiently issuing in absentia removal orders.

4. Decreases in Individual Calendar Hearings

Individual calendar hearings (ICHs) are evidentiary hearings at which noncitizens can contest the government’s removal charges or seek relief like asylum, cancellation of removal, or adjustment of status that can lead to green cards. They can submit briefs and documentary evidence, testify, present witnesses, object to the government’s evidence, cross-examine opposing witnesses, and deliver opening and closing statements. Historically, a significant percentage of noncitizens won at these hearings. The share of completed cases with at least one ICH rose steadily from 24.4% in 2005 to a peak of 60.2% in 2018. This era coincided with the EOIR reforms that contributed to the professionalization of the immigration judiciary, including the revamping of the Immigration Judge Benchbook and the creation of the Immigration Court Practice Manual. However, there has recently been a decrease in the rate at which removal cases include an ICH. Specifically, the share of completed removal cases with at least one ICH has plummeted since 2018, about halfway through the first Trump Administration. Since 2018, the percentage of cases with at least one ICH has fallen precipitously to 25.7%, not far from its 2005 level of 24.4%. Most removal orders today are entered in cases that never had a merits hearing: in 2025 only 28.1% of cases in which a removal order was entered had an ICH, compared to 52.6% in 2018.

There are various possible explanations for the decreasing share of case completions with at least one merits hearing. Policies like the MPP and accelerated dockets during the first Trump Administration produced an increase in in absentia orders of removal without any ICH occurring. In absentia orders of removal decreased during the pandemic, but the number of ICHs also initially decreased due to pandemic-related disruptions. During the Biden years following the pandemic, in absentia orders of removal again began to increase. At the same time, many cases were terminated or dismissed as a result of prosecutorial-discretion policies that favored immigrants with long ties to the United States, without criminal records, and with other sympathetic factors. These policies, which were beneficial to many immigrants, may have also contributed to the continued trend away from case resolution through ICHs. From 2022 through 2024, total case completions increased much faster than the number of completed cases with an ICH, causing the share of completions with an ICH to fall from 43.7% to 27.7%.

The use of prosecutorial discretion to systematically terminate nonpriority removal cases ended sharply with the second Trump Administration, but the annual share of completions with an ICH has remained low. The summary removal policies discussed above likely contributed to the continued low share of case completions with an ICH.

The increase in removal orders at master calendar hearings and the falling share of cases with an ICH reflect a system in which most cases are now completed without any evidentiary hearing. Instead, today’s Deportation Judges increasingly decide cases in a summary fashion that is beginning to resemble the expedited-removal process designed for cases at the border.

II. courts as legitimators

Judicial independence has long been considered critical to the integrity of the United States’s political system. Historically, judicial independence has been considered important for maintaining separation of powers and for protecting minorities who are vulnerable in a majoritarian political process. The ability of judges to decide cases based on the facts and law, not the preferences of political leaders, is central to the rule of law. Ideally, judges are protected from political influence with job security, decent salaries, and judicial control of court administration. Commentators generally agree that even courts housed in administrative agencies should be able to decide cases free of political control.

In contrast, judicial independence and the rule of law can be threats to authoritarian systems. Nonetheless, countries with authoritarian governments have often maintained court systems to achieve a variety of goals, such as reassuring foreign investors and legitimating systems of repression and social control. To balance the threat and benefit of a judiciary, authoritarian governments use several means to tightly control judicial appointment, removal of judges, and court administration. The Trump Administration has drawn from some of this authoritarian playbook, purging the ranks of IJs and imposing new adjudicatory policies that have effectively dictated a radical shift in case outcomes.

A. The Purpose of Courts in Authoritarian Systems

Courts in authoritarian systems sometimes operate like courts in nonauthoritarian systems, for example, resolving disputes in ordinary matters involving property or contracts. This ongoing functioning can serve to assure investors, and the broader international community, that some version of the rule of law continues to exist. Yet courts in authoritarian systems may also help an authoritarian regime punish political opponents and monitor and discipline government agents. For example, in the Soviet Union, Stalin used Troika tribunals to sentence political opponents to execution or labor camps during the Great Terror of 1937-1938.

Additionally, authoritarian regimes use courts to provide cover for controversial or unpopular policies. Egyptian Supreme Constitutional Court (SCC) rulings enabled the government of Hosni Mubarak to overturn the socialist-oriented policies of the Nasser Era without drawing direct opposition from groups opposed to economic liberalization. Diverting controversial matters to courts can help authoritarian governments moderate dissent.

Relatedly, courts can bolster regime legitimacy. As Alexis de Tocqueville wrote, “[g]overnments in general have only two methods of overcoming the resistance of the governed: their own physical force and the moral force supplied to them by the decisions of the courts.” Courts legitimate authoritarianism by presenting a rule-of-law facade while sanctioning or refusing to intervene in the face of state oppression. This was the case, for example, in Chile under Pinochet, when Chile’s courts rejected almost all recursos de amparo, or challenges to confinement, abdicated review over the decisions of military tribunals, and rejected challenges to the constitutionality of military policies. Whether standing idly by in the face of oppression or presiding over show trials, courts offer symbolic authority that can support authoritarian governance and increase legitimacy in the eyes of the international community.

B. Methods of Manipulating Courts

On April 7, 1933, Adolf Hitler and two of his ministers enacted the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service. “Restoring” the civil service, for Nazi Germany, meant discriminating against judges and other civil servants based on their religion, ethnicity, and political views, as the law was a decree to purge non-Aryans and those with undesirable past political activity from positions in the Civil Service, including the judiciary. Although the Nazi law was a particularly brazen example, Germany’s attacks on judicial independence are not unique. More recently, Mexico, Poland, and Hungary have all politicized judicial appointments and limited the ability of the judiciary to self-govern. The tension between judicial independence and accountability is both a long-running and topical theme for democracies and authoritarian governments alike.

Legal theorists increasingly conceptualize authoritarianism and democracy as porous, with institutional forms sometimes migrating across regimes. Beginning with German legal theorist Ernst Fraenkel’s “dual state,” political scientists have discussed various forms of authoritarian-democratic hybridization, including “competitive authoritarianism,” “abusive constitutional borrowing,” “autocratic legalism,” and “democratic erosion.” Courts play a central role in this interplay between authoritarian and democratic forms. Depending on the culture and conditions surrounding courts, they can defend against or support democratic erosion and legitimate or resist authoritarianism.

Autocratic governments deploy various techniques to control their courts and to prevent them from becoming a base for political opposition. The most basic measures involve controlling the recruitment, appointment, training, retention, promotion, and removal of judges and the overall administration of courts. Hungary, both during the communist era from 1956-1988 under János Kádár and under Viktor Orbán from 2010-2026, offers a prime example of government manipulation of the judiciary. During the earlier period, the Communist Party controlled the appointment of court presidents, who in turn controlled the operation of courts, allocation of cases, and promotion of judges. Independent decision-making was constrained by rigid statutory law, the requirement that judges uphold “socialist legality,” the existence of a Communist Party–dominated “Coordination Committee” for overseeing criminal matters, and the ability of the President of the Supreme Court to take over and decide any court case at any time.

Democratic reforms in the 1980s brought greater judicial independence. However, a landslide election in 2010 gave power to Viktor Orbán and his Fidesz party, and afterward the government pursued what effectively amounted to a purge of the judiciary. It enacted constitutional and legislative reforms that forced out the President of the Supreme Court and required that about 10% of serving judges retire. The President of the National Office for the Judiciary gained wide-ranging powers to control the administration of the courts, and the new constitution imposed binding methods of legal interpretation on judges.

Cooperation between the military and judiciary is common in authoritarian systems, which in some cases have replaced ordinary courts with military courts, and in other instances have staffed courts with both members of the military and judges. For example, the António de Oliveira Salazar regime in Portugal created special military tribunals in 1933 to judge political crimes, although the military adjudicators were later replaced with civilian judges. The Brazilian (1964-1985) and Chilean (1973-1990) military regimes likewise used military courts, with Brazil’s courts incorporating both military and civilian judges.

Another common technique of manipulation is to create what Tamir Moustafa calls “fragmented judicial systems.” In these fragmented systems, independent courts exist alongside special courts for politically sensitive cases, where “the executive retains tight controls through non-tenured political appointments, heavily circumscribed due process rights, and retaining the ability to order retrials if it wishes.” Historical examples of fragmented courts include multiple types of special courts in Francoist Spain, military courts in Brazil from 1964 to 1985, Emergency State Security Courts and military courts in Egypt, the Tribunale Speciale per la Sicurezza dello Stato in Fascist Italy, and the Tribunais Plenários under Salazar in Portugal.

C. Making Deportation Judges

Historically, the goal of immigration courts has been to provide a system for fairly and accurately deciding deportation cases. As President Eisenhower wrote to Congress after the passage of the INA, deportation proceedings give noncitizens their “day in court.” The immigration courts also offer a backstop against mistakes, such as the erroneous deportation of a citizen. EOIR under the Trump Administration espouses a similar mission “to adjudicate immigration cases by fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly interpreting and administering the Nation’s immigration laws.”

However, recent statistics belie the Administration’s professed commitment to fairness. Asylum denial rates in immigration courts have grown from 61% in January 2025 at the beginning of the Trump Administration to 94% in July 2026. Removal orders went from 32,848 in the month of January 2025 to 77,234 in August 2026—a 135% increase. Evidentiary adjudication in general has declined as the agency has focused on summary procedures, with most removal orders today being issued in cases that never had a merits hearing.

In its recent memoranda, EOIR has repeatedly emphasized the importance of efficiency. The statistics concerning asylum denials and removal orders suggest that Deportation Judges are efficiently doing one thing: issuing removal orders. It has become difficult to even get an evidentiary hearing in immigration court, let alone win it. At the beginning of the Trump Administration, nearly a third (30%) of asylum applicants won their immigration court cases; in July 2026, only 5.19%, or approximately one out of every nineteen applicants, won. Formally, DOJ’s immigration courts are separate from DHS, the prosecuting agency for removal cases, but functionally, Deportation Judges seem to be committed to DHS’s mission of removing noncitizens from the United States as efficiently as possible.

The Trump Administration has achieved these outcomes by adopting many of the methods of court manipulation used in authoritarian systems like Hungary under Viktor Orbán and János Kádár. It has stripped IJs of civil-service job protections; purged IJs with higher relief rates and replaced them with DHS officers, former prosecutors, and military lawyers; arrested court attendees and summarily deported them outside the court process; and issued decisions and memoranda reinforcing hierarchy and restricting IJs’ ability to grant relief to noncitizens. Its measures to purge and replace IJs and tightly control court procedures resemble Hungary under Orbán, which forced out the President of the Supreme Court and required that about 10% of serving judges retire. The Administration’s heavy reliance on Judge Advocate General or former military lawyers for its Deportation Judges recalls authoritarian systems like Brazil that heavily incorporated military officers into civilian court systems.

Immigration courts under the Trump Administration closely resemble “fragmented” court systems like those in certain authoritarian regimes like Francoist Spain. There, relatively independent courts existed alongside highly controlled ones for deciding politically sensitive cases. As in those fragmented systems, Deportation Judges are tightly controlled by the executive branch and noncitizens’ due-process rights have been circumscribed. The use of immigration courts to pursue deportation charges based on speech calls to mind the use of fragmented courts like the Tribunal de Orden Público in Francoist Spain, which handled cases including speech-based offenses such as sedition, public disturbance, and illegal propaganda. The Trump Administration has similarly used immigration courts to attempt to deport noncitizens for their speech, like Mahmoud Khalil, who was charged with removal for his pro-Palestinian advocacy under an extraordinarily vague and broad provision allowing for the removal of any noncitizen whose “presence or activities in the United States . . . would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States,” as determined by the Secretary of State.

Just as in those systems, Deportation Judges exist in a larger landscape that includes an independent judiciary. A notable difference, however, between immigration courts and other fragmented court systems is that noncitizens retain the ability to seek judicial review of immigration-court decisions by federal courts. In some cases, circuit courts operate as a meaningful check on severe due-process violations. However, Congress has progressively restricted federal judicial review of removal decisions, and court-invented restrictions further limit federal court intervention. Without representation, noncitizens rarely appeal to the BIA, let alone the federal court of appeals. BIA appeals have also become extremely difficult to win and very expensive, yet it is not possible to appeal to federal court without first exhausting administrative remedies with a BIA appeal. Relatedly, detention markedly limits noncitizens’ ability to obtain legal representation or otherwise support their case, for example through the collection of evidence. The number of noncitizens in detention has increased as a result of the Trump Administration’s policies, leaving even fewer noncitizens able to challenge their removal orders with federal litigation.

Although immigration courts appear to be collaborating with the prosecuting agency for removal cases, they nonetheless offer legitimacy to the system. IJs are not just deportation collaborators; they are deportation legitimators, lending the gravitas of a formal court system to a policy of mass deportation and lulling the public into believing that removals are being conducted with appropriate care and caution. In contrast to expedited removal, which is administered by immigration officers, Deportation Judges lend the trappings of a judicial system to removal while generating similar outcomes.

At the same time, the overall statistical record, the Board’s published decisions, EOIR’s policy memoranda, media reports of courthouse arrests, and the appointment of military lawyers as IJs all strongly resonate with the Administration’s pro-enforcement immigration policies. Therefore, immigration courts not only legitimate deportation through a judicial process; they also promote a pro-enforcement immigration policy, a function that is underscored by IJs’ retitling as “Deportation Judges.” This public relations aspect of the immigration courts might be important, given that the Administration is far from its stated goal of deporting all undocumented immigrants from the United States. Thus, Deportation Judges stand today as an effective rebuke both to anyone who might question whether the Administration is pursuing removal to the maximum extent and to anyone who might question whether the Administration is pursuing removal with fairness and care.

In this sense, the President’s Deportation Judges serve a political purpose in addition to a legal one. They mobilize the supporters of the Administration’s immigration policies by offering evidence that it is faithfully pursuing removal. For those who might be ambivalent about mass deportation, immigration courts authenticate the Administration’s policies with the imprimatur of a judicial process. For noncitizens, widespread reports of arrests and routinized removal orders in court discourage any effort to mount a defense.

Adherents of a strong version of the unitary-executive theory might argue that all this is appropriate for a court system housed within the executive branch and staffed by judges who serve at the pleasure of the AG, rather than a concerning slip into authoritarianism. Under one version of this theory, the President has the ability to cancel or supplant the decisions of inferior officers, including adjudications, because Article II vests all executive power in the President. Unitary-executive theorists might view the President’s power to dictate outcomes in immigration courts as an asset: the President can act quickly in response to changing circumstances and is politically accountable to the electorate. Some might also point to the President’s sweeping authority over foreign affairs and arguably plenary power over immigration law as additional justifications for presidential domination over immigration courts.

However, the Constitution is not just a document about power allocation; it also creates a set of rights and responsibilities. The President is not only vested with executive power but also has a duty to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” Ultimately, it is Congress, not the President, which has legislated immigration law. Congress passed the INA, which mandates a system for adjudicating removal cases through evidentiary hearings at which noncitizens have rights. When Congress has acted to create a system for adjudicating outcomes, an effort by the Executive to dictate those outcomes subverts Congress, raises separation-of-powers concerns, and is inconsistent with the Take Care Clause.

The prioritization of mass deportation at the cost of fair adjudication also implicates the due-process rights of noncitizens. In contrast to adjudication, the political process cannot adequately protect important personal interests against majoritarian preferences. That is particularly the case in an administrative system like immigration courts, which decide cases involving a discrete and insular minority who enjoy limited political participation. It is for this reason that Justice Robert Jackson held in 1950 that noncitizens have a right to a neutral decision-maker. The President’s Deportation Judges exist in fundamental tension with that commitment.

III. rehabilitating courts

The systemic capture of immigration courts to serve as deportation collaborators may not be a holocaust, a guerra sucia, or a killing field. But the immigrants whose cases have been heard by Deportation Judges deserved better. The asylum applicants whose cases, in recent months, have been overwhelmingly denied almost all fled some form of threat or violence before coming to the United States. Many were survivors of rape, beatings, detention, and torture. Others were children who have been abused, neglected, and abandoned, making them eligible for SIJS had they been given time to pursue that process. There are a host of other immigration defenses and remedies that might have received serious attention from IJs in another era, but that have been given short shrift by Deportation Judges. Win or lose, all removal cases deserve a fair process. The construction of a system designed to turn a blind eye to these claims is an affront to the rule of law and an abdication of the United States’s commitments under international humanitarian law. It raises the question of how to move forward in the wake of a trauma that has not only impacted deported noncitizens, but their families, communities, and the nation as a whole.

Change from authoritarian regimes begins with resistance. In time, resistance can lead to reform and a search for transitional justice—“the conception of justice associated with periods of political change, characterized by legal responses to confront the wrongdoings of repressive predecessor regimes.” Courts have sometimes played a role in resistance to authoritarianism: court cases can galvanize supporters and generate media attention and international scrutiny. This Part describes the role that courts can play in resistance to authoritarianism in the short term, and proposes that in the long term, meaningful reform should incorporate a transitional-justice approach into preexisting recommendations for immigration-court reform. That approach contextualizes reform alongside the harms that have occurred, the claims they have generated, and the political constraints of transition. It does not supply easy answers but offers a set of considerations and a holistic process involving impacted communities.

A. Resistance and Immigration Courts

The political-science literature concerning courts reveals that they can be captured and used as an agent for democratic erosion. However, in other cases, courts can be sites of resistance to authoritarianism. Tamir Moustafa explains that courts in authoritarian systems “never advance the interests of authoritarian rulers in a straightforward manner. Rather, courts inevitably serve as dual-use institutions, simultaneously consolidating the functions of the authoritarian state while paradoxically opening new avenues for activists to challenge regime policy.” Moustafa describes how the Anwar Sadat regime allowed for the creation of the SCC in Egypt as a device to encourage foreign investment, but afterward it also became a venue for human-rights activists to challenge political oppression.

Immigration-court cases have become extraordinarily difficult for noncitizens to win, but immigrants and their advocates can appeal, publicize, and organize around them as part of a strategy on behalf of individual clients or a broader resistance movement. High-profile immigration-court cases have generated litigation, protests, media attention, and political-organizing campaigns. This environment offers reason to believe that the capture of immigration courts not only makes them a possible starting point for authoritarian drift, but also a site of resistance.

B. Transitional Justice and Reform

Like a skin cancer that has metastasized, the severe immigration enforcement environment of the border has now spread throughout the United States and into immigration courts, challenging basic presumptions about courts and the rule of law. It is not just noncitizens and their families who have been harmed but concerned citizens who have watched the degradation of the justice system with horror. Transitional justice grapples with the question of how best to restore faith in civil society in the wake of mass wrongdoing: with truth commissions, punishment, dialogue, restitution, reparations, or something new?

Transitional justice, in different times and places, has drawn on international legal norms as well as the realities of a country’s transitional political context to develop a response to past wrongdoing. In some cases, such as the post–World War II era, it has involved prosecutions before international tribunals; in others, such as South Africa, the political context has led to decisions that prioritize truth-seeking, peace, and restorative measures over prosecutions. Transitional justice is holistic, offering a range of approaches to restore public trust, depending both on what happened and what response is politically feasible.

Retributive measures to address the harms caused by Deportation Judges would be problematic because they occurred under color of law, were often inflicted by actors who sincerely believed in what they were doing, responsibility for them is highly diffuse, and such efforts would be politically near impossible. Rather, the most meaningful remedy for noncitizens impacted by Deportation Judges would be to create a system that gives them a legitimate chance to make their case. There is no shortage of thought that has already been put into the reform of immigration courts. A growing consensus of scholars favors the creation of an independent Article I immigration court similar to the Tax Court. Rather than being housed in an executive-branch agency and subject to complete executive oversight, an Article I court would be created by Congress and would involve an unbiased appointment process and built-in protections for its judges.

Scholars and policymakers have already developed reasonable blueprints for an Article I immigration court. But recent developments make it necessary to reconsider reform from a transitional justice perspective. The use of authoritarian methods to capture immigration courts to legitimize mass deportation raises unique issues that ought to be addressed. What should be done with the current corps of Deportation Judges, hand selected to pave the path to removal? Should they be grandfathered into IJ positions on a new Article I immigration court, allowed to compete for them, or prohibited from holding them? What should happen with the body of case law and policy memoranda that has developed during the Trump Administration that has created and enabled the current state of affairs?

And what about the backlog of 3.1 million cases pending before immigration courts? The backlog is at least partly a creation of harsh enforcement policies while also being a justification for the summary removal procedures implemented by the Trump Administration. Strict immigration enforcement precipitates a never-ending emergency that justifies the abandonment of due process and the funneling of more cases into expedited-removal processes outside immigration court. At the same time, the continued existence of immigration courts, which give the semblance of greater due process, offers token legitimacy to a system that has drifted far from the rule of law. As long as a broken immigration court exists, it offers a rebuttal to any attempt to make something better.

The answers to these questions are not easy, but transitional justice supplies a framework for answering them: a holistic and collective process that balances justice alongside reconciliation. What is needed is not just reform, but a focus on rehabilitation drawn from the literature on transitional justice. Postauthoritarian societies have rebuilt their judicial systems, reworked their substantive law, appointed new judges, and developed mechanisms for reconsidering the past judgments of authoritarian courts. In the wake of Argentina’s military dictatorship, for example, the Argentinian Congress passed a bill that created a habeas corpus remedy through which civilians sentenced by military courts could seek to have their sentences nullified by civil courts. Subsequently, Argentina also granted jurisdiction to the civilian Cámara Federal de Apelaciones to review military judgments. After reunification, Germany similarly passed the Strafrechtliches Rehabilitierungsgesetz, or Criminal Rehabilitation Act of November 1992, “allow[ing] for the annulment of verdicts and other judicial decisions of the Soviet occupation zone and the [German Democratic Republic], as far as they [were] inconsistent with the rule of law.” What these efforts have in common is recognition that the judgments of authoritarian courts are potentially unsound and that persons affected by these decisions should have an opportunity to have them reconsidered.

Along those lines, a transitional justice approach should focus not only on remaking immigration courts, but on creating a mechanism to reconsider judgments and addressing the substantive law that has contributed to the cycle of mass enforcement and summary removal. Immigration law already allows for reopening removal cases in some circumstances, but a broader remedy could be created as seen in Argentinian and German laws. Congress would need to explicitly address the circumstances under which a noncitizen with a removal order could seek reopening and, potentially, return to the United States, including the timeline for filing the motion and the legal standard for prevailing.

Moving forward, a different standard for adjudicating some immigration-court cases might be developed based on transitional-justice principles. There is one domestic parallel that offers a model. In the 1980s, the United States government routinely coerced Central American refugees into taking voluntary departure and denied approximately 97% of their asylum claims, while granting asylum at relatively high rates for noncitizens fleeing other countries. This unfair treatment provoked lawsuits and, in time, a political accounting. First, a court-ordered settlement in the American Baptist Churches v. Thornburgh (ABC) case required the government to reopen and give de novo reconsideration to Salvadoran and Guatemalan migrants’ previously denied asylum cases. Subsequently, Congress’s passage of the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act (NACARA) created streamlined procedures for favorably adjudicating some Central American cases, a form of recompense for the adjudicatory failures of the 1980s. The government worked through a heavy volume of cases afterward, granting a high percentage of them.

This came about as a result of the sanctuary movement and the political advocacy, litigation, and persistence of activists, lawyers, religious leaders, and, most importantly, immigrants themselves. Their sustained campaign brought refuge, at last, to a population that had fled devastating political violence only to face decades of denials, delays, and bureaucratic hurdles in the United States. The story of ABC and NACARA reveals that even in the face of seemingly insurmountable odds, the “maneuverings [of immigrants and their allies can] occasionally result in social change or transformative visions of social existence.”

Today’s population of asylum seekers has run a similar gauntlet, and something like the streamlined approach of the late 1990s may be needed to address the backlog of cases and offer restitution for the practices of Deportation Judges. As Professor Sarah Sherman-Stokes has argued, Congress might create simplified standards for relief for some class of persons as a form of reparations. The precise contours of any new remedy would necessarily involve value judgments and the prioritization of some cases over others. Congress might consider family ties, length of time in the United States, and past harm experienced by applicants—all factors that have already been incorporated in various ways into immigration law.

A streamlined approach to some cases should not permanently displace the need for evidentiary adjudication in others. To restore integrity to immigration courts, it will be important to not substitute the current system of summary removal for one of summary approval. Reforms to the immigration court and the appointment of new IJs should be accompanied by new substantive law. Congress will need to not only assess the fate of those in the immigration system now, but those who will come in the future. It will need to develop workable priorities for admission and sustainable expectations for enforcement.

Conclusion

The manipulation of immigration courts is part of a worldwide pattern of democratic erosion in which elected governments use democratic institutions to subvert democracy itself. The rule of law is a pivotal bulwark against authoritarianism and courts have long been at the center of struggles for democracy. Authoritarian governments manipulate courts to serve and legitimate their agenda, yet even in authoritarian systems, courts can become sites for resistance. Conversely, democracies hope that courts will protect against authoritarian drift, but they have been captured and manipulated in some cases by competitive authoritarian regimes.

The capture of American immigration courts raises serious issues related to separation of powers and individual rights. Immigration courts decide life-and-death matters for millions. Under the INA, IJs are required to decide cases based on the evidence in each case. If IJs can be dismissed because of how they decide cases, the law can be reworked by executive officials, and court procedures can be modified to transform evidentiary hearings into summary dispositions, then there is a larger problem for the country’s constitutional system. A threat to the independence of immigration courts is a threat to American democracy.

The solution to that problem might come from immigration courts and the immigrants whose cases are decided there. At another time when the country turned its back on refugees, a coalition of immigrants, religious leaders, and lawyers formed the sanctuary movement, leading to the ABC settlement and NACARA as a form of recompense for immigrants whose cases had been dismissed. The authoritarian tilt of Deportation Judges creates the possibility that immigration courts might become contemporary sites of resistance. Authoritarianism produces repression, but in time, resistance can lead to transitional justice and meaningful restitution.

text:
Immigration lawyers challenging how the Department of Homeland Security provides records needed for asylum and deportation cases have lost their federal appeal after judges ruled that the additional time and expense of obtaining those documents did not give them standing to sue.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled October 29, 2026, that the attorneys and a legal aid organization also failed to establish a uniform DHS policy requiring immigrants to obtain records through Freedom of Information Act requests. The decision upholds the dismissal of their lawsuit while leaving the government's underlying disclosure obligations undecided.

Greater Boston Legal Services, attorneys Annelise Araujo and Stefanie Fisher, and their law firm sued DHS in January 2021, alleging that immigration agencies routinely directed clients to file Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests for documents needed to prepare their cases. Those records included earlier visa applications, asylum interview notes, immigration filings and documents from previous deportation proceedings.

Delayed and incomplete responses forced attorneys to reconstruct their clients' immigration histories through interviews, court records and requests to previous lawyers, according to the lawsuit. Some sought postponements in immigration court while waiting for documents, increasing the cost of representation and limiting the number of additional clients they could accept.

Federal law generally requires agencies to respond to FOIA requests within 20 business days, with an additional 10 days permitted under certain circumstances. The attorneys alleged that immigration agencies regularly missed those deadlines or returned records with missing or redacted information.

Writing for the three-judge panel, Judge Gustavo Gelpí found that the attorneys had combined different records-access practices across U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Customs and Border Protection into an alleged DHS-wide policy. The agencies used different disclosure procedures, and the court found the alleged injuries too speculative to establish standing.

Even assuming such a policy existed, the judges ruled that additional legal expenses and a reduced capacity to represent clients did not amount to the concrete injury required to sue. The court found that the lawyers could continue obtaining records through other means, despite the additional work involved.

U.S. District Judge Denise Casper in Massachusetts had dismissed the claims involving deportation proceedings and later ruled for DHS on the remaining asylum-related challenge. During appellate arguments on May 7, the First Circuit raised the standing question and requested additional briefing before affirming the judgment on different grounds.

The lawyers had also relied on a 2010 Ninth Circuit decision, Dent v. Holder, which recognized access to immigration files for certain people required to establish lawful presence during deportation proceedings. They alleged that ICE limited its compliance with that ruling to cases within the Ninth Circuit while continuing to direct immigrants elsewhere to FOIA requests.

text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is threatening U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement with new legal action over the use of city lots.

Mamdani says ICE using those areas for staging is illegal, and an unauthorized use of city property.

"We want to make very clear that we mean what we say when we talk about sanctuary city policies and we talk about the fact that our city will not assist in immigration enforcement," Mamdani said Monday. "What we've seen all too often is ICE's flouting of those directives and those laws. And this is a letter to make clear that ICE has no right to use any city property or lots for anti-immigrant operations and that we are willing to go to court if they continue to do so."

The mayor's office says ICE agents have reportedly parked vehicles and held meetings in a number of city-owned lots, including at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx and Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens.

The mayor also unveiled a new policy Monday instructing parks workers to deny ICE agents if they ask to use city lots or enter any non-public parts of a park without a warrant. Parks workers who don't comply with the new policy could face discipline, officials said, adding, the policy also instructs them to not engage in any verbal or physical altercations with ICE agents.

Last month, Mamdani urged private parking lot owners to keep ICE out after reports surfaced that agents staged in one in Marble Hill before the shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal.

The Department of Homeland Security pushed back against the mayor's directive, saying ICE presence is fully authorized under federal law.

"Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won't," a DHS spokesperson said. "Luckily, no terminated parking will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make New York safe again. We need New York to cooperate with our officers and stop releasing criminals from their jails into New York's neighborhoods. Seven of the 10 safest cities in America cooperate with ICE."

Queens City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino, a Republican, accuses the mayor of overstepping.

"And the feds, of course, are going to completely ignore him, as they should," Paladino said. "New York is not an independent nation that operates on its own immigration policies. Okay? Last I checked, we were still part of the United States of America."

Gov. Kathy Hochul and Public Advocate Jumaane Williams offered Mamdani their unwavering support.

"No family in New York should fear that going to the park or walking through their neighborhood could mean being torn away from their loved ones," Hochul said. "I am deeply disturbed by reports that ICE is using public property to carry out aggressive immigration enforcement operations ... I stand with Mayor Mamdani in demanding an end to the unauthorized use of city property for these operations."

"When we say ICE out of New York, we mean it -- and we're not going to let this rogue agency use city property to terrorize our city's residents," Williams said.

"I hope that [ICE] do heed this warning, but I think the city will end up having to take legal action against them," added Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition.

text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who is accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston turned himself in Monday, his attorney said.

Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales, 33, on Friday.

During Monday’s hearing, Judge Matthew Peneguy set bond at $30,000. Prosecutors had asked that bond be set at $75,000, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.

Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. Other encounters have come under investigation.

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales’ vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Surveillance camera video shows Morales’ vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

David Lindenmuth, Morales’ attorney, has said his client was “truly a good man” and did not commit a crime.

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.

Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. He unsuccessfully ran for Congress this year and previously served in the Army.

Catch Up

Immigration activists sue Tennessee over new rule denying driver’s licenses to legal non-U.S. citizens

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - A judge signed a temporary restraining order in Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition’s (TIRRC) lawsuit against the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security (TDOS).

The lawsuit challenges the TDOS’s new rule regarding issuing new driver’s licenses to non-U.S. citizens who are legally permitted to be in the country.

The organization shared news of the ruling Monday night, saying a judge signed a temporary restraining order in their lawsuit’s case.

“The order is temporary and will be in effect once a bond is posted, which we intend to do tomorrow,” the TIRRC said.

What the ruling does

The TIRRC said that the TDOS is “not allowed to require that people provide a visa or I-94 in order to get a license.”

Instead, the TDOS must comply with the regulations that the department has practiced for several years, accepting work permits and other federal documents as proof of federally authorized presence under the order, the organization said.

The TIRRC filed the lawsuit Friday alongside the National Immigration Law Center and Bass Berry and Sims, LLC, saying that the TDOS’s new policy “blocks many non-U.S. citizens from getting temporary driver’s licenses, even when they have authorization from the federal government to be present in the U.S.”

Old policy vs. new rule

The TIRRC said Tennesseans who could prove they had permission from the federal government to be in the U.S. have been able to obtain driver’s licenses for many years, adding that they routinely accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legality in the U.S. for a period of time.

In recent weeks, however, the TIRRC said the TDOS abruptly changed this policy, and now only issues driver’s licenses to certain non-citizens who can present a valid visa, I-94,I94W or temporary green card.

“The new rule excludes thousands of people living in Tennessee with federal authorization who have relied for decades on the agency’s prior practice,” the TIRRC said.
