title: Mass Deportation Has Put the House Out of Reach for Republicans. Here's Why.
description:
VOTERS HAVE SEEN WHAT ICE IS DOING When mass deportation agents brutally killed U.S. citizens Renée Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis this year, their deaths reverberated far beyond the state.
There have been over 500 documented cases of U.S. citizens detained by mass deportation agents, including at least 70 children and teens.
MASS DEPORTATION IS INCREASING COSTS FOR AMERICAN FAMILIES The 2024 campaign promise that mass deportation would lead to a more prosperous America was a wicked lie.
Voters connect the dots: by 62-38%, they say mass deportation is hurting the economy and raising costs.
“I’ll never go Republican again.” CONGRESSIONAL REPUBLICANS CHAMPIONED MASS DEPORTATION.
text:
Five reasons the immigration backlash will help shape Tuesday’s results

Whatever happens on Election Day, we believe that the Trump administration’s violent, lawless and costly mass deportation agenda stands to be one of the most critical factors when it comes to the fight for the House. It’s already playing a role in early voting, including among Latino voters who cast their ballot for Donald Trump in 2024 and now feel his immigration enforcement actions have gone too far and are coming out in “staggering” numbers. Here are five reasons why we think the administration’s anti-immigrant ugliness will be a defining factor in which party ultimately holds the speaker’s gavel come January.

VOTERS HAVE SEEN WHAT ICE IS DOING

When mass deportation agents brutally killed U.S. citizens Renée Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis this year, their deaths reverberated far beyond the state. Their killings were part of a pattern of abuse that began in year one and has only grown deadlier in year two. There have been over 500 documented cases of U.S. citizens detained by mass deportation agents, including at least 70 children and teens. ICE is now arresting parents and labeling their children “unaccompanied”, and Brookings estimates more than 145,000 U.S. citizen children have had a parent detained by ICE since the administration began. Voters didn’t need a campaign ad to learn this, they saw firsthand – in their own neighborhoods, schools, and businesses.

MASS DEPORTATION IS INCREASING COSTS FOR AMERICAN FAMILIES

The 2024 campaign promise that mass deportation would lead to a more prosperous America was a wicked lie. America’s Voice’s End the ICE Tax report found that the administration’s surge cost an estimated 668,000 jobs. In Minnesota – ground zero of the bloody Operation Metro Surge – some immigrant-owned businesses said they lost up to 100% of their revenue. Russ Adams, manager for Minneapolis’ corridor recovery initiatives, called it “an economic crisis of catastrophic proportions.” In industries where immigrant labor matters the most – such as healthcare and agriculture – prices have risen the fastest: home health care is up 10.7% in a year, while fruits, vegetables, and milk have jumped between 6% and 32%. Voters connect the dots: by 62-38%, they say mass deportation is hurting the economy and raising costs.

THE MASS DEPORTATION AGENDA IS INCREASINGLY REJECTED BY VOTERS

As AV’s October polling memo documented, 56% of Americans now say Trump is going too far on deportations, his immigration approval has fallen to a second-term low of 38%, and Democrats now edge Republicans on trust in immigration – an issue Republicans led by double digits before 2024. Pew also found that ICE is now the least popular of 12 polled federal agencies, including the IRS. Even judges appointed by Trump have condemned ICE’s lawlessness, with a New York court last month rebuking the agency for lying and faking records. Officers were “inexperienced, possessed little understanding of the law and used ‘false testimony to conceal these failings,’” the judge ruled according to The New York Times. The issue Trump called his strongest has become a liability for him and every Republican tied to it.

LATINO VOTERS HAVE MOVED SHARPLY AWAY FROM REPUBLICANS

Latino voters now prefer Democratic control of Congress 59-35%, double the margin at this point in 2024. Democrats lead Hispanic likely voters 64-29% in an average of high-quality polls, up from a seven-point Harris lead. The shift is playing out district by district: in Texas’s 15th, a majority-Latino seat Trump carried by 18 points in 2024, Democrat Bobby Pulido leads Rep. Monica De La Cruz 51-44% among likely voters, and 57-40% among Latino likely voters. In Arizona, a Latina who voted for Trump in 2024 regrets her vote after seeing the effects of his agenda on her community. “There are a lot of people who are being harassed for the color of their skin, and that’s not right,” Sandra Ramírez told the AP. “I’ll never go Republican again.”

CONGRESSIONAL REPUBLICANS CHAMPIONED MASS DEPORTATION. THEY OWN THE FALLOUT.

U.S. Reps. María Elvira Salazar (FL-27), Monica De La Cruz (TX-15), David Valadao (CA-22), and Gabe Evans (CO-8) all repeatedly voted to make ICE the nation’s highest-funded law enforcement agency by giving DHS $261 billion. But once these masked agents began to target their constituents – such as DACA recipients, farmworkers and other essential workers critical to their local economies – they laughably attempted to distance themselves from the agenda they funded no fewer than three times. Voters remember their actions. One Florida immigrant said that while Salazar “presented herself as our advocate” and “spoke about legalization, solutions and dignity,” she has “manipulated us all; she’s taken advantage of the uncertainty and fear that we live with.”

WHAT COMES NEXT

The polling has been unequivocal, with voters rejecting mass deportation month after month. In just a matter of hours, voters who have seen their communities targeted and harassed under the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant agenda will render their decision at the ballot box. The question for the next Congress is what comes after the election. In 2027, the debate turns to accountability for the immense harm done to our country and humane solutions to protect America’s immigrant communities and our nation’s economy. That must include a path to citizenship for the millions of our neighbors who have lived, worked, and raised families in the U.S. for decades, an approach that majorities across party lines already prefer over mass deportation.

name: Human Rights
title: USA: midterm elections on a skewed field - CIVICUS LENS
description:
On 23 September, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which has observed every US federal election since 2002, announced it hadn’t received an invitation.
The government’s decision places the USA alongside Belarus and Russia, which also refused to admit OSCE observers in their latest national elections.
Days later, Trump urged Republicans to ‘nationalize’ voting, arguing that states run elections as agents of the federal government.
It gives states the power to run elections and allows Congress to set rules for federal elections, while it gives no role to the president.
That month, civil rights organisations, the city of Denver and the Democratic Party filed lawsuits to keep armed federal agents away from voting sites.
text:
Across Michigan, volunteers are preparing to watch polling stations and counting centres. They’ve been recruited and trained by the Ford-Carter Election Observation Network, a partnership between the Carter Center and the Gerald R. Ford Presidential Foundation, to monitor each stage of the state’s election process and check whether election laws and procedures are applied consistently. Having observed over 100 elections around the world, mostly in fragile or fledgling democracies, the Carter Center first observed a US election in 2020, when it focused on Georgia’s presidential recount. It then monitored other elections in Georgia in 2022 and 2024. Now it’s taking that work beyond its home state.

As domestic observation expands, international observers have been shut out. On 23 September, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which has observed every US federal election since 2002, announced it hadn’t received an invitation. The government’s decision places the USA alongside Belarus and Russia, which also refused to admit OSCE observers in their latest national elections.

Instead, the government is sending its own observers. In its largest operation ever, the Justice Department is deploying around 1,000 monitors in all 50 states. Federal monitors normally visit areas with histories of discrimination to safeguard voting access, but this time, on stated ‘election security’ grounds, they’ll mostly target Democratic strongholds and seek to get inside polling places. Following legal challenges by civil rights groups concerned that voters would be put at risk, the department had to file a declaration that it wouldn’t deploy federal law enforcement and immigration agents as monitors. Some states plan to keep the department’s monitors at a distance from polling stations.

That the USA is closing itself off from foreign scrutiny while domestic bodies are using election-monitoring tools designed for fragile or backsliding democracies says much about the state of US democracy. Under Donald Trump’s second administration, the country is on its way to becoming a competitive authoritarian regime, where elections take place and the opposition can still win, but the incumbent abuses state power to tilt the playing field.

To weaken democratic checks, Trump has sought to silence those who scrutinise and challenge power, which has put civic freedoms in the firing line. In March 2025, the CIVICUS Monitor placed the USA on its Watchlist, which flags countries experiencing rapid declines in civic freedoms. In December 2025, the USA’s civic space rating was downgraded to obstructed, indicating serious restrictions, including harassment of civil society, repression of protests and pressure on the media. While the midterms offer a chance to reverse course, institutional manipulation makes it an uphill struggle.

Redistricting and racial gerrymandering

Congressional districts are typically redrawn to reflect population changes once a decade following the census. But in 2025, facing poor poll showings, Trump pressured Republican-led states to redraw their maps ahead of schedule, manipulating boundaries to win more seats. In August, Texas added five Republican-leaning seats. Gerrymandering has a long history in US politics, but this was the first coordinated national campaign to manufacture a congressional majority ahead of expected losses.

Democrats’ counter-efforts saw mixed results. California voters passed a map adding five Democratic-leaning seats, but in Virginia, the state Supreme Court blocked a voter-approved redistricting amendment. Overall, nine states – Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah – are voting under new maps. Only in California and Utah do changes favour Democrats. The new maps could hand Republicans up to 15 additional seats compared with six for Democrats, meaning that Republicans could lose a significant share of the vote without it costing them a corresponding number of seats.

Much of the redistricting blurred the line between partisan and racial gerrymandering. Since 2019, federal courts have refused to hear challenges to partisan gerrymandering, but drawing districts to dilute the votes of racial minorities remains unconstitutional. In practice, the two are hard to separate, particularly in the south, where Black voters overwhelmingly support Democratic candidates. Maps drawn to eliminate Democratic seats often do so by breaking up districts with substantial numbers of voters of colour.

The conservative-dominated Supreme Court has made racial gerrymandering easier to carry out and harder to challenge. In November 2025, a federal court blocked Texas’s new map after finding it was likely a racial gerrymander, but the Supreme Court reversed the ruling, accepting the state’s argument that its motive was partisan. This cleared the way for the map to be used in the midterms. On 29 April, the Supreme Court went further, striking down a Louisiana map that created a second majority-Black district to comply with Section 2 of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, the main legal tool voters of colour have to contest discriminatory maps. Before, they could win a case by showing that a map weakened their votes, whatever lawmakers intended. Now they must show a map was drawn with the aim of discriminating, which is much harder to prove.

The day after the ruling, Louisiana’s governor postponed the state’s congressional primaries so the legislature could redraw the districts. The new map, which he signed into law a month later, eliminated a majority-Black district and is expected to give Republicans an extra seat. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, historically charged with enforcing voting rights, has pledged to review districts drawn to comply with Section 2 in every state, and its head has predicted that districts will be redrawn across almost all southern states in the coming years. Southern Black voters, whose representation was won through decades of struggle, stand to lose most.

Citizenship checks and voter purges

On the basis of the false claim that large numbers of non-citizens vote, the Justice Department has demanded complete voter registration lists from 49 states and the District of Columbia, including birthdates, partial Social Security numbers and driver’s licence numbers. In doing so, it has invoked the Civil Rights Act, which requires election officials to preserve voting records and allows the attorney general to inspect them. Passed in 1960 so the department could investigate discrimination against southern Black voters, the Act is now being invoked to obtain data that could be used to remove voters from the rolls.

Several states complied and handed over their files, and the Justice Department sued the 31 jurisdictions that refused. Oklahoma agreed to hand over its data in exchange for the lawsuit being dropped. All 26 judges who had ruled by mid-October threw out the lawsuits, and the only appeals court to decide so far upheld the dismissal of the Michigan case.

In March, the Justice Department gave the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) access to the voter rolls it had collected. In July, Trump claimed that a DHS review had found around 278,000 non-citizens registered to vote in four states, including as many as 15,903 in Nevada. The figure came from matching state voter files against federal databases, a method DHS staff warned would vastly overstate the numbers. A month later, DHS officials admitted they’d confirmed only 185 cases in Nevada, and when the state checked those names, it found every one was a citizen.

On 9 October, in a lawsuit brought by the civil society organisation Common Cause, a federal judge in Washington, DC, struck down the Justice Department’s programme of collecting voter rolls and checking them against federal databases. The judge concluded that no law authorised this, that it violated federal privacy law and that the department had ignored the risk of eligible voters being removed from the rolls. On 15 October, the Electronic Privacy Information Center, the League of United Latin American Citizens and the League of Women Voters sued DHS, alleging it has secretly amassed voter files from at least 47 states, including some handed over by the Justice Department, and combined them with commercial data to hunt for supposed ‘illegal voters’.

DHS has also pushed states to check voters’ citizenship through the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system, a database built to verify immigrants’ eligibility for public benefits. Since 2025, DHS has overhauled the system and fed it confidential data from across the federal government, so states can now run bulk checks on their voter rolls. DHS’s internal assessments warned in mid-2025 that inaccurate data could produce false results, but over half of states are using it regardless.

In early 2026, a ProPublica and Texas Tribune investigation found that the system had made numerous mistakes, particularly affecting citizens born abroad, whose Social Security records are often not updated when they naturalise. DHS has had to correct the results it gave to at least five states. Even counting the errors, the checks haven’t borne out claims of widespread non-citizen voting. In seven states with around 35 million registered voters, they flagged roughly 4,200 people, around 0.01 per cent of the electorate. In Missouri, hundreds were wrongly flagged and temporarily barred from voting, and in Texas the system wrongly flagged at least 87 voters across 29 counties. Some citizens whose registrations were cancelled were unable to vote in the March 2026 primary.

The Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of Women Voters challenged the overhaul in court, and in June a federal judge ruled that it broke federal law. In September, however, the Supreme Court paused the ruling, allowing the system to keep running.

Other measures target voter registration. Since 2024, eight states have passed laws requiring people to show documents such as birth certificates or passports to register to vote. Trump and his allies in Congress want to extend the requirement to the whole country. In February, the House passed the SAVE America Act, which would impose the registration requirement nationwide and mandate photo IDs to cast a ballot, but the bill has stalled in the Senate. Over 20 million voting-age citizens lack ready access to such documents. Those most affected would be low-income people, young people and married women whose names no longer match their birth certificates.

Pressure on election systems and staff

US elections are run by states and counties. This decentralised system, which in 2020 withstood Trump’s attempt to overturn his defeat, is now under pressure.

In January, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agents executed a search warrant at the election hub of Fulton County, Georgia, seizing hundreds of boxes of 2020 ballots. The county, which includes most of Atlanta and votes heavily Democratic, has been at the centre of false fraud claims since 2020, even though its ballots were counted three times, with the results confirmed each time. The raid was a clear attempt to sow doubt about election integrity. Days later, Trump urged Republicans to ‘nationalize’ voting, arguing that states run elections as agents of the federal government. But the US Constitution says otherwise. It gives states the power to run elections and allows Congress to set rules for federal elections, while it gives no role to the president.

In the final weeks of the campaign, Trump has laid the groundwork for disputing results. On 23 October, the Justice Department sued Alaska to stop certification of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses by fewer votes than those received by a little-known namesake on the ballot. Trump said he ordered the lawsuit himself. Three days later, he offered a US$1 million reward for information leading to convictions for voter fraud in past elections or the midterms.

While asserting control, the federal government has withdrawn protection. Since 2018, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has helped election officials defend their systems against cyberattacks and foreign interference. The administration has cut almost 1,000 of its staff, around a third of the workforce, and ended funding for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, through which election offices shared threat information. Several states reported that CISA services they relied on were not available ahead of the midterms, and the agency published its election security plan just 40 days before the vote. The administration’s 2027 budget proposal would eliminate CISA’s election security programme, even though the head of US Cyber Command has warned that foreign adversaries are likely to try to interfere.

The election workforce is also being worn down. Turnover among local election officials reached 41 per cent in 2024, the highest in at least 25 years, driven partly by burnout, harassment and threats that intensified with the false claims that followed the 2020 election. Experience is draining away. The share of chief local election officials with six or more years in the job fell from 60 per cent in 2006 to 47 per cent in 2024. In a recent survey by the Brennan Center for Justice, 32 per cent of local election officials reported abuse, harassment or threats. Half said they were worried about political leaders interfering in how elections are run and three-quarters said their state or local government hadn’t replaced lost federal funding.

Voter targeting

In February, far-right former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents would ‘surround the polls’ in November, and the White House press secretary said she couldn’t guarantee that ICE agents wouldn’t be near polling locations. Weeks later, a senior DHS official told state election officials there’d be no ICE presence at polling places. But at his confirmation hearing in March, DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin said agents could be sent in response to a ‘specific threat’.

In June, during New York’s primary, two ICE officers confronted a poll worker at her polling site in Syracuse and handed her a warning over social media posts criticising ICE. In September, the FBI director declined to commit to keeping agents away from polling places. That month, civil rights organisations, the city of Denver and the Democratic Party filed lawsuits to keep armed federal agents away from voting sites. They cited evidence that fear is already depressing participation. In Minnesota, for instance, an organisation working with African immigrant communities reported only one new voter registered this year, compared with hundreds in previous years.

Intimidation has reached voters’ doorsteps. Under what DHS calls its ‘Unlawful Voter Initiative’, armed agents went door to door in several states to question people suspected of voting or registering while ineligible, including naturalised citizens. Their target lists were built from voter rolls and commercial data, some generated by unidentified AI tools. DHS stepped up the operation just as early voting began. On 21 October, a federal judge ruled that this probably amounted to voter intimidation in violation of the Voting Rights Act and barred agents from questioning people likely to be citizens until the polls close. The case had been brought by two nurses’ unions, the Voto Latino Foundation, the city and county of San Francisco and Santa Clara County. On 30 October, an appeals court refused to suspend the judge’s ban while the government appeals, pointing to the questionable timing of the operation. This left the ban in force through to election day.

title: 260. Elections and the Base Rate Fallacy - One First | Steve Vladeck
description:
It’s how many eligible voters we’re prepared to disenfranchise in the course of hunting for ineligible ones.
But the relevant comparison has never been between some ineligible voting and no ineligible voting.
It’s between some ineligible voting and the costs of the tools we use to find it.
What DOJ wanted instead was to put the burden on 20,000 voters at once, after sitting on DHS’s claims since July.
These arguments share the same blind spot—treating the government’s interest in stopping ineligible votes as concrete and the risk to eligible voters as abstract.
text:
Welcome back to “One First,” a newsletter that aims to make the U.S. Supreme Court more accessible to lawyers and non-lawyers alike. I’m grateful to all of you for your continued support, and I hope that you’ll consider sharing some of what we’re doing with your networks.

Share

If you’re not already a subscriber, please consider becoming one—and upgrading to a paid subscription if and when your circumstances permit:

The “base rate fallacy” is a term psychologists and statisticians use to describe how, when we judge how likely something is, we tend to fixate on the details in front of us and forget how rare the thing was to begin with. The classic example is a screening test for a rare disease. When the thing you’re screening for has a very low incidence, even an accurate test administered to a large population will flag far more people who don’t have the condition than who do. For instance, a test that catches 999 of every 1,000 real cases, and wrongly flags only 1 of every 1,000 healthy people, sounds terrific. But run it across a population of 100 million people where the condition turns up about once in every 400,000, and nearly everyone it flags will turn out to be fine. Of the roughly 100,250 people the test will flag, only about 250 actually have the condition. The other 100,000 (~99.75 percent!) are false alarms, even though the test is exceptionally accurate.

As we head into tomorrow’s elections, I have base rates on the brain, largely because the Trump administration’s fight with California over roughly 20,000 mail ballots is really a fight about them. So I want to use today’s “Long Read” to make two points that the California litigation—and most of the coverage thereof—has buried, but that we’d all do well to remember: American electorates are enormous, and ineligible voting in our elections is exceedingly rare.

That means the question that should worry us is not whether a handful of ineligible ballots get counted. It’s how many eligible voters we’re prepared to disenfranchise in the course of hunting for ineligible ones. I certainly don’t endorse voting by anyone who isn’t legally registered to do so. But (1) such voting is statistically insignificant once we take the denominator into account; and (2) it’s just as problematic, if not more so, to formally or functionally disenfranchise significant numbers of eligible voters in the name of preventing such a marginal number of ineligible votes (that’s where the base rate comes in). On both of these points, the California case is a pretty good—and troubling—illustration.

More on all of that below. But first, the Supreme Court-specific news.

On the Docket

The Merits Docket

It was another quiet week on the merits docket. The Court didn’t issue any regular orders, so no new cases were added to the roster for the October 2026 Term. We’re currently at 34 merits cases, two of which are consolidated—so 33 arguments in granted cases to date. If the Court’s recent pattern (since OT2019) holds, that should be a little more than half of the total cases the Court will resolve through plenary review between now and next summer.

The Emergency Docket

The only formal action by the full Court last week was Tuesday’s denial, over no public dissents, of the emergency application in City of Baltimore v. Texas. I wrote in detail about that case for last Thursday’s bonus issue.

Once more, the real news on the emergency docket is the Court’s inaction on several high-profile pending applications—including the K.M.K. case (about the challenge to Washington state allowing a wrestler who identifies as a transgender woman to compete in high school competitions), which has been fully briefed since October 15; and the Trump administration’s application in the border wall case, which is also now fully briefed. It’s a good bet that we get one or both of those rulings between now and Friday.

The Week Ahead

The justices will be back on the bench at 10 ET this morning for the beginning of the November argument session, which features a total of seven arguments over five days (M–W this week; M–T next week). The next Conference is scheduled for this Friday, which should lead to a full Order List next Monday (November 9) at 9:30 ET.

The One First “Long Read”:

“I Was Told There Would Be No Math…”

In July, DHS announced that as many as 190,000 noncitizens might be on California’s rolls, and then gave the state nothing more until after ballots went out. In October, DOJ sent state and Los Angeles County officials a list of more than 20,000 “likely” noncitizens (on a thumb drive), gave them 48 hours to review it, and sued on October 15.

Los Angeles County, to its credit, actually checked. Of the 20,930 records, 7,035 had county addresses. In a sample of 200 of those 7,035, 112 belonged to canceled or inactive registrations, so no ballot had been mailed to them at all. More than 71 percent had never voted. And among records that meaningfully reported a birthplace, 38.9 percent listed the United States, which the county called “strong evidence of citizenship.” A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) official told the court that the agency’s records showed none of the sampled people were U.S.-born, though he acknowledged 189 records with “minor data discrepancies.” On Saturday, a UCLA analysis reported that 8,880 names (42 percent of the list) didn’t match anyone on California’s current voter file. It further estimated that nearly 7,500 naturalized citizens were “highly likely” to be wrongly flagged.

The courts, to put it mildly, have not been impressed. After the Ninth Circuit on Monday rejected a premature DOJ appeal, Judge David Carter denied a temporary restraining order last Wednesday, holding that DOJ likely lacked standing and a cause of action and that its remedy would likely violate federal voting laws. He noted that DOJ had charged 28 alleged noncitizens the same day it sought emergency relief. “Go out and indict,” he said from the bench. On Friday, a divided Ninth Circuit panel refused DOJ’s request for emergency relief from Carter’s Wednesday ruling, accepting the finding that DOJ’s process was “not credible.” Meanwhile, county employees have been subpoenaed to appear before a federal grand jury on November 4, the morning after Election Day.

The numerator and the denominator

Fights about election “integrity” are, in an important sense, fights about a fraction. We spend almost all of our time arguing about the top half of it. It seems worth taking a minute to talk about the bottom half, too.

After the 2016 election, the Brennan Center surveyed officials in 42 jurisdictions with large noncitizen populations. Those officials oversaw 23.5 million votes and referred about 30 suspected incidents of noncitizen voting, or roughly 0.0001 percent (so roughly one ineligible vote for every 780,000 total votes). In 2024, Georgia’s Republican Secretary of State ran what he called the most comprehensive citizenship check in the state’s history. It found 20 noncitizens among 8.2 million registrants, only nine of whom had ever voted (across multiple elections), mostly before 2012. That’s 1.1 ineligible votes per million. This summer, DHS told Nevada it might have 15,903 noncitizens on its rolls, then conceded it had confirmed only 185. Nevada checked and reported back that “our records indicate that they were [all] citizens.”

To be clear, none of this means the number of noncitizens on these voter rolls is zero. As noted above, Georgia did find 20 such registered voters, DOJ has charged 28 more in California, and those cases ought to be taken seriously. But the relevant comparison has never been between some ineligible voting and no ineligible voting. It’s between some ineligible voting and the costs of the tools we use to find it.

Running the numbers

Here’s a deliberately simple illustration, using my numbers rather than anyone’s findings: California has about 23 million registered voters. At Georgia’s rate of roughly one noncitizen per 410,000 registered voters, you’d expect something like 56 noncitizens on the rolls. Now assume that DHS has a screening tool with a false-positive rate of just 0.1 percent (I am very skeptical that such a precise tool exists, but work with me). Run across 23 million records, it would flag about 23,000 citizens. Even if it caught all 56 noncitizens, more than 99.7 percent of the flagged names would be eligible voters—who would all be at serious risk of disenfranchisement.

DOJ’s list, for what it’s worth, has 20,930 names. No one outside the government knows what methodology was used to create it. Nor do we have any idea what the false-positive rate is (or any reason to believe that the false-positive error rate is less than 0.1 percent). And when the true rate (of noncitizens on voter rolls, let alone noncitizen voting) is that low, a list of 20,000 “likely” noncitizens is roughly what you’d expect from noise alone. Even a modest error rate, multiplied by a denominator in the tens of millions, will swamp a numerator that may be, at most, in the dozens.

The dilution concern runs both ways

The government’s best answer is dilution. Bill Essayli, the not-quite-U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, framed the “ongoing emergency” as one that “disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” and one of Judge Patrick Bumatay’s two dissents from last week’s Ninth Circuit doubleheader likewise warned that counting the suspect ballots would threaten “to dilute the vote of eligible citizens.” I don’t doubt that an unlawful ballot dilutes lawful ones. But even assuming noncitizens on the voter rolls are also voting (because dilution isn’t an issue if they’re not), dilution is a two-way street. An eligible citizen voter whose ballot is set aside loses her vote entirely, and that distorts the tally every bit as much as a wrongly counted noncitizen vote does. And although you wouldn’t know it from Essayli or Judge Bumatay, once the base rates are back in the picture, the wrongful exclusion side of the ledger is larger than the wrongful inclusion side—by more than two orders of magnitude.

There’s also a difference in the kind of error involved. Scattered individual mistakes in a giant electorate tend to wash out. A screening program, by contrast, tends to make the same mistake over and over, and against the same kinds of people, including naturalized citizens and people with stale or incomplete records. The UCLA estimate about naturalized citizens is a warning on exactly this point, as is the researchers’ observation that voter ID numbers were apparently stripped from the list.

“What’s the harm in checking?”

The response I’ve heard most often from those defending DOJ’s position is that, even if the list is imperfect, there’s no harm in checking. That argument, too, depends on completely ignoring the base rate problem.

DOJ didn’t ask for an investigation on a normal timeline; it wanted an order, on 48 hours’ notice and in the middle of an election, to segregate every listed voter’s ballot and not count it until her citizenship was verified. Yet DOJ’s own complaint conceded that it was “not practicable or feasible” for federal investigators to look into “thousands, let alone tens of thousands,” of these voters before the election ended, and the county has no citizenship information beyond each voter’s sworn attestation. The upshot is that a voter who swore under penalty of perjury that she’s a citizen becomes a suspect because a database (of not-exactly-clear provenance) said so.

Congress has also, in a sense, already answered the question. The National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) bars systematic removal programs within 90 days of a federal election—precisely because last-minute sweeps catch eligible voters with no time to fix the error. Indeed, among lots of other things, Judge Carter found that DOJ’s request would probably violate that rule.

Nor is anyone arguing that the government can’t ever go after illegal voters. It can, through individualized investigation and prosecution, with the burden on the government. Even Judge Bumatay acknowledged that California “appears correct” that prosecution remains available after the fact. What DOJ wanted instead was to put the burden on 20,000 voters at once, after sitting on DHS’s claims since July. Two Ninth Circuit judges called that emergency, at least in part, “a self-constructed one.” And when the next step is grand jury subpoenas for the people counting the ballots, it gets harder and harder to describe all of this as just “checking.” To the contrary, it seems like a calculated effort to use the specter of noncitizen voting as a mechanism for both (1) kicking a lot of eligible voters (of particular demographic groups) off the voter rolls; and (2) sowing the seeds of doubt about the integrity of the results. If the choice is between potentially counting 50 ineligible votes and not counting thousands of eligible votes (again, in a state with 23 million voters), I would like to think that we’d all pick the former.

What the Ninth Circuit’s dissents miss

Last week’s three relevant Ninth Circuit opinions (the two rulings in United States v. California and the separate but related denial of en banc rehearing in California Nurses Association v. Mullin) are worth reading in full, in part because the dissents illustrate the base rate problem better than any hypothetical I could have come up with.

Friday’s unsigned majority opinion in United States v. California recounted the district court’s findings that the government offered “no error rates” or “validation against a reliable benchmark,” and that “[i]t remains unknown how Lexis Nexis performed its analysis.” DOJ, in other words, wanted a list of more than 20,000 names used to sequester potentially thousands of ballots on the strength of a tool whose false-positive rate nobody has yet disclosed.

Judge Bumatay, who had also dissented from the dismissal of the government’s first appeal earlier in the week, dissented from the denial of a stay on appeal #2. He framed the case as about the federal government’s power “to stop this potential attack on the integrity of our elections.” And he called DOJ’s request “a modest remedy” that “would not cancel any vote” while faulting California’s “lax system for verifying citizenship.” He also noted that when the government ran the county’s sample through its own systems, “it confirmed that none were born here,” while the county offered nothing “beyond the say-so of the potential voters themselves.”

That’s certainly the strongest version of the government’s case. But it rests on an unspoken (and deeply contestable) assumption on which the entire argument depends. When two sets of records disagree about the same person, someone has to bear the risk that the government is wrong, and Bumatay puts that risk on the voter. Her “say-so,” though, is a citizenship attestation under penalty of perjury, the one the NVRA’s federal mail registration form is built around, as Judge Mark Bennett explained. California also requires “extraordinary proof” to challenge a mail ballot. What Bumatay calls a “lax system,” in other words, reflects a deliberate choice about who should bear the risk of error, and I’d argue that it’s an eminently sensible one in a system in which nearly everyone who gets challenged turns out to be eligible. Again, properly accounting for the base rate problem would—or, at least, should—properly shape the legal analysis.

As for “would not cancel any vote,” the majority pointed out that treating the list as proof would require canceling registrations under California law. Judge Bennett identified “a material risk” that verification couldn’t finish before certification. A ballot that’s segregated and never cleared is, for all practical purposes, a vote lost. Indeed, DOJ’s own theory was that continued processing causes “untraceable disenfranchisement.” DOJ is right that wrongly counted ballots dilute the votes of lawful voters; the evidence just suggests far more disenfranchisement on the other side. And when Judge Bumatay invoked the risk to “a close election,” Judge Gabriel Sanchez had the answer: the uncounted ballots the government was seeking “could be greater than the margin of victory in races.” It’s exceedingly unlikely, in contrast, that that the same could be said about any ineligible votes.

Judge Eric Tung’s dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc in the California Nurses case (a challenge to DHS’s door-to-door investigations of suspected noncitizen voters) is, if anything, more revealing. A district judge had barred, through Election Day, field operations likely to involve people the government should suspect are citizens. Writing for seven judges who dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc (on a court with 29 active judges), Tung accused that judge of having “confused investigation for intimidation.” He rejected the plaintiffs’ standing in part because “[b]oth USCIS and HSI would have to miss the citizen in their respective reviews.”

But a second layer of review helps only if each layer is reasonably accurate and their errors are independent of each other. We don’t know either layer’s error rate, and both draw on overlapping government records, so a naturalized citizen whose old immigration file was never updated is likely to trip both. Nor do we have to guess how this pipeline performs. Judge Bennett described the California list as the product of the same two agencies, and the 185 Nevada names that had gone through “manual review” all turned out to be citizens.

Judge Tung’s answer to these kinds of mathematical points is to assert that it misses the point to doubt how much fraud exists, because “even the appearance of impropriety” undermines public confidence. But if appearances are enough, the actual numerator will never matter (to say nothing of the denominator). That’s about as good a summary of the problem as I can offer.

None of these dissents is the law, of course. But they’re a pretty good summary of what too many folks appear to genuinely believe—and also of what the Supreme Court will have to confront if Essayli is right that this case is headed its way. These arguments share the same blind spot—treating the government’s interest in stopping ineligible votes as concrete and the risk to eligible voters as abstract. The arithmetic suggests it’s entirely the other way around. Judge Carter put it best in just ten words: “A ballot segregated, in effect, would be a ballot removed.” If the government can demand the segregation of ballots on the strength of a list like this one, it will remove thousands of lawful votes to reach, at most, a few dozen unlawful ones.

***

Even though Election Day is tomorrow, and there’s no sign of DOJ seeking Supreme Court intervention before then, this dispute could be far from over. Judge Carter plans to rule on a preliminary injunction after a November 13 evidentiary hearing with a special master. Essayli has said he expects the case to reach the Supreme Court (at some point?). And the grand jury subpoenas suggest the pressure on election workers will get worse before it gets better.

But whatever happens in court, I hope the broader lesson sticks. The serious risk to our elections was never the 20 Georgians or the 30 suspected cases out of 23.5 million votes in the Brennan Center’s survey. It’s the screening programs, purges, and documentation rules, each defended in the name of a tiny numerator, that quietly remove a larger number of eligible voters from a very large denominator. Until we start asking how many eligible voters a given rule disenfranchises for every ineligible voter it stops, we’re going to keep getting that tradeoff wrong. I hope folks keep that in mind when the results start coming in tomorrow—and especially as politicians, pundits, and everyone in between try to raise amorphous “election integrity” concerns without accounting for the base rate problem.

Math, it turns out, matters.

SCOTUS Trivia: Go Vote!

No trivia today. Just a link to the League of Women Voters’ “VOTE411” website, which can provide you with specific information about what’s on your ballot (if you’re already registered)—and, in states with same-day registration, how you can still register.

If you haven’t voted yet, and you can, I sure hope you will.

I hope that you’ve found this installment of “One First” useful. If you have feedback about today’s issue, or thoughts about future topics, please feel free to e-mail me. And if you liked it, please help spread the word!

title: ICE officer indicted on allegations he ran over undocumented Mexican immigrant appears in court
description:

Parra Hernandez, 48, and another occupant in the vehicle with him began to flee on foot after Morales pursued their vehicle, Teare said.

text:
The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of running over an undocumented immigrant from Mexico with a vehicle was released on a $30,000 bond Monday after appearing in court for a bond hearing, according to his attorney.

A grand jury indicted Mario Alberto Morales Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly struck the man, causing multiple leg fractures. Morales’ next court hearing is set for December 2, according to his attorney David Lindenmuth.

Morales was driving an ICE vehicle, a Jeep Grand Cherokee, near Houston on October 10 when he started to pursue a vehicle driven by Miguel Parra Hernandez, an ICE spokesperson said. Parra Hernandez, who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years, has no criminal record and had no deportation order at the time of the incident, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said at a news conference Friday.

Parra Hernandez, 48, and another occupant in the vehicle with him began to flee on foot after Morales pursued their vehicle, Teare said. “What happened next shocked our entire community,” the district attorney said before playing video he said showed Morales striking Parra Hernandez with his vehicle.

ICE said it “immediately contacted EMS and provided aid” to Parra Hernandez. The agency claimed Parra Hernandez “ran in front of an ICE vehicle,” which Teare said contradicts findings of his investigation.

An ICE spokesperson called the allegations that Morales struck Parra Hernandez intentionally “RECKLESS and FALSE” in a statement to The Associated Press, adding local officials are not authorized to investigate federal officers following their duties.

CNN has not reviewed the indictment and has reached out to the Harris County District Clerk and the Harris County District Attorney’s Office to request a copy.

When contacted by CNN for comment on the indictment and the district attorney’s comments about Morales, a DHS spokesperson responded: “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are in the United States illegally—period.”

“I’ve reviewed hundreds of cases, some very similar to this,” Teare said at the news conference, citing his background leading the division in the office responsible for prosecuting vehicular crimes. “The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” he added.

Lindenmuth accused the district attorney of a “politically motivated prosecution.”

“It’s offensive that an elected DA would do anything like this, especially to a former service member. Morales is a good man. You would think he’s a monster based on what you’ve heard from the elected DA,” Lindenmuth told CNN.

The attorney said he believed the incident was an “accident” and claimed his client did not commit a crime.

Morales is a former corrections officer, pastor and military veteran who filed to run for Texas’ 34th Congressional District in 2025 and later dropped out, Lindenmuth said. He said Morales was contracted by ICE as a transportation officer.

The consequences of the incident have been “devastating and horrible” for Parra Hernandez, leaving him with life-threatening injuries, his attorney Kim Bruno said at a separate news conference Friday.

“He has suffered fractures, nerve damage, and has had surgery, and continues to face mobility limitations and chronic pain,” Bruno said, adding he has also suffered from anxiety and depression since the incident.

After a three-hour conversation with her client on Thursday, Bruno said, “All he wants is accountability,” and “assurance that this will not happen to anybody else. He is so sympathetic, and all he cares about are the other people, but he’s the one in the bed suffering.”

ICE pursued wrong man, DA says

The other occupant in the car with Parra Hernandez was identified by ICE as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was the target of the operation. But Teare said the man by that name has been “apparently dead for nine years” and did not identify the other man with Parra Hernandez inside the vehicle.

In a previous interview with CNN, Parra Hernandez’s brother said the other man in the truck was not Mendoza-Cervantes, the person ICE said it was trying to arrest. “We don’t know him,” said Rodolfo Parra Garcia. “The person ICE was looking for was not the person with my brother.”

Parra Hernandez was on his way to work at a nearby construction site with another man and had just gotten water from a nearby gas station when ICE officers started the enforcement action, his brother said.

“My heart broke, seeing my brother lying in a bed without being a criminal,” Parra Garcia said.

Parra Hernandez was still in the hospital on October 25, according to a GoFundMe page created by his brother.

The incident is one of several examples involving federal agents where witness accounts and video footage have at times contradicted the federal account of what transpired, such as the fatal shooting of US citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis.

It also comes amid heightened scrutiny over vehicle stops in immigration enforcement operations after two immigrants, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, were fatally shot in July by ICE officers in separate incidents about a week apart.

Morales “aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra Hernandez,” Teare said, leaving him “seriously injured and hospitalized to this day” before calling 911 to report the Mexican national had “hit his car.”

In the 911 call played by Teare during the news conference, Morales told dispatch: “We’re following this guy, trying to pull him over. He jumped out of the vehicle. I tried to get around him and he hit my car.”

In the audio of the call, Parra Hernandez can be heard crying out after the incident.

Body camera and surveillance video footage of the incident was also displayed during the news conference, showing the moment Morales allegedly struck the man with the vehicle as well as the aftermath when Parra Hernandez was on the ground.

Parra Hernandez’s attorney said the video footage of the incident tells “a different story than what was offered” by ICE, showing her client “running away from the vehicle and not in front of the vehicle.”

Surveillance video previously reviewed by CNN appeared to show the two men jumping out of a white pickup truck and running away as the ICE vehicle accelerated and hit Parra Hernandez as he fled on foot, but the video did not clearly show the moment of impact.

“Prosecutors synced up surveillance video from a local business with the ICE officer’s body camera footage from the incident, and just before Parra Hernandez is struck by the SUV, we see the officer make a hard left turn, steering the heavy vehicle toward the man,” said Josh Campbell, CNN Senior Correspondent and former FBI Supervisory Special Agent.

“There isn’t a law enforcement agency in this country that permits its officers to use a vehicle as a deadly weapon against someone who poses no imminent threat,” Campbell added.

Even before the strike, Campbell said there were numerous questionable tactics employed by the ICE officer, which appear to mirror other controversial immigration enforcement encounters of late.

“The officer is in an unmarked SUV, with no emergency warning lights flashing as he barrels over a traffic median. We also learned from local authorities that the whole time the ICE officer was chasing Parra Hernandez, there were two other prisoners from unrelated arrests in the back of his SUV not seat-belted in.”

In early October, CNN reported on new internal agency guidance, which said ICE officers would be allowed to conduct vehicle stops only if they have completed related training courses and must ensure vehicles used for stops are equipped with lights and sirens.

ICE officer was a ‘surge’ hire last year

Morales was one of the “surge hires” by ICE in August 2025 and Teare’s office has not received any training records, he said during the news conference.

Without being able to go into detail regarding the officer’s past work history, Teare said: “I can unequivocally tell you that I’ve reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I’m not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person, based on his past.”

It’s not the first time Teare’s office has investigated a federal law enforcement officer for allegedly injuring or killing members of his community. The case against Morales shares similarities with the investigation into the fatal ICE shooting of Salgado Araujo in his van in July, Teare said.

“In all honesty, this was not even in the back of my mind that I would be having to investigate multiple instances of federal officers harming our community members,” Teare said.

As CNN reported, a byproduct of President Donald Trump’s nationwide surge has been a ramped-up effort to hire more immigration agents while slashing in half the amount of time they are trained before hitting the streets, Campbell said.

“Federal law enforcement officers have incredible powers,” Campbell said, “which include the powers to deny someone their liberty and even legally kill someone who might present a threat. The public expects that anyone hired to carry out the duties of a federal agent will be someone with exceptional judgment who is provided intensive training before being given a badge and gun.”

Evidence in case against Morales is clear, DA says

Teare stressed his office’s “utmost respect and admiration for law enforcement,” adding all local, state and federal officers should be properly vetted, trained and expected to follow standard law enforcement practices, especially as it relates to vehicle pursuits and stops.

“An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone,” Teare said, adding he hopes the prosecution of Morales sends a “loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels they have a free pass to terrorize our streets.”

At the news conference, Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez said investigators at his office gathered video evidence, interviewed witnesses and worked closely with prosecutors to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Investigators “developed serious concerns about the actions of the agent involved” and the office presented the findings of the investigation to the district attorney, Gonzalez said.

“Behind every investigation is a human being whose life has been affected, and we should never lose sight of that,” the sheriff added.

CNN’s Lauren Mascarenhas contributed to this report.

title: Venezuela TPS: October 30 Court Ruling Explained | Martha Arias
description:
Today, this decision by the Supreme Court, in practical terms, what does it mean?
That suspension, which the Supreme Court authorized last year, on October 3, 2025, has an expiration date of November 6.
This means that, while the litigation continues, because sadly the litigation continues, TPS would be reinstated for Venezuelans.
I repeat, it would be a temporary reinstatement of TPS while the TPS litigation continues in court.
[Unclear fragment in the original text: “se en casa.”] ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS: Thank you, very kind of you.
text:
English Translation

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

We continue. This is America. We introduce our guest. We are changing the structure of today’s program in light of this news that has just become known in the last few minutes.

Joining us is Martha Arias. She is an attorney, an immigration expert, specializing in immigration, and it is precisely in relation, attorney, to this decision announced by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which rejected this Friday, October 30, the request by President Donald Trump’s administration to keep suspended a court order that declared unlawful the measures adopted to withdraw TPS from Venezuelans.

What is this measure about? How does it materialize for the Venezuelan community?

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

Well, yes, greetings to you, Mr. Pernalete, and to your entire audience.

Indeed, today, October 30, 2026, in the case called National TPS Alliance v. Mullin, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which we already know is in California, determined that, um, that is, the pause that the Supreme Court had approved in October 2025 must expire or must be lifted.

That pause was supposed to expire on November 6. Today, this decision by the Supreme Court, in practical terms, what does it mean? It means that beginning November 6, TPS may be reinstated. That is, what I mean is that TPS may be reinstated starting Friday, November 6 of this year, 2026.

The only thing that can stop the reinstatement of this TPS on November 6 is if the Supreme Court of the United States intervenes. In other words, this is an almost final decision, and the last word on whether it would not be reinstated would belong to the Supreme Court, which could intervene as it did the previous year.

But this, then, is the good news for Venezuelans today.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Now, litigation is what has predominated around decisions concerning immigration matters. During this administration, we have seen how the government, versus the cases that continue moving up through the courts, continues precisely to extend uncertainty.

Everything points to the possibility that, within a week, Venezuelans who properly applied for TPS and were approved for TPS may once again have this benefit, attorney, in a week, if absolutely nothing happens in this regard, if there is no ruling, it would be from the Supreme Court. Could there be a reversal in this regard?

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

That reversal could come only from the Supreme Court. That is to say, the Court of Appeals has full autonomy to issue the decision it issued today, saying that the litigation continues. So that you all know, the litigation continues.

What happened is that, within the litigation, a pause had been requested. That is called a stay, so that the government could suspend this TPS while the litigation continued.

That suspension, which the Supreme Court authorized last year, on October 3, 2025, has an expiration date of November 6. And today the Ninth District Court said, the Ninth Circuit, excuse me, said: the stay stops now, it is revoked, it is removed. In other words, we are removing the pause. That means TPS is reinstated beginning November 6.

What can happen here is that two things can happen. Let’s put it in practical terms.

One would be that the Supreme Court, within these eight days, well, fewer than eight days, five business days, acts and says: no, we are going to reinstate, we, the Supreme Court, that it be reinstated, that the pause continue. And the government, obviously, would have to ask the Supreme Court for this.

Or it could happen that the government does not ask the Supreme Court for anything and this decision by the Ninth Circuit panel remains as the final decision. This means that, while the litigation continues, because sadly the litigation continues, TPS would be reinstated for Venezuelans.

Until the litigation ends. When the litigation ends, we will then have a decision on whether that TPS is reinstated permanently or whether it truly ends.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Attorney, what exactly is the immigration status of this group of Venezuelans affected by the TPS decision who have not applied for another type of immigration benefit?

In other words, what should they do? I want to take advantage of this conversation to provide some responsible guidance, without triumphalism, without getting ahead of what may happen, because, as you say, we do not know what may happen, but we can suggest some steps to our Venezuelan brothers and sisters here.

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

I am not going to venture to say what the immigration status is of Venezuelans whose TPS was suspended or terminated at this moment, because unfortunately that status also varies.

It varies depending on whether it is the 2021 designation, whether it is the 2023 designation, whether the person obtained an extension in January 2025, and so on.

So, let’s say that the majority of Venezuelans whose TPS status was terminated or suspended may have it reinstated on November 6. This means that they may continue with their work permits and remain in the United States.

However, people should not rely on that possibility. People must continue looking for a remedy. One. Two, if the only remedy in court, if, for example, they are already in court in deportation proceedings, and the last remedy, the only benefit or remedy they have in court, is asylum, but TPS is reinstated, then surely they can ask the court to close the case or to terminate it because their TPS has been reinstated.

Here I see a problem for us, for us attorneys and for the people we work for, our people, and that is that recently the Supreme Court also said that the government has the right not to administratively close cases in the courts.

So, if that new decision, which is very recent, from last week, which says that cases cannot be administratively closed, is in effect, then if we are going to request administrative closure based on the reinstatement of TPS, will the court or the judge not allow the case to be administratively closed? That is a question we do not know the answer to.

The other question would be: then, can we go to the prosecutors, to DHS, to the attorney who represents DHS, and say to them: do you agree to help us close the case because of this situation?

Those other possibilities, will they agree? We do not know. Or will it be an administrative policy? The government is the one that tells the prosecutors what they can or cannot do, because there are policies that the government has that tell them: you have to do this. Well, we do not know what those policies will be.

So there would be many questions about what we attorneys will be able to do in court and what the people who are in court will be able to do, especially because they are the ones who have an imminent immigration problem, because they are in court.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Attorney, what do you say? I am not going to ask you for your intuition, because with so many things that have happened over the last few years, I believe that even with experience, one continues learning, despite that experience, given how politics is being conducted differently today in the United States and around the world.

But is there any case law that can give us some guidance regarding TPS?

What should the natural steps be, if we set aside the obligation to extend TPS? What would be the legal steps for its termination, rather than doing so in such an unexpected manner?

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

If I understand your question, it is: what can we, or what can the people who benefit from TPS or the attorneys do to prevent the government from ending TPS abruptly?

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Yes, that is, TPS at this moment has already been ended in a very unexpected way, but TPS, as a legal obligation, I believe provides for certain time periods.

In what way should those time periods have been observed, without complying with the extension?

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

The termination of TPS has to be announced a few months before it ends. The government has to say whether it is going to extend it or not.

Here, what happened is that the government, President Biden, during Mr. Biden’s presidency, extended it. He extended it a little earlier than the deadline when it would normally have to be done, and extended it for both the 2021 TPS and the 2022 TPS.

When the new administration came in, the new administration wanted to end that extension that covered both TPS designations, and that is where this lawsuit and this entire situation arose.

The government has, I think two… I think it is a month and a half, normally six months, 60 days before termination.

I do not remember at this moment whether it is 60 days, whether it is about a month and a half. Before termination, the government has to announce whether it is ending it or not, but it cannot end it in an untimely manner as this administration did.

So, but still, it is not much time, Mr. Pernalete, that the law gives or allows the government to terminate TPS. It is relatively quick.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

And the time periods, yes, and the time periods for litigation. Let’s say they have six months, 60 days, for the announced termination under the protocol established by law.

But if the litigation continues, that is indefinite. We would have to have a crystal ball to know when it will reach a successful conclusion.

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

Of course, of course, because in federal litigation, many, let’s say, little lawsuits arise within a big lawsuit, which is the federal litigation. Many other little disputes arise.

So, among these is, for example, the one we are seeing, which is when the government requests a stay, that is, that the suspension not be applied; in other words, that the suspension continue.

Then that becomes a small litigation within the larger litigation, and that makes federal litigation last a long time.

So federal litigation does not only have the main issue, in this case the main issue of whether the government can terminate TPS or not, but other subissues arise, other little disputes arise, and that is what we are seeing now.

So it is impossible to determine when federal litigation may conclude. Just as it can be quick, it can take years to reach that point. In fact, we know that this litigation has already lasted a little more than a year.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Attorney, I do not want to end this conversation without first asking you, drawing on your experience, to summarize this news of partial relief for the Venezuelan community with the accuracy that is required to understand it, please.

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

The news would be this: there is a possibility that Venezuela’s TPS may be reinstated beginning, at least temporarily, while the litigation continues, beginning November 7, 2026.

I repeat, it would be a temporary reinstatement of TPS while the TPS litigation continues in court. That is, in other words, if it is reinstated on November 6 of this year, it is not permanent. It would still be temporary while the litigation continues.

Obviously, it is a relief, but it remains a temporary relief.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Attorney, thank you very much for your timely and your [unclear wording in the original transcript] participation today, because there is a great demand for certainty, clarity, and transparency, especially regarding decisions that affect each of the families involved in this immigration relief.

Thank you very much. See you later. [Unclear fragment in the original text: “se en casa.”]

ATTORNEY MARTHA ARIAS:

Thank you, very kind of you. Until next time.

JOSÉ PERNALETE (VPItv):

Thank you. Until next time. Until next time.

We spoke with Martha Arias. She is an immigration attorney. She was connected with us digitally regarding this news that has just emerged, a developing news story.

We repeat for you: the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected today, Friday, October 30, the request by President Donald Trump’s administration to keep suspended a court order that declared unlawful the measures adopted to withdraw Temporary Protected Status, TPS by its English initials, a benefit granted to the Venezuelan community in the United States.

With this, we have reached the end of today’s program. Friends, until next time.

Share:

A coalition of immigration attorneys is suing Tennessee over a new policy that denies drivers’ licenses to thousands of immigrants in the state.

For years, non-U.S. citizens could get a temporary drivers’ license using a valid work permit to show they had federal permission to be in the U.S.

In recent weeks, the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security has stopped accepting work permits as documentation for license applications and renewals.

The change means asylum seekers and immigrants protected by DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, won’t be able to legally drive in the state.

L.R., a nurse and DACA recipient in East Tennessee, has an hour-long commute to the rural hospital in which he works. At a Friday press conference, he told reporters it’s impossible to find a ride to work and too costly to Uber.

“We are already experiencing a nursing shortage,” he said. “With one less nurse on the floor, this has left them dealing with higher patient-to-nurse ratios.”

L.R., like the six plaintiffs who signed onto the lawsuit, are not using their full name to protect their identity.

For many, losing the ability to drive has meant losing their job. Ale Z. had been working as a therapist for children with disabilities before the state rejected her license renewal. Now, she said, she’s out of work and doesn’t have the means to take her own son to medical appointments.

State response

The new rule stems from a 2025 omnibus immigration law that established a new state division to coordinate immigration enforcement between federal and state agencies. Although the law has been fully in effect since Jan. 1, the department didn’t announce the change until September.

Department of Safety may have violated its own rules around policy changes, according to a lawsuit filed Friday by the National Immigration Law Center, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and law firm Bass, Berry & Sims. The agency did not allow for public comment or wait to 90 days to implement the change after formally announcing it, as required by Tennessee code.

Gov. Bill Lee told reporters Wednesday that he had just been made aware of the change and was looking into the possibility of legislative “unintended consequences.” The 2025 sweeping immigration law was the product of a special session Lee called to, in part, address immigration enforcement in the state.

The Tennessee General Assembly has continued focusing on immigration, passing a host of laws crafted in coordination with the Trump administration. One law requiring beneficiaries of public programs to prove their immigration status drew similar scrutiny in June when it jeopardized the medical care of severely sick and disabled children.

At the time, the legislation’s sponsor, Sen. Ed Jackson, R-Jackson, said he hadn’t intended for the restrictions to apply to children. A group of doctors sued on behalf of their patients, and a judge temporarily blocked the law’s enforcement.

The lawsuit over licenses is making a similar ask: for the court to stop enforcement of the law while the legal challenge moves forward.

What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation, House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations.

In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status.

Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases.

Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.

What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS.

DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”

“These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica.

Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents.

description:
